69. Powers to arrest to be applied judiciously Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, empowers authorised GST officers to arrest individuals for certain offences under the GST law. This provision is designed to prevent tax evasion and ensure compliance with the law.

The power to arrest relies solely on the Commissioner's "reason to believe" that an offence under clauses (a) to (d) of Section 132(1) has been committed. The ability to arrest based on "reason to believe" without stringent procedural checks opens the door to potential abuse and arbitrary detention.

It is recommended that the GST provisions be amended to seek specific approval from the Principal Chief Commissioner before arrests can be made. Further, the proper officers seeking approval must present written evidence justifying the arrest.

Recently, the Supreme Court expressed concerns about the ambiguity in Section 69. The Supreme Court instructed the Centre to refrain from employing "threat and coercion" tactics during search and seizure operations to recover GST from traders. It emphasised its commitment to interpreting the law in a manner that upholds individual liberties and prevents undue harassment of citizens. Thus, once implemented, these changes will address the concerns raised by the Hon'ble Supreme Court regarding the potential misuse of Section 69.

70. Offences should be mentioned explicitly

Section 132 of the CGST Act prescribes punishments for specified offences. However, certain clauses in this section raise concerns due to their broad, generic nature, which could lead to misuse and harassment.

Relevant text of the provision:

(h)

acquires possession of, or in any way concerns himself in transporting, removing, depositing, keeping, concealing, supplying, or purchasing or in any other manner deals with, any goods which he knows or has reasons to believe are liable to confiscation under this Act or the rules made thereunder;

(i)

receives or is in any way concerned with the supply of, or in any other manner deals with any supply of services which he knows or has reasons to believe are in contravention of any provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder;

(l)

attempts to commit, or abets the commission of any of the offences mentioned in [clauses (a) to (f) and clauses (h) and (i)] of this section,

These clauses are overly broad and generic. They do not require evidence of intentional tax evasion by the defaulter.

It is therefore recommended that the GST provisions be amended by removing them entirely from Section 132(1) to prevent their misuse. The GST provisions should be suitably amended so as to replace criminal liability for non-compliance with a token penalty, ensuring fairness in enforcement.

71. Malicious intent should be the basis for a penalty

The relevant text of Clause (c) of Section 132(1) of the CGST Act:

(c)

Avails input tax credit using the invoice or bill referred to in clause (b) or….

This provision penalises individuals availing input tax credit under the circumstances outlined in clause (b) of Section 132(1). It does not consider whether the individual acted with malicious intent (mens rea).

It is recommended that this clause be modified to adhere to the legal maxim "actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea," which means that an act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

Either the first part of clause (c) should be deleted entirely, or the term 'fraudulently' should be inserted at the beginning of clause (c) to limit its scope to deliberate offences. For unintentional non-compliance, the Government may consider imposing a token penalty rather than criminal liability.

72. No criminal proceedings for self-rectified defaults

Criminal proceedings under Section 132(1) of the CGST Act can be initiated even when the defaulter has voluntarily identified the default and corrected it before the proceedings are initiated.

It is therefore recommended that criminal action be restricted to cases where defaults persist when proceedings are initiated. In cases of self-rectification of defaults, the law may prescribe levying a token penalty for non-compliance instead of initiating criminal proceedings. This approach encourages proactive adherence to tax laws.

(ix) What procedure is to be followed for making an order for provisional attachment ? - As per rule 3, the following procedure shall be adopted in making provisional attachment of property :

(a )The Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise, on being satisfied that a provisional attachment is necessary in the interest of revenue, prepare a proposal in the prescribed format and forward the same to the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise for his approval.

As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, normally the proposal should be forwarded within one month of the issue of show-cause notice.

In case the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending before the Commissioner of Central Excise, he himself shall initiate the attachment.

(b )The Commissioner of Central Excise may, on being satisfied, that the circumstances of the case justify provisional attachment, cause service of a notice on the person (in default). The notice shall state reasons for initiating provisional attachment and details of property to be attached.

(c )The notice shall require the person (in default) to make submissions, in writing or in person or both, within 15 days of service of the notice, as to why the property belonging to him and specified in the notice, should not be provisionally attached.

(d )The CBEC in its Circular dated July 1, 2008 has clarified that the said notice should also specify the condition that the noticee should not sell, transfer, mortgage, charge, lease or otherwise alienate or encumber the property specified in the notice, till the decision of the said notice. In case of proposal for provisional attachment of immovable property, the notice should also be sent to the concerned registration authorities with a direction not to allow any sale, transfer, mortgage, etc., of the property.

(e )After considering the materials placed before him, in writing or in person or both, by the person (in default), the Commissioner of Central Excise may grant approval to the provisional attachment of the specified property. As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, such an order should be made within 15 days of holding of personal hearing. Thereafter, the Central Excise Officer, before whom the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending, may order, in writing, to attach the said property.

(f )A copy of the order of provisional attachment shall be served on that person as per the provisions of section 37C of the Central Excise Act, 1944, as extended to service tax matters.

(x) For what period an order of attachment shall continue to be in effect ? - As per rule 6 of the Rules, an order of provisional attachment shall continue to be in force for a period of six months from the date of service of the order on the person in default, or till the date the entire ‘pending revenue’ along with interest thereon is paid, whichever is earlier. However, the aforesaid period of six months may be extended by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise, after recording reasons for the same in writing, for such further period(s) as he thinks fit. However, the total period of extension shall not exceed two years.

(xi) What procedure is to be followed in effecting attachment ? - Section 73C as well as the Rules, both are again silent on this issue. As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, the following points merit consideration :

(a )The provisional attachment of the property of the concerned person by arrest or distrain shall be made after sunrise and before sunset and not otherwise.

(b )After provisional attachment of the property, the Central Excise Officer shall prepare an inventory of the property attached and specify in it the place where it is lodged or kept and shall hand over a copy of the same to defaulter or the person from whose charge the property is distrained.

(xii) Is the person whose property has been attached, obliged to exercise any restraint in respect of the said property ? - In terms of rule 5, the person whose property has been attached or his representative shall not mortgage, lease, transfer, deliver or deal with the attached property in any manner except with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise. The Rules, however, do not provide as to whether any action can be initiated if the person acts in definance of rule 5, and as to what shall be the position of the rights of the third party who deals unknowingly, with that person.

The CBEC’s circular, however, states that where a provisional attachment has been made, any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any debt, dividend or other moneys, contrary to such provisional attachment, shall be void as against all claims enforceable under the provisional attachment.

TAX RECOVERY

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY UNDER SERVICE TAX PROVISIONS

ASHHOK SAXENA*

The Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 have been made effective to curtail growing tax evasion, particularly by the big service providers. Provisional attachment is to be resorted only in cases where the defaulted amount alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakhs. Being a harsh measure of extraordinary nature, it should not be applied routinely and, therefore, an elaborate procedure has been prescribed which needs to be followed before attachment of property. In this article, the modus operandi of these measures has been explained. The author is of the view that such measures though harsh, should not remain paper-measures because of the involvement of heavy-weights, but need to be implemented effectively if the interests of revenue are to be protected.

Introduction

1. Section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994 was inserted with effect from April 18, 2006 1 to provide for the provisional attachment of property. This provision was made effective with a view to protect the interests of revenue during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 2 or section 73A 3. Framing of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 4 is a step in the direction of implementing these provisions more comprehensively.

Keeping in view that the provisional attachment of property is a harsh measure directed towards the defaulting assessees, the CBEC has issued comprehensive instructions 5 so that no injustice is meted out.

Pending revenue

2. Provisional attachment of property is to be resorted to during the pendency of revenue which means the circumstances should exist where any service tax has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded and in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A. As regards justification for provisional attachment, the CBEC Circular states as under :—

"It is important to note that there should be sufficient justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The remedy of attachment being, by its very nature, extraordinary, has to be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. The grounds on which the Central Excise Officer entertains the reasonable belief that the notice would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any, should be clearly stated while seeking the approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise."

2.1 Amount alleged to be involved - There is a prescription regarding the amount of service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved for the provisional attachment of property. Presently, such amount should be more than Rs. 25 lakhs.

Offences which call for provisional attachment of property

3. The circular enumerates certain types of offences which if committed by a service provider or an exporter may be considered for provisional attachment of property. These are as under :—

uProvision of a taxable service without the cover of an invoice or any other document, as prescribed, and without payment of tax;

uProvision of a taxable service without declaring the correct value for payment of service tax, where a portion of value of taxable service, in excess of invoice price, is received by him or on his behalf but not accounted for in the books of account;

uTaking of CENVAT credit without the receipt of goods or services specified in the document based on which the said credit has been taken;

uTaking of CENVAT credit on invoices or other documents which a person has reasons to believe as not genuine;

uIssue of service tax invoice or any other document, without providing or to be providing a taxable service, as specified in the said invoice or other document;

uClaiming of refund or rebate in a fraudulent manner such as on invoice or other documents, which a person has reason to believe as not genuine.

Procedural aspects

4. An elaborate procedure is contemplated for provisional attachment of property, mainly because of the fact that such measures being extraordinary by nature, should not be resorted to as a routine. Following procedure is to be adopted for the purpose :—

(i) Issue of Show-Cause Notice (SCN) - The proceedings for provisional attachment can be initiated only where SCN has been issued under section 73 or section 73A. In other words, the department cannot proceed to attach the property of the defaulter provisionally as and when it wishes to take action. The circular prescribes that normally, the proposal for attachment should be forwarded within one month’s period of the issue of SCN.

In the course of business, various liabilities like dues to the Government and Statutory Agencies, like Sales Tax/VAT dues, etc. and now Goods and Service Tax (GST) under Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 arise. The dues under GST arise as tax is collected from the recipient of supply of goods or services from the 'taxable person' ('dealer' under earlier Sales Tax/VAT laws and 'taxable person' under CGST Act, 2017) and it is the responsibility of such "taxable person" to deposit the tax collected with the Government. Section 83 empowered the Commissioner to attach the properties of the 'taxable person' to recover the dues. It is a general notion that the said dues, being the dues payable to the Government, have the priority or first right to recover from the properties of the taxable person over all other creditors' dues. This article discusses whether recovery of GST tax dues, in fact, has any priority under the law vis-a-vis other creditors.

CROWN DEBTS : It was held by the Supreme Court in the case of Dena Bankv. Bikhabhai Prabhudas Parekh & Co1 where the debts of the Government (Crown Debts) and Subjects conflict, the Debts due to Government get precedence and priority over all other debts except the Secured Creditors. The Court explained the doctrine of priority of 'Crown Debts' as under:

"What is common law doctrine of priority or precedence of crown debts? Halsbury, dealing with general rights of the crown in relation to property, states where the Crown's right and that of a subject meet at one and the same time, that of the Crown is in general preferred, the rule being "detur digniori" Herbert Brown states - "Quanta jus domini Regis et submit concurrent jus Regis preferred debt - Where the title of the king and the title of a subject concur, the king's title must be preferred. In this case detur digniori is the rule... where the titles of the king and of a subject concur, the king takes the whole... where the king's title and that of a subject concur, or are in conflict, the king's title is to be preferred" This common law doctrine of priority of State's debts has been recognised by the High Courts of India as applicable in British India before 1950 and hence the doctrine has been treated as "law in force" within the meaning of Article 372(1) of Constitution.

The principle of priority of Government debts is founded on the rule of necessity and of public policy. The basic justification for the claim for priority of state debts rests on the well recognised principle that the State is entitled to raise money by taxation because unless adequate revenue is received by the State, it would not be able to function as a sovereign government at all. It is essential that as a sovereign, the State should be able to discharge its primary governmental functions and in order to be able to discharge such functions efficiently, it must be in possession of necessary funds and this consideration emphasises the necessity and the wisdom of conceding to the State, the right to claim priority in respect of its tax dues.

However, the Crown's preferential right to recovery of debts over other creditors is confined to ordinary or unsecured creditors. The Common Law of England or the principles of equity and good conscience (as applicable to India) do not accord the Crown a preferential right for recovery of its debts over a mortgagee or pledgee of goods or a secured creditor. It is only in cases where the Crown's right and that of the subject meet at one and the same time that the Crown is in general preferred. Where the right of the subject is complete and perfect before that of the King commences, the rule does not apply, for there is no point of time at which the two rights are at conflict, nor can there be a question which of the two ought to prevail in a case where one, that of the subject has prevailed already. In Giles v. Grover 1832 131 ER 563 it has been held that the Crown has no precedence over a pledgee of goods. In Bank of Bihar v. State of Bihar and Ors. [AIR1971SC1210] , the principle has been recognised by this Court holding that the rights of the pawnee who has parted with money in favour of the pawnor on the security of the goods cannot be extinguished even by lawful seizure of goods by making money available to other creditors of the pawnor without the claim of the pawnee being first fully satisfied. Rashbehary Ghose states in Law of Mortgage - 'It seems a Government debt in India is not entitled to precedence over a prior secured debt."

21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.

The relevant text of Clause (c) of Section 132(1):

(c) Avails input tax credit using the invoice or bill referred to in clause (b) or….

This provision penalises individuals availing input tax credit under circumstances outlined in clause (b) of Section 132(1). It does not consider whether the individual acted with malicious intent (mens rea).

It is recommended that this clause be modified to adhere to the legal maxim "actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea," which means that an act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty. 11. State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act; Section 53 of IBC doesn't override Section 48 of GVAT Act: SC

IBC | State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 157/174 SCL 250 (SC)

In the landmark ruling, the Supreme Court held that the State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

In the instant case, the following questions were placed before the Supreme Court:

(a)

Is State a secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes under Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act)?

(b)

Whether Section 53 of IBC overrides Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act) or not?

The Apex Court held that the State is a secured creditor under the GVAT Act. Section 3(30) of the IBC defines the secured creditor as "a creditor in favour of whom security interest is created".

The court further held that such security interest could be created by the operation of law. The definition of a secured creditor in the IBC does not exclude any Government or Governmental Authority. Therefore, the State will be treated as the secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes.

In view of the above, the Supreme Court concluded that State is a secured creditor for VAT under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

With regard to the overriding effect of Section 53 of the IBC, it was held that Section 48 of the GVAT Act is not contrary to or inconsistent with Section 53 or any other provisions of the IBC. Section 53 of the IBC deals with the distributions of the asset. As per Section 53, proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets shall be distributed in the order of priority and within such period as prescribed in the provision.

Under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), the debts owed to a secured creditor, which would include the State under the GVAT Act, shall rank equally with other specified debts, including debts on account of workman's dues for 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.

The term "Secured Creditor", as defined under the IBC, is comprehensive and wide enough to cover all types of security interests, namely, the right, title, interest or a claim to the property created in favour of or provided for a secured creditor by a transaction, which secures payment or performance of an obligation and includes mortgage, charge, hypothecation, assignment and encumbrance or any other agreement or arrangement securing payment or performance of any obligation of any person.

In view of the statutory charge in terms of Section 48 of the GVAT Act, the claim of the tax department of the State squarely falls within the definition of "Security Interest" under Section 3(31) of the IBC, and the State becomes a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the Code.

A considered answer to the above query will be that a Superintendent of Central Excise cannot make a proposal as contemplated under rule 3(1) ibid. Reasons for this position are as follows: The term 'Central Excise Officer' mentioned in section 73(1) ibid is a general category, whereas the expressions 'Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise' used in rule 3(1) ibid are specific expressions. The rule of interpretation applicable in such situations is 'Specialia generalibus derogant'. Where a special provision is made on a certain matter, that matter is to be excluded from the general provision. (See: Venkateshwar Rao v. Govt. of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1966 SC 828; CIT v. Shahzada Nand & Sons [1966] 60 ITR 392 (SC); State of Gujarat v. Patel Ramajibhai Danabhai AIR 1979 SC 1098, etc.).

The above position is also fortified by the contrast in the expressions used in section 73(1) and rule 3(1). Section 73(1) uses the expression "the Central Excise Officer is of opinion that", while the expressions in rule 3(1) are "the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is satisfied that …". Thus, the mental state necessary under rule 3(1) is that of satisfaction which is much higher than the opinion as contemplated under section 73(1), and the former is expected of an officer of a higher level than the one entertaining an opinion. There again, the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is supposed to make a proposal for attachment 'after due verification of the facts, and the circumstances of the case', which further underlines the gravity of the matter. It should be so, because attachment of property is a very serious matter and the same should be resorted to only in highly necessary and appropriate cases.

Analysis

4. In summary, it can be said that the term 'Central Excise Officer' mentioned in section 73(1) ibid denotes an Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise, and not any officer of Central Excise below the rank of an Assistant Commissioner.

This does not, however, mean that attachment of property cannot be resorted to in a case where adjudication is pending before a Superintendent of Central Excise. (Even in monetary terms attachment may be vital if there are several cases pertaining to the same assessee pending before a Superintendent/Superintendents). In such cases, the Commissioner of Central Excise can cause service of notice for attachment on his own satisfaction, under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008. If attachment of property is felt necessary in a matter pending before a Superintendent of Central Excise, the Superintendent will have to inform the Commissioner accordingly, not under rule 3(1) of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008, but in general terms. Commissioner will have to call for the file under section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994 (read with section 12E of the Central Excise Act, 1944), examine the matter, record his satisfaction under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 ibid, and proceed to issue notice for attachment. But if the Superintendent makes a proposal under rule 3(1) ibid, such proposal will be incompetent, and if the Commissioner acts on such a proposal per se without examining the matter and recording his own personal satisfaction under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 ibid, and proceeds to issue notice for attachment, the whole proceedings will be incompetent and vitiated and will be liable to be struck down by a competent Court of law, for lack of satisfaction on the part of the Commissioner.

11. Some Substantive provisions :

Section 3 – Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 3 of the Ordinance places a blanket ban on Unregulated Deposit Schemes and prohibits deposit taker from promoting, operating, issuing any advertisement soliciting participation or enrolment in or accepting deposits in pursuance of an Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 4 – Fraudulent default in Regulated Deposit Schemes

Section 4 of the Ordinance prohibits deposit taker, while accepting deposits under a Regulated Deposit Scheme, from commission of fraudulent default in the repayment or return of deposit on maturity or in rendering any specified service promised against such deposit.

It may be noted that Section 4 is not applicable to companies (as per proviso to Section 27 of the Ordinance)

Section 5 – Wrongful inducement in relation to Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 5 of the Ordinance prohibits any person from knowingly making any statement, promise or forecast which is false, deceptive or misleading in material facts or deliberately conceal any material facts, to induce another person to invest in, or become a member or participant of any Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 6 – Certain scheme to be Unregulated Deposit Scheme

Section 6 of the Ordinance provides that prize chit or a money circulation scheme banned under the provisions of the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 shall be deemed to be an Unregulated Deposit Scheme under this Ordinance.

Section 7 – Provisional Attachment

The power for provisional attachment in cases of contravention of section 3 has been vested with a Competent Authority. This Competent Authority is an officer appointed by appropriate Government who is not below the rank of Secretary to that Government.

As per section 7(3) of the Ordinance, where the Competent Authority, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of such information and particulars as may be prescribed that any deposit taker is soliciting deposits in contravention of section 3, he may, by order in writing, provisionally attach the deposits held by the deposit taker and the money or other property acquired either in the name of the deposit taker or in the name of any other person on behalf of the deposit taker.

It is pertinent to mention that section 7(3) of the Ordinance is not properly drafted and does not provide for giving any show cause notice to the deposit taker prior to provisionally attaching deposits. Not providing an opportunity of being heard prior to provisional attachment tantamount a contravention of principles of Natural Justice and vitiates the pre-requisites of a fair trial. As this law will evolve, there is a high possibility that section 7(3) may be read down by the Courts to the extent it fails in providing a show cause notice prior to provisional attachment. It will be tested in future.

Section 14 and 15 – Confirmation of attachment by Designated Court

(i)

Section 14 of the Ordinance requires the Competent Authority to file an application before the Designated Court for making the provisional attachment absolute within a period of 30 days (which may extend upto 60 days) from the date of the order of provisional attachment. This period may be extended up to sixty days, for reasons to be recorded in writing.

(ii)

As per section 15(1) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall then issue notice to the deposit taker or any person whose property is attached under section 14, to show cause, within a period of 30 days, as to why the order of attachment should not be made absolute and the properties so attached be sold.

As per section 15(2) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall issue notice to all other persons represented to it as having or being likely to claim any interest or title in the property to appear on the same date as persons referred to in section 15(1) to raise objections, if they so desire, to the attachment of the property.

It is mandatory for them to provide statement of particulars or specific information on various subjects more particularly may be understood as inadmissible or admissible list of items in statutory prescribed Form 3CD. Clause 44 in Form 3CD (tax audit reporting) in particular require break up of total expenditure both for entities registered and not registered under GST.

The ICAI Guidance Note

The ICAI in their August 2022 guidance note has further prescribed a tabular format to the taxpayers in paragraph 82.17 to capture entity wise details of total expenditure including capital expenditure for reporting purpose. Paragraph 82.17 further states that the tax auditor needs to obtain from the assessee the required details and should verify the details furnished with the underlying document. In other words he merely has to report the total expenditure in a tabular format without envisaging the underlying purpose of such compilation.

Form 3CD ingredients

From a close look at the form 3CD contents one would notice that it asks for specific information starting clauses 12 onwards until clause 43. However clause 44 is drafted to gather very general and non specific information which serve no purpose to the Act. For instance clause 12 seeks to know whether any part of the profit represent income qualifying for presumptive taxation. Clause 13 call for details of ICDS backed adjustments to the declared net profit. Clause14 attempts to gather information on increase and decrease in inventory due to change in method of valuation of inventory. Clause 15 call for information on conversion of capital asset to inventory. Clause 16 and 17 seek details on unbooked items. Clause 18 is specific to admissible amount of depreciation under the Act. Clause 19 and 20 similarly seek details of deduction admissible under the Act. Clause 21 and 22 is specific to inadmissible items. Clause 23 seeks information on payments to related parties. Clause 24 and 25 call for information on deemed incomes under the Act. Clause 26 is specific to statutory payments defaults and disallowances. Clause 27 is specific to previous year items for disallowance purpose. Clauses 28 and 29 call for details of incomes assessable under the head income from other sources. Clause 30 is specific to hundis borrowed, Transfer Pricing adjustments, GAAR adjustments. Clause 31 is specific to loan or deposit otherwise than in the acceptable modes as per the Act. Clause 32 is statement of admissible losses as per the Act. Clause 33 is to admissible deductions as per the Act. Clause 34 is specific to TDS compliances and non compliances. Clause 35 is specific to inventory tally. Clause 36 is specific to deemed dividends information as per the Act. Clause 37, 38 and 39 is for any disqualification in cost audit, excise and customs and GST audit reports. Clause 40 is specific to assessment of financial ratios and their comparison to preceding year ratios. Clause 41 is specific to demand raised and refunds realized under other laws for tax implications if any. Clause 42 and 43 is specific to non compliance. The last clause 44 seeks break-up of total expenditure of entities registered or not registered under the GST. Thus clause 44 compilations appear to be a kind odd item with no underlying purpose.

Predated Inquiry

Section 133(6) of the income tax Act (power to call for information) empowers tax authorities to requisition only information which will be useful for or relevant to any enquiry or proceeding under the Act. The question therefore arises whether it is proper to statutorily seek information on total expenditure under clause 44 in the absence of any enquiry or pending proceedings. This is statutorily possible only with the prior approval of Principal Director/Director or the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner, as the case may be. (Karnataka Bank Ltd. v. Secretary, Government of India [2002] 123 Taxman 219/255 ITR 508 (SC). When we seek break of total expenditure in a certain manner and that too for parties registered as well as parties unregistered we are attempting to scrutinize both general ledger and party ledger account details and that is equivalent to seeking of details or information in any proceedings or inquiry without any prior authorization under the Act.

There is seemingly san attempt to predate inquiry under section 133(6) by enforcing tax auditor/taxpayer to verify and furnish entity wise details of total expenditure under Clause 44 of Form 3CD. This is also a clear instance of roving or fishing inquiry which is impermissible under the law.

This quirky clause 44 in my humble opinion is undesirable as it does not serve any purpose of the Act and therefore must be lifted from Form 3CD.

19. ITAT to apply the decision of a larger bench if there are conflicting decisions of non-jurisdictional High Courts: ITAT

Income-tax | Wockhardt Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2022] 144 taxmann.com 27 (Mumbai - Trib.)

The issue before the Mumbai Tribunal was in what manner and to what extent the decisions of non-jurisdictional High Courts bind the lower judicial forums outside their jurisdiction.

The Mumbai Tribunal held that when there are conflicting decisions of non-jurisdictional High Courts and no decision of a jurisdictional High Court on an issue, the ITAT should not follow the rule to apply the favourable view to the assessee. It's a conscious call that must be taken for the question of whether the non-jurisdictional High Court is required to be followed on the facts of a particular situation.

For Tribunal, it is a compulsion by law to follow a jurisdictional High Court decision. However, following a non-jurisdictional High Court is a call for judicial propriety. The decisions of the non-jurisdictional High Court are followed in letter and spirit if there is no contrary decision by the jurisdictional High Court.

Difficulties arise when there are conflicting views of the non-jurisdictional High Courts. Tribunal can't choose the views of one of the High Courts based on its perceptions.

In the given case, there was one decision of the division bench consisting of two Hon'ble judges and another decision of a single judge bench consisting of only one Hon'ble judge.

The Tribunal has much simpler and more objective criteria readily available, which is the strength of the bench of the Hon'ble non-jurisdictional High Court which has rendered the judgment.

The plurality in the decision-making process makes the decisions of benches with a larger number of Hon'ble judges being placed on a higher pedestal than the decisions of the benches with fewer Hon'ble judges.

Between a division bench decision of a non-jurisdictional High Court and a single judge bench of a non-jurisdictional High Court, a simple objective criterion of choice is the division bench decision to be preferred over the single judge bench decision.

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY

The author in this article discusses the salient features of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 which empowers the Government to provisionally attach the property of the assessee. By way of conclusion, he opines that notification of the Rules is one of the very stringent measures adopted by the Government to ensure recovery of amount and that the rules are framed with very good objective, but it is to be seen that its implementation shall not destroy the object.

Introduction

1. Of late, there have been number of instances where the department was unable to recover the amount of taxes even after the issue has been finally decided against the assessee. The final decision on any issue normally takes around 10 - 15 years. Both the assessee or the Government always tries to fight out the issue up to the Supreme Court. The organization may be closed or become insolvent or may not have any asset in the span of 10 - 15 years. Some of the organizations may deliberately sell or dispose of the asset of the organization in order to reduce the chances of recovery of tax by selling the asset. As per the provisions of the Central Excise Act or Service Tax Rules, the amount due from the assessee can be recovered as arrears of land revenue, i.e., by attaching and selling the asset belonging to the assessee. However, if the assessee has no asset, the Government was unable to recover any amount of tax from the assessee in spite of writing to the District Collector to recover the amount.

The Government has, therefore, notified the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 (‘the Rules’) which empowers the Government to provisionally attach the property of the assessee.

Applicability

2. Rule 2(b ) defines the words ‘pending revenue’ as any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A.

Section 73(1) empowers the Central Excise Officer to issue notice to the person chargeable to service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom such tax refund has been erroneously granted requiring the person to show cause as to why the amount specified in the notice should not be recovered. The notice normally gives the information about the nature of service provided by the assessee, the category under which tax is payable, basis of arriving at the demanded amount, etc. The notice shall be served within one year from the relevant date as defined in sub-section (6) of section 73. The relevant date in the normal course is when periodical return is to be filed, date on which said return is filed and where no such return is filed, the last date on which return has to be filed under the Rules. Thus, the show-cause notice has to be issued within one year from the date on which return is required to be filed. For example, return for April-September 2007 is required to be filed by October 25, 2007; the period of one year, therefore, will be counted from October 25, 2007 and the notice shall be issued for recovery of service tax on or before October 24, 2008.

However, when the tax has not been levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid by reason of fraud, collusion, wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts or contravention of any of the provisions of this Chapter, with intent to evade payment of service tax, the period of one year gets extended to 5 years.

The definition of ‘pending revenue’ as is in rule 2(b ) covers both the situations where the notice is issued within one year or 5 years as provided in proviso to section 73(1).

Section 73A provides for recovery of service tax from any person who has collected the amount as service tax (irrespective of fact whether such person is liable to pay service tax or not). He must deposit the amount with the Central Government as per the provisions contained in section 73A. Where any person who has collected any amount as tax and not deposited same with the Government, the Proper Officer may serve show-cause notice requiring the person to show-cause as to why the said amount should not be recovered.

Extension of Inverted Duty Structure (IDS) refund to 'input services' and 'capital goods'

Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, read with Rule 89(5) of the CGST Rules, prescribes the mechanism for granting refunds of unutilised input tax credit (ITC) arising from an inverted duty structure. However, the statutory formula restricts the scope of 'Net ITC' exclusively to input tax credit availed on input goods, explicitly excluding input services and capital goods from the refund computation.

As a result, taxpayers operating under an inverted tax structure accumulate substantial unutilised ITC on account of input services (such as job work, freight, utilities, professional services, etc.) and capital goods, which remain permanently blocked. While large enterprises are generally able to absorb such accumulation due to diversified product portfolios and higher-rated outward supplies, MSMEs and smaller manufacturers, particularly those engaged in single-product or low-margin businesses, face severe working capital constraints due to the non-refundability of such credits.

The adverse impact of this restriction has been further exacerbated by recent GST rate rationalisation measures, which have reduced output tax rates without a corresponding alignment of input tax rates, intensifying inverted duty structures across several sectors.

In this context, it is recommended that the refund mechanism under Rule 89(5) be suitably amended to include input services and capital goods within the scope of 'Net ITC' for the purpose of inverted duty structure refunds. Such a measure would align the refund framework with the fundamental GST principle of tax neutrality, prevent tax cascading, and significantly improve liquidity, thereby promoting ease of doing business and enhancing manufacturing competitiveness.

67. IDS refunds should be allowed for inputs and outputs at the same GST rate

Under Section 54 of the CGST Act, taxpayers are entitled to claim refunds for accumulated input tax credit on account of an inverted duty structure (IDS), i.e., where the rate of tax on inputs exceeds the rate of tax on outward supplies. However, tax authorities have often denied refunds under Section 54(3) read with Rule 89 of the CGST Rules, where the input tax rate on certain goods exceeds the output tax rate, even when the principal input and output attract the same GST rate. This has created uncertainty and impacted cash flow for businesses.

Recent judicial developments indicate a more purposive interpretation of the IDS provisions. In Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs. Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax [2025] 174.taxmann.com 1 (Karnataka), the Karnataka High Court observed that an IDS refund cannot be denied merely because some inputs are taxed at a higher rate than the output, so long as the principal input and the outward supply attract the same GST rate and the accumulation of ITC is otherwise attributable to the rate structure.

Further, during the 56th GST Council meeting, the government indicated its intent to simplify IDS refund processes, hinting at regulatory changes in the near future. Taxpayers can anticipate a more streamlined and predictable mechanism for claiming IDS refunds, potentially reducing litigation and enhancing liquidity management.

68. Blocking of the electronic credit ledger with zero or negative ITC may be reviewed

Rule 86A of the CGST Rules was inserted videNotification No. 75/2019- Central Tax, dated 26-12-2019, empowering the GST authorities to restrict the utilisation of ITC in the ECL under exceptional circumstances.

In practice, instances have been observed where tax authorities have blocked the ECL on a negative basis, i.e., restricted utilisation of ITC in excess of the balance actually available in the ECL at the time of passing the order. Such negative blocking effectively prevents utilisation of future credits, leading to severe cash-flow constraints for taxpayers, particularly during audits or verification proceedings.

Recently, the Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue's Special Leave Petition in Kings Security Guard Services (P.) Ltd. 174 taxmann.com 982, thereby affirming the decision of the Delhi High Court. The High Court, relying on its earlier ruling in Best Crop Science (P.) Ltd. [2024] 166 taxmann.com 654, held that Rule 86A of CGST Rules is not a machinery provision for recovery of tax or dues under CGST Act but an emergent measure for protection of revenue by temporarily not allowing debit of available ITC in ECL order disallowing debit from ECL, in excess of ITC available in ECL at the time of passing the order.

In view of the above judicial pronouncements, it is recommended that the scope and application of Rule 86A of the CGST Rules be reviewed and clarified to prevent its use as a recovery mechanism. However, appropriate safeguards may continue to be retained to allow restriction of ITC utilisation in genuine cases involving fraud or wilful misuse of input tax credit, subject to due process and statutory limitations.

In this regard, it is important to refer to a recent judgment in the case of Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator, ABG Shipyard.17

The facts before the Hon'ble Supreme Court were that ABG Shipyard ("ABG") had imported certain goods which were stored in the Customs Bonded Warehouse and Container Freight Station. ABG had also availed the benefit of the Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme ("EPCG Scheme"). An insolvency resolution process was initiated against ABG, and the liquidator sought to dispose of the goods lying at the customs warehouse. The Customs Department issued notices to ABG seeking demand of customs duty for non-fulfilment of the obligation under the EPCG Scheme. ABG approached the NCLT seeking directions to dispose of the goods. The application was allowed stating that Customs Department would allow ABG to remove the goods from the warehouse, and the Customs was free to lodge a claim before the liquidator. In the meantime, Customs Department also issued notice to ABG under Section 72(1) of the Customs Act seeking to demand customs dues in respect of goods warehoused.

At this juncture, it would be pertinent to discuss Sections 71 and 72 of the Customs Act. Section 71 of the Customs Act states that goods warehoused shall only be taken out of a warehouse on (i) clearance for home consumption or (ii) export, or (iii) removal to another warehouse or (iv) as provided under the Customs Act. Thus, Section 71 of the Customs Act allows the removal of goods from a warehouse only under four specific situations. Section 72 of the Customs Act is a recovery provision in relation to warehoused goods. It allows an officer of customs to demand duty along with interest and penalties on goods (i) which have been improperly removed from the warehouse, (ii) where goods which have been kept in the warehouse beyond the period allowed and (iii) where goods have been kept under a bond but have not been cleared for home consumption or export.

TIME-LIMIT

Extension - Extension of attachment and extension of uppermost time limit for attachment are two different aspects; at no stage, Department is precluded from extending attachment if it is open to do in law [Asstt. CIT v. Soham Securities Ltd. [2013] 36 taxmann.com 582 (Guj.)].

GENERAL

Constitutional validity - Section 281B gives guidelines for making provisional attachment and is, thus, constitutionally valid [Dar International v. Asstt. DIT [1995] 82 Taxman 75 (Delhi)].

Search proceedings - Such proceedings which are to be necessarily commenced as a result of search are to be treated as 'proceedings' within meaning of section 281B(1). SARFAESI Act - In the absence of any specific provision under the Securitisation Act creating first charge on bank, section 281B r/w Rule 16 of Second Schedule will have an overriding effect on section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act [UCO Bank-Regional Office v. UOI [2009] 182 Taxman 26 (Guj.)].

PROPERTY

Exercise of power - Power of attachment of property u/s 281B should be exercised by the AO only if there is reasonable apprehension that assessee is about to dispose of whole or any part of his property with a view to thwart ultimate collection of demand [Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 (Bom.)].

The power conferred upon the AO u/s 281B is a very drastic far-reaching power and that power has to be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons. To ensure that this power is not misused, a number of safeguards have been provided in the section itself. One thing is clear that this power should be exercised by the AO only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution. It should not be exercised unless there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of the demand [Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas v. CIT [2001] 119 Taxman 289 (AP)].

Attachment of assessee's property only - Attachment order was to be limited to plot owner by person against whom order was passed and not extended to plots owned by others in residential area [Mutta Venkata Ramana v. ITO [2013] 40 taxmann.com 531/[2014] 221 Taxman 222 (Mag.) (AP); Raghunandan Enterprise v. Asstt. CIT [2022] 139 taxmann.com 51 (Guj.)].

Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 (Bom.); Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas v. CIT [2001] 119 Taxman 289 (AP)].

The nature of Personal Deposit Account is explained by the High Court in Kurumber Betta Estate v. ITO [2002] 257 ITR 328/124 Taxman 161 (Ker.) as follows:

"We are informed that under administrative circulars, amounts which were not to be appropriated to the revenue are held in personal deposit account to be kept in the name of certain officers, including TRO. These amounts are actually treated as amounts of the Government over which the bank has no authority. In other words, instead of depositing the amount in the treasury, the bank holds it as an agent of the treasury for the purpose of holding the money. Such amounts which are held as security cannot be utilised by the bank, would not bear any interest, and the revenue also would not be entitled to any interest on such amount held. The notes/disclaimers in Clause 3 of Form 3CA/Clause 5 of Form 3CB must not exceed 1000 characters. (1) Whether Conversion Charges paid in cash to as payee's bank account was frozen by attachment order of ESIC?

Where the assessee-company had paid conversion charges to a company in cash as a bank account of the said company was frozen by an order of attachment passed by the ESI department, the assessee was entitled to exemption under rule 6DD and; thus, no disallowance under section 40A(3) was called for. What is crucial while testing such a claim and the applicability of section 40A(3) is the facts of each particular case. Therefore, a decision cannot be taken without referring to facts. The assessee seeks to bring its case under two limbs, namely, there was no banking facility and it was a business expediency. The assessee by stating that there was no banking facility does not seek to bring their case under clause (j) of rule 6DD but on account of the factual position. On 29-11-2002, the Punjab National Bank sends a letter to SLM directing them to close the bank account with State Bank of India and directs them to do all banking transactions only through the Punjab National Bank. This direction has come because the said Bank was appointed as the operating agency to implement a scheme of revival of SLM as framed by the BIFR. Therefore, SLM cannot flout the direction. The said company was carrying on business and it appears that the assessee was one of the major entities with whom they had entered into agreement. There was an agreement for 'conversion job-work' dated 1-4-2003. Even prior to that, on 27-2-2004, the Punjab National bank informs SLM that their bank account with them has been attached pursuant to an order passed by the Employees State Insurance Corporation, Madurai and the interest payable towards Punjab National Bank cannot be serviced from the very same account. On receipt of the letter on 2-4-2004, SLM writes to the assessee informing this development and requesting them to pay cash for meeting the wages, salary and other expenses for their unit to run smoothly. Further, they have represented for payment of additional conversion charges depending upon the quality of the product as they have incurred lot of expenses in modernising the machineries. These factors led to the assessee effecting payments in cash. The words 'extent of banking facilities available' in proviso to section 40A(3) has to be interpreted in the facts of a given case and all such cases will not be covered under clause (j) of rule 6DD which has been subsequently deleted. In the instant case, banking facility was available but the bank account of SLM could not be operated by the very bank themselves because of an order of attachment passed by the ESI department. SLM virtually came to the assessee with the begging bowl and requested to effect payment in cash. The assessee has entered into an agreement for conversion on job work basis. The assessee is required to act as a prudent businessman, so that the job-work is completed to his satisfaction with optimum quality. This has led the assessee to effect payments in cash The argument of the revenue is on the ground that in order to avoid the attachment of the bank account the assessee has effected payment in cash. It is to be noted that what is relevant to be seen insofar as section 40A(3) is concerned is the conduct of the assessee and not the payee and the question would be did the assessee have a reasonable cause to effect payment in cash. If the assessee has a reasonable Explanation, then the proviso under section 40A(3) would stand attracted and the assessee would be entitled to relief. It maybe true that merely because the payee is identifiable, it will automatically exonerate the assessee. The Court is not laying down any such broad principle. The fact that the payee was identifiable and not a fictitious person would go to show the bona fides of the transaction. This is what is required to be considered from the angle of a commercially expedient and prudent business house [Pr. CIT v. Sumukha Synthetics [2020] 119 taxmann.com 234 (Madras)]

42.13 Continuation and validation of certain recovery proceedings if amount increased/reduced in appeal

Where any notice of demand in respect of any tax, penalty, interest or any other amount payable under this Act, (hereinafter in this section referred to as "Government dues"), is served upon any taxable person and any appeal, revision application is filed or other proceedings is initiated in respect of such Government dues, then, if Government dues are enhanced in appeal, revision or other proceedings, the proceedings shall continue. Fresh proceedings are not required - section 84(a) of CGST Act.

If Government dues are reduced in appeal, revision or other proceedings, fresh demand notice is not required. Only reduced Government dues will be recovered.

Recovery proceedings initiated on the basis of the demand served upon him prior to the disposal of such appeal, revision application or other proceeding may be continued in relation to the amount so reduced from the stage at which such proceedings stood immediately before such disposal - section 84 of CGST Act.

Intimation or notice for reduction or enhancement of any demand under section 84 shall be in form GST DRC-25 - rule 161 of CGST Rules, 2017 [words in italics inserted w.e.f. 26-12-2022]

42.14 Liability in some specified cases

GST Law has made specific provisions relating to liability in various situations and cases. These are summarised below.

42.14-1 Liability in case of transfer of business

Where a taxable person, liable to pay tax under this Act, transfers his business in whole or in part, by sale, gift, lease, leave and license, hire or in any other manner whatsoever, the taxable person and the person to whom the business is so transferred shall jointly and severally be liable wholly or, as the case may be, to the extent of such transfer, to pay the tax, interest or any penalty due from the taxable person up to the time of such transfer, whether such tax, interest or penalty has been determined before such transfer, but has remained unpaid or is determined thereafter - section 85(1) of CGST Act.

Where the transferee or the lessee of a business referred to in section 86(1) carries on such business either in his own name or in some other name, he shall be liable to pay tax on the supply of goods or services or both effected by him with effect from the date of such transfer and shall, if he is an existing taxable person, apply within the prescribed time for amendment of his certificate of registration - section 85(2) of CGST Act.

42.14-2 Liability of agent and principal

Where an agent supplies or receives any taxable goods on behalf of his principal, such agent and his principal shall be jointly and severally liable to pay the tax payable on such goods under the Act - section 86 of CGST Act.

42.14-3 Liability in case of company in liquidation

When any company is being wound up whether under the orders of a court or Tribunal or otherwise, every person appointed as receiver of any assets of a company (hereinafter referred to as the "liquidator"), shall, within thirty days after his appointment, give intimation of his appointment to the Commissioner- section 88(1) of CGST Act.

The Commissioner shall, after making such inquiry or calling for such information as he may deem fit, notify the liquidator within three months from the date on which he receives intimation of the appointment of the liquidator, the amount which in the opinion of the Commissioner would be sufficient to provide for any tax, interest or penalty which is then, or is likely thereafter to become, payable by the company - section 88(2) of CGST Act.

Notice to liquidator shall be issued by Commissioner in form GST DRC-24.

17.5-5 Impracticable seizure of bank lockers and bank accounts [Section 247(4) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(3) of the ITA 1961)] While Section 132(1) of the ITA 1961 grants the power to seize money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable articles, Section 132(3) comes into play where it is not practicable to seize such assets. The Kerala High Court, in the case of ITO v. M. Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

In support of this amendment, the Ministry stated before the Select Committee that "During search, situations arise where a person though not possessing any books or other documents but is in the know of the business intricacies or is a key person managing business e.g. accountant, machine operator in the manufacturing industry, gatekeepers who are maintaining exit records, quality control persons who have complete production information and so on. Statements of such persons also become extremely important. Therefore, practically, these statements are relevant to conduct investigations. It is relevant to note that such statements are taken during the course of the search and at the premises being searched. Thus, the amendment has been rightly made to rationalise the provision."

Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

PROCEEDS OF BENAMI PROPERTY DEPOSITED IN BANK

Cash and bank balance are treated as movable property/asset. Property under section 2(26) of PBPT Act, 1988 means asset of any kind, whether movable or immovable and proceeds of a such property. It is our common knowledge that on many occasions cash forms part of the proceeds of a benami property which gets deposited in bank. In such a situation, depending on the origin of cash and intention behind such a transaction, the balance in the bank account represented by proceeds of a benami property could form benami property. In other words, if the bank balance has a nexus with the proceeds of a benami property, it can partake the character of benami property subject to benami transaction. There may a case where there is no bank balance except leaving a very small balance and there is no trace of utilization of cash withdrawn. Action can be taken to attach the small amount of cash balance in the bank and then other consequences would follow. There is no monetary limit to initiate benami proceeding.

Steps to secure recovery of demand in high demand cases - It has been the experience in the past that on several occasions, the Assessing Officers create huge demands against assessees without obtaining the details of any known assets of the asses¬see. With the passage of time and in the absence of such details, no concrete action gets taken to recover this demand. As a re¬sult, Department is burdened with the responsibility to recover the huge arrears existing in its records, with little possibility of actual recovery in many cases. As on 1-4-2004, the arrears increased by 20% to Rs. 87,885 crore while the objective was to reduce arrears by 20% as compared to the preceding year.

2. The Board has, therefore, decided that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakh and above in big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolka¬ta, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Pune and Bangalore and Rs. 1 lakh and above elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that the recovery, in full or in part, could become difficult, it shall be the responsibility of the Assessing Officer, during the assessment proceedings itself, to enquire into all assets of the assessee and place under provisional attachment, in terms of provisions of section 281B, before the assessment is completed, the assets sufficient to cover the demand in question (or to the maximum extent, as the case may be). After completion of the assessment, if the provisional attachment cannot be continued till recovery, the same assets can be considered for attachment, etc., under section 222/226. In each of these cases, the Assessing Officer shall mention in an Office Note to the Assessment Order in question, the efforts made to locate the assets of the assessee, the details of assets located, the details of assets placed under provisional attachment, etc.

3. In search and seizure cases, huge demands are raised under block assessment and the recovery of the same is tedious and time-consuming. In this regard, it is extremely important for Assessing Officers in Central Charges to explore the possibility of invoking the provisions of section 281B. At the time of prepa¬ration of Appraisal Report, the DDIT(Inv.)/ADIT(Inv.) should take particular care in identifying the properties of the assessees which could be attached under this section and make a specific mention of the same in the Appraisal Report itself.

4. It shall be the responsibility of all Assessing Officers to follow the above procedure. If any demand becomes irrecoverable due to the failure of the Assessing Officer to follow these guidelines, he shall be held accountable for the loss caused to the Government, regardless of his subsequent posting.

5. While making a review of scrutiny assessments, the Commission¬ers of Income-tax and Chief Commissioners of Income-tax concerned shall specifically comment on this aspect.—Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2-9-2004.

CLARIFICATION ONE

1. Attention is invited to Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2nd September, 2004, wherein the Board directed that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakhs and above in big cities and Rs. 1 lakh elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that recovery, in full or in part, would be difficult, the Assessing Officer should place assets of suitable value under provisional attachment under section 281B.

2. Since the issue of this Instruction, some apprehensions have been expressed regarding the potential for its indiscriminate use. The purpose of the Instruction was to draw attention to the statutory provision (section 281B) that has been in existence since 1975. To safeguard against any indiscriminate use, the Board desires that the provisions of section 281B should be resorted to only in cases where there is a reasonable likelihood of the recovery becoming difficult due to inadequacy of assets. Where there are sufficient assets to cover the demand, the provisions of section 281B should not be resorted to, except under exceptional circumstances warranting the same, and after strictly complying with the conditions incorporated in section 281B.—F. No. 404/22/2004-ITCC, dated 5-11-2004.

Whether "any authority" would include income tax authority? As discussed earlier, the word 'any' is used before the word 'authority'. In the context of the provision, the word 'any' has wider meaning and accordingly, it implies that literally read, 'any authority' may include income-tax authority also. Therefore, in terms of the amendment, it can be said that 'reason to believe' as recorded by the income tax authorities is not required to be disclosed to any authority including income tax authority.

11.1-3c Appellate Tribunal - The Appellate Tribunal is defined under section 2(4) of the Act as under:

"Appellate Tribunal" means the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 252."

As discussed above, in terms of the amendment, income tax authority is not required to disclose 'reason to believe' to the Appellate Tribunal.

11.1-3d Effect on pending Cases - The amendment is made effective from 1-4-1962. Since above amendment is procedural in nature, it can have retrospective effect. Accordingly, it would have impact on pending cases.

11.1-3e Whether the amendment encourages search and seizure without recording of reason to believe? - Prima facie, answer is no, because there is no change in law in respect of recording of reason to believe before authorization of search. There is no additional power given to income-tax authority to conduct search without recording reasons. The specified authority is obliged to record the reason. However, only difference is that now such authority need not disclose the reason to any person, authority or the Appellate Tribunal. If search proceeding is challenged before High Court, such authority is bound to disclose the reason to High Court, if asked to do so.

However, in past, in many cases, search was conducted without recording concrete reason. In some cases, it was also found that the reason was recorded subsequent to the search proceeding or based on the material found during the search. In such circumstances, Court had struck down the order passed by the authorities treating it as illegal or invalid.

In terms of the amendment, now income-tax authorities are not required to disclose the reason to any person, authority or Appellate Tribunal. Therefore, in absence of transparency in process of decision making and recording reason by income tax authorities, it may encourage the search without recording a reason or recording reason subsequently.

In such cases only remedy available is to file a Writ petition before jurisdictional High Court which may be a costly affair.

11.1-3f Hardship, if search proceeding initiated in case of mistaken identity or incorrect information - It is possible that search proceeding may be initiated or conducted against a different person say due to same name mistakenly or based on incorrect information. In such circumstances, it may not be possible for such person to ask reason for initiating search or he cannot challenge validity of search before income-tax authorities/Appellate Tribunal. In such cases, it appears that it may cause hardship. Suppose, if he challenges validity of such proceedings before High Court by way of filing Writ petition, then apart from litigation cost, other consequences could be financial hardship, interruption of business, public reputation, goodwill, mental harassment, etc.

11.1-4 No disclosure of 'reason to suspect' [Section 132(1A)]

Section 132(1A) provides that where an authority mentioned therein, based on the information in his possession, has 'reason to suspect' of circumstances referred in the said sub-section, he may authorize an authority specified therein to carry out search and seizure of any building, place, vessel, vehicle or aircraft.

Finance Act, 2017 has inserted Explanation to section 132(1A) to provide that the reason to suspect as recorded by the income-tax authority shall not be disclosed to:

any person; or

any authority; or

Appellate Tribunal

The above amendment is similar to amendment made under sub-section (1) of section 132 as discussed above.

In terms of the provision, an authorised officer may provisionally attach any property in the following manner:
