invoking section 83 of Himachal Pradesh Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the HPGST Rules, 2017.

Appellant instituted Writ Petition under article 226 of Constitution challenging orders of provisional attachment.

High Court dismissed writ petition on ground that provisional attachment could not be challenged in a petition under article 226 on ground that an 'alternative and efficacious remedy' of an appeal under section 107 was available.

On appeal to Supreme Court: HELD: The marginal note to section 83 provides some indication of Parliamentary intent. Section 83 provides for 'provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases'. The first point to note is that the attachment is provisional - provisional in the sense that it is in aid of something else. The second point to note is that the purpose is to protect the revenue. The third point is the expression 'in certain cases' which shows that in order to effect a provisional attachment, the conditions which have been spelt out in the statute must be fulfilled. Marginal notes, it is well-settled, do not control a statutory provision but provide some guidance in regard to content. Put differently, a marginal note indicates the drift of the provision. With these prefatory comments, the judgment must turn to the essential task of statutory construction. The language of the statute has to be interpreted bearing in mind that it is a taxing statute which comes up for interpretation. The provision must be construed on its plain terms. Equally, in interpreting the statute, one must have regard to the purpose underlying the provision. An interpretation which effectuates the purpose must be preferred particularly when it is supported by the plain meaning of the words used. [Para 40]

Sub-Section (1) of section 83 can be bifurcated into several parts. The first part provides an insight on when in point of time or at which stage the power can be exercised. The second part specifies the authority to whom the power to order a provisional attachment is entrusted. The third part defines the conditions which must be fulfilled to validate the power or ordering a provisional attachment. The fourth part indicates the manner in which an attachment is to be levelled. The final and the fifth part defines the nature of the property which can be attached. Each of these special divisions which have been explained above is for convenience of exposition. While they are not watertight compartments, ultimately and together they aid in validating an understanding of the statute. Each of the above five parts is now interpreted and explained below:

(i)

The power to order a provisional attachment is entrusted during the pendency of proceedings under any one of six specified provisions:

sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 or 74. In other words, it is when a proceeding under any of these provisions is pending that a provisional attachment can be ordered;

(ii)

The power to order a provisional attachment has been vested by the legislature in the Commissioner;

(iii)

Before exercising the power, the Commissioner must be 'of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue, it is necessary so to do";

(iv)

The order for attachment must be in writing;

(v)

The provisional attachment which is contemplated is of any property including a bank account belonging to the taxable person; and

(vi)

The manner in which a provisional attachment is levied must be specified in the rules made pursuant to the provisions of the statute. [Para 41]

Under sub-section (2) of section 83, a provisional attachment ceases to have effect upon the expiry of a period of one year of the order being passed under sub-section (1). The power to levy a provisional attachment has been entrusted to the Commissioner during the pendency of proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 or as the case may be, section 74. Section 62 contains provisions for assessment for non-filing of returns. Section 63 provides for assessment of unregistered persons. Section 64 contains provisions for summary assessment. Section 67 elucidates provisions for inspection, search and seizure. [Para 42]

A power is conferred by section 70 upon the proper officer to summon a person whose attendance is considered necessary to give evidence or produce a document or any other things in any enquiry in the manner which is provided in the case of a civil court under the CPC. [Para 43]

Sub- section (1) of section 74 empowers the proper officer to serve a notice on a person chargeable with tax where it appears that—

(i)

Any tax has not been paid;

(ii)

Tax has been short paid;

(iii)

Tax has been erroneously refunded; or

(iv)

Input tax credit has been wrongly availed or utilized by reason of fraud, wilful statement or suppression of fact to evade tax. [Para 45]

the Commissioner that it is not liable to be attached in the present. [Para 55]

The second significant aspect of sub-rule (5) is the mandatory requirement of furnishing an opportunity of being heard to the person whose property is attached. This is in consonance with the principles of natural justice and ensures that a fair procedure is observed. Sub-rule (5) provides for a post provisional attachment right of:

(i)

Submitting an objection to the attachment;

(ii)

An opportunity of being heard. Sub -rule (5) contains clear language to the effect that a person whose property is attached is entitled to two procedural entitlements: first, the right to submit an objection on the ground that the property was not or is not liable to be attached; and second, an opportunity of being heard to the person filing an objection. This is a clear indicator that in addition the filing of an objection, the person whose property is attached is entitled to an opportunity of being heard. It is not open to the Commissioner, as has been stated in the present case, to hold the view that the only safeguard under sub-rule 5 is to submit an objection without an opportunity of a personal hearing. Such a construction would be plainly contrary to sub-rule 5 which contemplates both the submission of an objection to the attachment and an opportunity of being heard. The opportunity of being heard can be availed of as a matter of right by the person whose property is attached. Both the right to submit an objection and to be afforded an opportunity of being heard are valuable safeguards. The consequence of a provisional attachment is serious. It displaces the person whose property is attached from dealing with the property. Where a bank account is attached, it prevents the person from operating the account. A business entity whose bank account is attached is seriously prejudiced by the inability to utilize the proceeds of the account for the purpose of business. The dual procedural safeguards inserted in sub-rule 5 of rule 159 demand strict compliance.

The Commissioner who hears the objections must pass a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the objections. To allow the Commissioner to get by without passing a reasoned order will make his decision subjective and defeat the purpose of subjecting it to judicial scrutiny. The Commissioner must deal with the objections and pass a reasoned order indicating whether, and if not, why the objections are not being accepted. Sub-rule 6 of rule 159 allows for the release of a property which either was or is no longer liable for attachment. The form in which such an order has to be passed, namely form GST DRC-23, states that 'now there is no such proceeding pending against the defaulting person which warrants attachment' of the account or as the case may be, the property. Sub -rules 5 and 6 do not expressly contemplate a situation in which the person whose property is attached can object on the ground that the attachment is in excess of the amount likely to be due for which proceedings have been launched under the Act. Nor does it provide for a specific opportunity to the taxable person to offer any alternative form of security in lieu of the attachment. Such an opportunity must be read into the provision to allow for a fair working in practice. Whether any alternative security that is furnished by the taxable person should be accepted and if so, its sufficiency, is a matter for the Commissioner to determine. Undoubtedly, the taxable person may not have a right to demand that only a particular form of security must be accepted. The Commissioner has to decide whether the form of security offered would secure the interest of the revenue. Where the taxable person sets up the plea that the extent of the attachment is excessive or where the taxable person offers an alternative form of security, these are also matters which ought to be determined by the Commissioner in the exercise of powers under rule 159(5). The scope of objection can also extend to the nature of the property which is being provisionally attached. Now, it is in this backdrop that it needs to be determined whether the petition under article 226 was maintainable and if it was, whether Commissioner exercised the powers under section 83 read with rule 159 in accordance with law. [Para 56]

HELD: The authority has come to a particular conclusion after satisfying itself on the basis of material which has already been produced by the assessee and found that action is necessitated in the interest of revenue. The proceedings in the form of show-cause notice of tax ascertained being payable by the assessee under section 74 of the Act has already been initiated and a specific notice in form GST DRC-01 is already issued under rule 142(1). It is quite clear that when the statutory function is being undertaken by authorities and when there is no allegation of specific mala fides, the function of the authority, in view of settled position of law, cannot be usurped by the High Court in exercise of extraordinary equitable jurisdiction when a satisfaction is arrived at by an authority that interest of revenue deserves to be protected. Hence, in the absence of any material or patent illegality such satisfaction cannot be disturbed or substituted for the sake of substitution and background of fact is such where the process cannot be intercepted when it has already commenced. When the substantial justice is pitted against technical consideration, predominance is given to the substantial justice. It has been clearly asserted by authority that amendment of section 83 of the CGST Act covers various chapters. The said chapters include the proceedings under section 70 of the Act. HELD: The only question that falls for consideration is whether the Competent Authority was justified in invoking section 83 for the purpose of passing an order of attachment of the bank accounts. [Para 22]

ance of the statutory preconditions by the Commissioner. While conditioning the exercise of the power on the formation of an opinion by the Commissioner that 'for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue, it is necessary so to do', it is evident that the statute has not left the formation of opinion to an unguided subjective discretion of the Commissioner. The formation of the opinion must bear a proximate and live nexus to the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue. [Para 48] By utilizing the expression 'it is necessary so to do' the legislature has evinced an intent that an attachment is authorized not merely because it is expedient to do so (or profitable or practicable for the revenue to do so) but because it is necessary to do so in order to protect interest of the government revenue. Necessity postulates that the interest of the revenue can be protected only by a provisional attachment without which the interest of the revenue would stand defeated. Necessity in other words postulates a more stringent requirement than a mere expediency. A provisional attachment under section 83 is contemplated during the pendency of certain proceedings, meaning thereby that a final demand or liability is yet to be crystallized. An anticipatory attachment of this nature must strictly conform to the requirements, both substantive and procedural, embodied in the statute and the rules. The exercise of unguided discretion cannot be permissible because it will leave citizens and their legitimate business activities to the peril of arbitrary power. Each of these ingredients must be strictly applied before a provisional attachment on the property of an assesses can be levied. The Commissioner must be alive to the fact that such provisions are not intended to authorize Commissioners to make pre-emptive strikes on the property of the assessee, merely because property is available for being attached. There must be a valid formation of the opinion that a provisional attachment is necessary for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue. [Para 49]

These expressions in regard to both the purpose and necessity of provisional attachment implicate the doctrine of proportionality. Proportionality mandates the existence of a proximate or live link between the need for the attachment and the purpose which it is intended to secure. It also postulates the maintenance of a proportion between the nature and extent of the attachment and the purpose which is sought to be served by ordering it. Moreover, the words embodied in sub-section (1) of section 83, as interpreted above, would leave no manner of doubt that while ordering a provisional attachment the Commissioner must in the formation of the opinion act on the basis of tangible material on the basis of which the formation of opinion is based in regard to the existence of the statutory requirement. [Para 50]

It is viewed that the formation of the opinion must be based on tangible material which indicates a live link to the necessity to order a provisional attachment to protect the interest of the government revenue. [Para 51]

Under sub-rule (1) of rule 159, an attachment of property by the Commissioner under section 83 is effected by passing an order mentioning the details of the property which is attached. The form in which the order is to be made is prescribed in form GST DRC-22. [Para 53]

Under sub-rule (5) of rule 159, the person whose property is attached is allowed seven days' time to file an objection that the property attached 'was or is not liable to attachment'. Sub-rule (5) stipulates that the Commissioner may 'after affording an opportunity of being heard to the person filing the objection' release the property by an order in form GSTDRC-23. Similarly, under sub-rule (6) upon being satisfied that the property was or is no longer liable to be attached, the Commissioner is empowered to release the property by issuing an order in Form GST DRC- 23 for the releasing of the property under attachment. [Para 54]

A significant aspect of rule 159(5) is that upon the levy of a provisional attachment, the person whose property is attached is empowered to file an objection within seven days on the ground that the property was or is not liable to attachment. In using the expression 'was or is no longer liable for attachment', the delegate of the legislature has comprehended two alternative situations. The first, evidenced by the use of the words 'was' indicates that the property was on the date of the attachment in the past not liable to be attached. That is the reason for the use of the past tense 'was'. The expression 'is not liable to attachment indicates a situation in praesenti. Even if the property, arguably, was validly attached in the past, the person whose property has been attached may demonstrate to the Commissioner that it is not liable to be attached in the present. [Para 55]

The second significant aspect of sub-rule (5) is the mandatory requirement of furnishing an opportunity of being heard to the person whose property is attached. This is in consonance with the principles of natural justice and ensures that a fair procedure is observed. Sub-rule (5) provides for a post provisional attachment right of:

(i)

Submitting an objection to the attachment;

(ii)

An opportunity of being heard.

Malice in its legal sense means such malice as may be assumed from the doing of a wrongful act intentionally but also without just cause or excuse or for want of reasonable or probably cause. Any use of discretionary power exercised for an unauthorized purpose amounts to malice in law. It is immaterial whether the authority acted in good faith or bad faith. [Para 42] When the search of the industrial premises of the writ applicant was undertaken, the further inquiry in that regard revealed that there were no goods involved, but there were only billing transactions. At the time of the search, goods worth Rs. 2,48,59,485 were found stored at the industrial premises of the writ applicant. The authority came to the conclusion that the tax liability which may be determined in future under section 74 may be to the tune of Rs. 1,60,00,000, and in such circumstances, thought fit to provisionally attach the goods worth only Rs. 1,60,00,000 from the total goods worth Rs. 2,48,59,485. [Para 43]

It would be a big mistake on the part of the respondents to understand that the reasons to believe necessary for the purpose of carrying out inspection, search and seizure under section 67 would be sufficient enough for the purpose of formation of the opinion that it is necessary to provisionally attach the goods or other articles for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. Section 83 stands altogether on a different footing. The considerations also are quite different for the purpose of exercising the power of provisional attachment under section 83. Just because, some proceedings are initiated under section 67 by itself would not be sufficient to arrive at the satisfaction that it is necessary to provisionally attach the property for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. The power has been specifically conferred upon the Commissioner to form such an opinion. The legislature was quite alive to the fact that an order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course. It is one of the drastic measures which the authority may be compelled to take if the situation demands for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue. Under section 67, the legislature has thought fit to use the words 'proper officer not below the rank of Joint Commissioner'. In section 83, even that discretion is taken away and it is only the Commissioner who has been empowered to act under section 83. Therefore, the subjective satisfaction, which is required for the purpose of section 83, is not dependent on section 67 or to put it in other words, just because, a search has been undertaken resulting in seizure of goods by itself may not be sufficient to arrive at the subjective satisfaction that it is necessary to pass an order of provisional attachment to protect Government revenue. [Para 44]

In the instant case, the challenge is also to the order in form GST DRC-07 (rule 142(5) of the Rules). This order dated 17-6-2019 is an assessment order purported to have been passed under section 74. [Para 45]

It appears from the materials on record that without issue of any show cause notice, the tax liability came to be determined under section 74. Section 74 makes it abundantly clear that the defaulter should be called upon to show cause as to why he should not be paid the amount specified in the notice along with the interest payable thereon. There could not have been any assessment under section 74 without giving any opportunity of hearing to the writ applicant. In such circumstances, the order is not tenable in law and deserves to be quashed and set aside. One also fails to understand as to on what basis the input tax credit could have been blocked by way of computer entry. At the most, the same could have been ordered to be provisionally attached, but how could the same have been blocked. Such action is also not sustainable in law. [Para 48]

Section 83 is in pari materia with the provisions of section 281B of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Section 281B of the Act, 1961 also provides for a provisional attachment of the property of an assessee pending the adjudication an assessment/reassessment proceedings where the income tax department believes that such attachment is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. [Para 49]

Thus, although the provisions of section 281B of the Income-tax Act is pari materia to section 83 of the State GST Act, yet one pertinent feature of section 281B of the Income-tax Act is that it gives guidelines for making the provisional attachment. Such guidelines are missing so far as section 83 of the State GST Act is concerned. [Para 51]

Conclusions:

(1)

The order of provisional attachment before the assessment order is made, may be justified if the Assessing Authority or any other authority empowered in law is of the opinion that it is necessary to protect the interest of revenue. However, the subjective satisfaction should be based on some credible materials or information and also should be supported by supervening factor. It is not any and every material, howsoever vague and indefinite or distant remote or far fetching, which would warrant the formation of the belief.

The contention that this could only mean 'cash' and not money in a bank account may be an attractive argument but not in the context in which the above expression occurs. It is certainly a valuable thing. In other words, a sum in a bank account is not outside the ambit of section 132(1) and can be subject to search and seizure. [Para 53] Thus, a person could be in possession of undisclosed income not only in his or her own account but in someone else's account. In the context of the instant petitions, therefore, when pursuant to the search warrant, the department proceeded to search and seize not only valuable things etc. found in the premises of 'M' but also those in the accounts of the 8 petitioner companies as well as that of VS who was actively involved in the day to day management of various companies controlled by 'M' and worked closely with him, they could do so as long as they were satisfied that what constitutes M's undisclosed income was in the accounts of the 8 companies and VS. [Para 54]

The second proviso to section 132(1) read with section 132(3) permits the department to require the bank in which the account that is subject to search is located to freeze it since it may not be possible 'to take physical possession' immediately of such 'valuable article or thing and remove it to a safe place.' Section 132B deals with the powers of the authorised officer to deal with the valuable thing which has been so seized and the conditions on which the restraint placed may be lifted. [Para 55]

The assertion by petitioners that this is realization of the debt owed by the bank to the petitioners and that the amount therein cannot be transferred to the department is based on an incorrect understanding of the legal position under section 281B. The said provision states that in order to protect the interests of the revenue, it may be necessary to go in for a provisional attachment. Therefore, the direction issued to RBL by the department does not mean that the money is finally taken over by the revenue. It will undoubtedly be kept in a suspense account like a PD Account to await the final orders in the assessment proceedings and the issues raised as a consequence thereof. For this purpose, the argument that this does not constitute 'assets' or 'money' within the meaning of section 132(1) read with section 133 has not merit. [Para 57]

■ It is the grievance expressed by the assessees that since the department has resorted to such draconian measure of provisional attachment of their properties, not for the first time, but for the fourth time, due to which, their business has almost come to a standstill, since, the properties, which were attached by the department were all the properties, which they have offered as securities to the banks, and because of such mortgaged properties were came to be attached, the banks are refusing to part with further working capital loans, at any moment, they would declare the assessees as non performing assets, if this situation continues, it will jeopardize the entire business of the assessees and it would also have a cascading effect of 5000 workers loosing their job, resulting in 5000 families landing on streets suffering for food and shelter. Thus, from the above backgrounds of the case it is clear that the first charge holders of the properties are the bankers and the department are only the second charge holders of the assessees’ properties. Therefore, the first charge holders of the assessees’ properties, being the bankers, the assessees have to first satisfy the bankers, for availing loan facility and only the bankers are satisfied they would come forward to lend loan facility to the assessees. The assessees have earned good reputation and credibility amongst the general public, based on which, the bankers have come forward to extend the loan facility and this is a continuous arrangements entered into between the bankers and the assessees, for the sake of running the business smoothly, and when the banks, having extended working capital loan facility to the assessees, certainly, they will monitor the same so as to protect their interest. The question of non-repayment would arise due to deficit in service of working capital loan extended to the assessees. Therefore, the department could have enabled the assessees to get their working capital loans extended by the bankers, and thereafter, monitor the assessees, whether such loan is being utilized by the assessees for the purpose, for which, such additional loan is extended, and by doing so, the interest of the revenue, is not going to be affected in any away, rather, it would promote much financial gain, and thereby, the interest of the revenue would also be safeguarded. Therefore, the department ought to have acted in such a way, in order to protect the interest of the revenue. Whereas, in the instant case, it is seen that, on earlier occasions, i.e., on 28.02.2022, 23.08.2022 and 17.02.2023, the department has issued the attachment orders and the same got lapsed on 27.08.2022, 22.02.2023 and 16.08.2023 respectively. Finally, for the fourth time, the department has issued the provisional attachment orders dated 16.08.2023 and the reasons assigned is that to protect the interest of the revenue.(Para 9)

■

Hence the Court posed a question to the department, whether the intention of the department is really to protect the interest of the revenue or whether to close down the business of the assessees by resorting to such draconian action. In reply to the said question, the department stated that it has no intention to cause hindrance or obstacles to the assessees’ running their business and the department is mainly concerned only about the safeguarding the interest of the revenue and in matters of revenue, there is no place for consideration of equity.(Para 10)

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority for recovery of excise dues of Rs. 55 lakhs had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to release attachment over bank accounts subject to assessee furnishing bank guarantee for Rs. 55 lakhs - Held, yes [Para 8][Partly in favour of assessee]GST: Where Competent Authority for recovery of excise dues of Rs. 55 lakhs had provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee, said authority was directed to release attachment over bank accounts subject to assessee furnishing bank guarantee for Rs. 55 lakhs

FACT: The Competent Authority for recovery of excise dues of Rs. 55 lakhs had provisionally attached bank accounts of the assessee.

On writ:

HELD: Section 83 provides for provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases and inter alia provides that where during the pendency of any proceeding under section 67, the Commissioner is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, it is necessary so to do, he may, by order in writing attach provisionally any property, including bank account, belonging to the taxable person in such manner as may be prescribed. Thus the object of the provision is to protect the interest of the Government revenue. In the instant case, attachment of the bank accounts of the assessee has resulted into various hardships to the assessee which would adversely affect its business and which may result in loss of revenue to the Government, instead if the assessee provides for some security towards its outstanding dues, the interest of the assessee as well as the revenue can be protected. [Para 6]

In view of the aforesaid, the interest of justice would be served if the assessee is permitted to pay the amount of Rs. 55 lakhs outstanding towards excise dues by way of equal monthly instalments within a period of eight months, subject to the assessee furnishing a bank guarantee for an equal amount towards security of such amount. [Para 7]

The Competent Authority is directed to forthwith release the attachment over the bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee shall furnish a bank guarantee for a sum of Rs. 55 lakhs to the Competent Authority. It shall also file an undertaking before the Court undertaking to pay the balance amount of Rs. 55 lakhs in equal monthly instalments within a period of eight months. In case the bank guarantee is not furnished as directed, it would be open for the Competent Authority to resort to the provisions of section 83 and attach the bank accounts of the assessee. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority initiated some proceedings against assessee under Central GST Act and attached his saving bank account provisionally - Assessee filed writ petition seeking directions to Competent Authority to dispose of representation dated 18-6-2019 sent by him and duly received by Competent Authority - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to dispose of assessee's representation on its own merits as expeditiously as possible - Held, yes [Para 7][In favour of assessee]GST: Where Competent Authority had initiated some proceedings against assessee under Central GST Act and attached his bank account provisionally, said authority was directed to dispose of assessee's representation dated 18-6-2019 on its own merits

FACT: The Competent Authority had initiated some proceedings against the assessee under the provisions of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and attached his saving bank account provisionally.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to dispose of the representation dated 18-6-2019 sent by him and duly received by the Competent Authority on 27-6-2019.

HELD: Vide the aforesaid representation, the assessee has written to the Competent Authority inter alia making a request to raise the aforesaid attachment. It is the specific case of the assessee that the aforesaid representation has not evoked any response or reply and there is inaction on the part of the Competent Authority. [Para 6]

The writ petition is disposed of with a direction to the Competent Authority to dispose of assessee's representation dated 18-6-2019 on its own merits and in accordance with law as expeditiously as possible and in any event within six weeks. Disposal of the representation shall be communicated to the assessee under due acknowledgement within seven working days. [Para 7]

the interest of the revenue it is necessary to do so. [Para 8]

The Delhi High Court in the case of V.L.S. Finance Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 246 ITR 707/ 112 Taxman 295 has held that opinion means something more than mere retaining of ‘gossip’ or ‘hearsay’, it means the judgment of belief that is a belief or conviction resulting from what one thinks on a particular question. [Para 9] So far as the question of opinion of the Assessing Officer was concerned, it was found that it was lacking in the instant case. The counter-affidavit sworn by ITO did not disclose any material on which requisite opinion to invoke the power under section 281 B could be formed. Only this much had been stated that FDRs valuing Rs. 44 lakhs were found. The nature and source of acquisition of those FDRs were required to be examined. The case of the assessee was that the aforesaid amount represented share application money received by the company. After filing of the counter-affidavit two more affidavits were also filed on behalf of the department. But in none of those affidavits any material or relevant circumstance had been mentioned on the basis of which it could be said that the assessee would not fulfil its obligation, namely, payment of demand of any tax which would be levied on it subsequently. Documents and account books, etc., seized by the officers of the Central Excise Department did not belong to the assessee-company nor did they relate to the business activities of the assessee-company. There was not a whisper even in any of the counter-affidavits that those documents belonged to the assessee. Such an averment was absent in the pleading of the department. The documents, thus, seized by the Central Excise Department and also requisitioned by the Income-tax Department did not relate to the business activities of either of the assessees. As a matter of fact, the enquiries on the basis of those documents were directed by the department against certain persons other than the assessees. [Para 10]

It is also settled that the powers vested with any authority under various provisions of law can be exercised only for the stated purpose and not for any other purpose. [Para 14]

The department could not show any material either from the counter-affidavit or from the supplementary affidavits to justify the action of the assessing authority under section 281B. Only this much was submitted by them that certain enquiries with regard to the nature and source of gifts in favour of the petitioner No. 2 were to be enquired into. That was the only ground which was stated in the counter-affidavit and was urged by the department. That ground was wholly insufficient to invoke section 281B. In every case, where the assessment has to take place, it is the bounden duty of the Assessing Officer to make such enquiries as are necessary to complete the assessment. Apart from the above the assessee-company was newly born assessee on the file of the Income-tax Department as it was incorporated only on 9-12-2001 and indisputably it filed returns of income up to the assessment year 2003-04, which were finalized by the department. There was no history of the assessee-company to show that on any occasion earlier it failed to discharge its liability. Apart from the above as has been held by the Bombay High Court in the case of Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 that the attachment of the bank accounts is the last resort. The department if it is of the opinion that the assessee is likely to dispose of its property to thwart the payment of income-tax dues, the department should provisionally attach the immovable property of such assessee first. Resort to blanket attachment of the entire bank accounts of an assessee has serious consequence on its rights to carry on the business. The action of the department in such circumstances should not give an impression to any body that it has indulged in any manner to hamper the business activities of the assessee. Power has been conferred under the said section to protect the interest of the revenue. Only so much asset or amount which would satisfy the future demand should be provisionally attached under section 281B leaving other assets including the amount standing in the bank account to enable the assessee to carry on the business. The passing of the impugned order in the instant case, amounted to stopping the business activities of the assessee, which instead of advancing the purpose of section 281B frustrated the interest of the revenue. [Para 15]

Even assuming that the Assessing Officer had power to attach the bank accounts provisionally, it does not give licence to conduct assessment proceedings at his leisure when the department was so apprehensive as to resort its power under section 281B which is to be used sparingly. It is expected in such matter from the department to conclude the assessment proceedings within a reasonable period. It is difficult to approve the callous approach of the Assessing Officer in such matters not to conclude the assessment proceedings within a reasonable period of time. [Para 16]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with rule 159 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 and copy of such order had not been served upon it - Whether notice required to be issued on Competent Authority - Held, yes [Para 3] [Matter pending]GST : Where Competent Authority had provisionally attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 of CGST Act and copy of such order had not been served upon it, notice was issued on Competent Authority

FACT: The Competent Authority of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Department had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the petitioner under section 83.

On writ:

HELD: No copy of any order under section 83 appears to have been served upon the petitioner. The order of provisional attachment of property under section 83 issued to the concerned bank is in Form DRC-22 which is referable to rule 159(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017. Sub-rule (5) of rule 159 provides that any person whose property is attached may within seven days of attachment under sub-rule (1) file an objection as provided in the said rule. However, it appears that the general practice of the department is to issue provisional attachment order on the concerned banks without furnishing copy of any such order to the concerned supplier. It is difficult to comprehend as to how the supplier whose property is attached would be in a position to file objection under sub-rule (5) of rule 159 if a copy of such order is not furnished to such supplier. [Para 2]

In view of the aforesaid, notice required to be issued on the Competent Authority. [Para 3]

HEADNOTE: Section 83, read with section 107, of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83, read with section 107 of the Himachal Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the Himachal Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Joint Commissioner provisionally attached appellant's receivable from its customer on ground that appellant was found to be involved in an ITC fraud - Appellant challenged said attachment by way of filing Writ Petition - However, High Court refused to entertain writ on ground that appellant had alternative and efficacious remedy of appeal under section 107 - It was found that order for provisional attachment was passed by Joint Commissioner to whom powers vested in Commissioner under section 83(1) were delegated - Thus, order passed by Joint Commissioner as a delegate of Commissioner was not subject to an appeal under section 107(1) and only remedy available was in form of invocation of writ jurisdiction under article 226 of Constitution - Whether therefore, High Court was clearly in error in declining to entertain writ proceedings - Held, yes - Whether power to order a provisional attachment of property of taxable person including a bank account is draconian in nature and conditions which are prescribed by statute for a valid exercise of power must be strictly fulfilled - Held, yes - Whether before ordering a provisional attachment, Commissioner must form an opinion on basis of tangible material that assessee is likely to defeat demand, if any and formation of opinion must bear a proximate and live nexus to purpose of protecting interest of government revenue - Held, yes - Whether dual procedural safeguards inserted in rule 159(5) i.e. (i) submitting an objection to attachment and (ii) an opportunity of being heard, demands strict compliance - Held, yes - Whether since there was a clear non-application of mind by Joint Commissioner to provisions of section 83, rendering provisional attachment illegal; therefore, impugned judgment and order of High Court was to be set aside and writ petition filed by appellant under article 226 of Constitution was to be allowed by setting aside orders of provisional attachment - Held, yes [Paras 72, 73 and 74]GST : Power to order a provisional attachment of property of taxable person including a bank account is draconian in nature; exercise of power for ordering a provisional attachment must be preceded by formation of an opinion by Commissioner that it is necessary so to do for purpose of protecting interest of government revenue

FACT: The appellant manufactures lead according to specific requirements of its clients, and has a factory in Himachal Pradesh. The appellant had been in the same line of business since 2008. Upon introduction of the Goods and Services Tax, the appellant migrated to and was registered under GST.

A 'detection' case was filed and registered against one of the suppliers (GM Powertech) of the appellant in 2018. As a consequence, the appellant was also issued a notice to appear before the authorities and explain the alleged illegal claim of Input Tax Credit (ITC) made by it during 2017-18 and 2018-19. The appellant appeared before the authorities and contended that the ITC claimed by it was valid and after fulfilling all necessary conditions. The appellant also contended in its petition that its ITC was blocked despite the explanation provided.

Subsequently, one of the debtors of the appellant was issued a notice, provisionally attaching the receivables of the appellant amounting to Rs. 5 crores. The appellant in its petition claimed that such attachment was done without affording an opportunity of being heard. However, later the provisional attachment order was withdrawn.

Subsequently, after almost a year and half, Joint Commissioner of State Taxes and Excise, provisionally attached appellant's receivables from its customers, F and D, on ground that the appellant was involved in ITC fraud. Provisional attachment was ordered against appellant while invoking section 83 of Himachal Pradesh Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the HPGST Rules, 2017.

Appellant instituted Writ Petition under article 226 of Constitution challenging orders of provisional attachment.

High Court dismissed writ petition on ground that provisional attachment could not be challenged in a petition under article 226 on ground that an 'alternative and efficacious remedy' of an appeal under section 107 was available.

On appeal to Supreme Court:

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority vide two separate orders provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee under section 83 - Assessee objected to orders of provisional attachment by its representations and sought for revocation thereof - Competent Authority overruled objection raised by assessee and prayer for revoking provisional attachment orders rejected - Whether as impugned order suffered from infirmity of lack of application of mind as well as breach of principles of natural justice, it was unsustainable and deserved to be set aside - Held, yes - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to de novo consider objection of assessee in accordance with law - Held, yes [Paras 10, 24 and 25] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where assessee objected to orders of provisional attachment and sought for its revocation but Competent Authority overruled objection raised by assessee without considering same, since there was lack of application of mind as well as breach of principles of natural justice, order of Authority deserved to be set aside

FACT: The Competent Authority vide two separate orders dated 27-4-2021 provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee under section 83.

The assessee objected to the orders of provisional attachment by its representations dated 7-5-2021 and 17-5-2021 and sought for revocation thereof on diverse grounds.

The Competent Authority passed an order dated 21-5-2021, whereby objection raised to the orders of provisional attachment had been overruled and the prayer for revoking the said orders rejected.

On writ:

HELD: The prayer of the assessee for revoking the orders of provisional attachment ought to be considered de novo by the Competent Authority. This is for the reason that although the Competent Authority has written a detailed order spread over nine pages as to why the provisional attachment ought to continue, it suffers from the infirmity of lack of application of mind as well as breach of principles of natural justice.

The grounds on which the judicial review is available are well established. Non consideration of relevant materials and consideration of extraneous matters together with non access of the part affected to materials relied on in reaching conclusions, if substantiated, would provide sufficient ground for judicial review. In the instant case, the order dated 21-5-2021 is unsustainable. [Para 24]

The impugned order dated 21-5-2021 stands set aside. The Competent Authority is directed to de novo consider the objection of the assessee dated 7-5-2021 and 17-5-2021 in accordance with law as early as possible but not later than three weeks of receipt of copy of this order. [Para 25]

In the event the Competent Authority refuses to lift the orders of provisional attachment once again, appropriate reasons shall be assigned. [Para 26]

HEADNOTE: Section 83, read with  section 74, of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159, of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83, read with  section 74, of the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and rule 159 of the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Whether order of provisional attachment is required to be communicated to party affected and this requirement is necessary for a meaningful exercise of right conferred under rule 159(2) - Held, yes - Petitioner was a dealer engaged in B2B e-commerce trading in white goods including mobile handsets - Pursuant to investigation carried out by DGGI against few suppliers of petitioner for issuing fake invoices to pass fraudulent ITC, premises of petitioner were searched under section 67 and statements were recorded under section 70 - Thereafter, DGGI attached bank accounts of petitioner under section 83 by citing pendency of proceedings under section 74 and petitioner's failure to pay tax dues - Petitioner filed a representation before DGGI against attachment order but no hearing was granted by DGGI - Hence, petitioner filed instant writ petition to quash attachment order - Whether requirement of provisional attachment as contained under rule 159 would require passing of order to affected person to enable him in filing of objections, and passing an order after affording an opportunity of being heard - Held, yes - Whether since investigation against petitioner was an outcome of investigation against suppliers, no show cause notice under section 74 was issued to petitioner; thus, it could not be said that on date of issuing attachment order, any proceedings were pending against petitioner - Held, yes - Whether further, since DGGI had neither considered or given hearing to petitioner on its representation, nor issued attachment order in prescribed form, revenue had not complied with procedure prescribed under rule 159 - Held, yes - Whether therefore, provisional order of attachment was to be lifted - Held, yes [Paras 18, 23, 24, 25, 28, 29, 34 and 36] [In favour of petitioner]GST : Where pursuant to investigation, on suppliers of petitioner, bank accounts of petitioner were attached, however, no show cause notice under section 74 was issued to petitioner, it could not be said that on date of issuing attachment order, any proceedings were pending against petitioner; hence provisional order of attachment was to be lifted

FACT: The petitioner was engaged in the Business to Business ('B2B') e-commerce trading in 'white goods' including mobile handsets. The respondent No. 2 (Additional Director General of GST Intelligence) was conducting certain investigation in respect of Pal Overseas, a registered entity under the GST Act and also as regards other entities relating to the alleged issuance of bogus/fake invoices without supply of goods and were seeking to claim Input Tax Credit of Goods and Services Tax. It is stated that the petitioner was purchasing the mobile handsets from these suppliers and was selling to its customers. The respondent No. 2 conducted a search at the Head Office of the petitioner. During the search, the respondent No. 2 issued summons to the Associate Director of the petitioner Company and had recorded their statements.

The said representatives of petitioner Company responded to the notice, appeared before the Authorities and also made their statements, which had been duly recorded.

On 21-9-2020, the respondent No. 2 sought details of the bank accounts of the petitioner which were provided on the same day. It is stated that the respondent No. 2 attached the bank accounts of the petitioner purportedly in exercise of power under section 83.

The petitioner made representation in terms of rule 159(5) seeking release of attachment and defreezing of bank accounts, but such request was neither considered nor any order was passed as required under the applicable Rules.

On writ Petition:

HELD: At the very outset, it must be noted that the order of provisional attachment is required to be communicated to the party affected and this requirement is necessary for a meaningful exercise of the right conferred under rule 159(2) of CGST Rules.[Para 18]

It must be noted that while the petitioner has drawn attention to communication dated 21-9-2020, addressed to the Bank Manager, HDFC Bank, Bengaluru regarding the provisional attachment of bank account of the petitioner in exercise of power under section 83, it is pointed out that such communication does not have any copy addressed to the petitioner.[Para 19]

HEADNOTE: Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent authority for recovery of dues from assessee, a private company, had provisionally attached bank accounts of directors - Whether impugned order was without any authority of law - Held, yes - Whether Competent Authority was to be directed to release attachment of bank accounts of directors - Held, yes [Paras 1 and 2] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where Competent Authority for recovery of dues from assessee, a private company, had provisionally attached bank accounts of directors, impugned order was without any authority of law and Competent Authority was directed to release attachment of bank accounts of directors

FACT: The Competent Authority for recovery of dues from the assessee, a private company, had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the directors.

On writ:

HELD: A perusal of the provisions of section 83 shows that the same empowers the Commissioner, if the circumstances therein are satisfied, to attach provisionally any property, including bank account, belonging to the taxable person, in such manner as may be prescribed. The term 'taxable person' has been defined under sub-section (107) of section 2 to mean a person who is registered or liable to be registered under section 22 or section 24. In the instant case, it is the assessee which is registered under the provisions of the CGST Act and is, therefore, the taxable person. Under the circumstances, if at all, the provisions of section 83 could have been invoked against the assessee herein. However, under no circumstances, the same could have been invoked against the directors. [Para 1]

The revenue has placed reliance upon the provisions of section 89 to submit that the same permits recovery of the dues of the private company from its directors in case such amount cannot be recovered from the company. The reliance placed upon section 89 is thoroughly misconceived inasmuch as the same relates to recovery of any tax, interest or penalty due from a private company in respect of supply of goods or services. Moreover even if such amount cannot be recovered from the assessee, the directors of the company do not ipso facto become liable to pay such amount and it is only if the director fails to prove that non recovery cannot be attributed to any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part in relation to the affairs of the company, that the same can be invoked. However, in any case, at this stage, section 83 does not apply to the directors.

In view of the aforesaid, the impugned order was without any authority of law.

The Competent Authority was to be directed to release the attachment of the bank accounts of the directors. [Para 2]

The case be fixed for 14-2-2019. [Para 3]

FACT: The assessee was a private limited company engaged in the business of procurement, supply and distribution of Xiaomi products in India bearing various brand names including mobile phones, accessories, computers etc. As part of its business, assessee had to pay royalty to Qualcomm and Beijing Xiaomi Mobile Software Company Ltd. During the period from 2019 to March 2022, there were proceedings between the assessee and Income-tax Department and the proceedings in relation to alleged payment of income tax by the assessee petitioner. Meanwhile, the Enforcement Directorate passed a seizure order, seizing the bank accounts of the assessee petitioner to an extent of INR 5,551 crores under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA).

The said order having been challenged by the petitioner, instant Court passed an interim order, staying the operation of the seizure order, subject to the condition that the petitioner was not entitled to make payments to foreign entities in the form of royalty or any other form. Subsequently, this Court issued a further clarification that the petitioner was at liberty to take overdrafts and make payments from such overdrafts to foreign entities excluding payment of royalty.

Subsequently, by final order, instant Court disposed of Writ Petition by relegating the petitioner to the Commissioner of Customs (Appeals) and further directed that the aforesaid earlier interim orders to continue till disposal of the proceedings.

Subsequently, in the proceedings before the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO), the petitioner contested the proceedings and filed the detailed submissions with regard to payment of royalty to the foreign entities and the TPO passed an order under section 92CA(3) whilst making transfer pricing adjustment.

The revenue issued show cause notice upon the assessee with respect to disallowance of royalty payments made to foreign entities i.e., Qualcomm and Beijing Xiaomi.

During the pendency of assessment, the revenue passed order under section 281B after obtaining requisite approval for provisionally attaching assessee's fixed deposits with two banks amounting to Rs. 3700 crores for a period of 6 months.

On Writ Petition:

HELD: A perusal of the impugned order will indicate that except for stating that there is likely addition of the amount mentioned in the order, no reasons, much less valid or cogent reasons are assigned by the Deputy Commissioner as to how and why he has formed an opinion that it was necessary to provisionally attach the fixed deposits of the assessee for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue. [Para 10]

In the instant case, a perusal of the impugned order will clearly indicate that the same is arbitrary and reflects premeditated conclusion without recording either an opinion or necessary to attach the property; the doctrine of proportionality which is implicated in the purpose and necessity of provisional attachment mandates the existence of a proximate or a live link between the need for the attachment and the purpose which it is intended to secure. [Para 12]

Further, mere apprehension that huge tax demands are likely to be raised on completion of assessment is not sufficient for the purpose of passing a provisional attachment order and the exercise of the same must necessarily be preceded by the formation of an opinion that it was necessary to do so for the purpose of protecting the interest of Government revenue, that too on the basis of tangible material that the assessee was not likely to fulfil the demand and on the other hand, was likely to defeat the demand, which is conspicuously missing and absent in the impugned order. [Para 13]

The impugned order also discloses that the same has been passed mechanically and is based on borrowed satisfaction and does not meet the test of formation of an opinion of the Assessing Officer who seems to have been influenced by the findings of the Investigation Wing and TPO and have not independently formed an opinion on the likely additions to be made during assessment proceedings. [Para 14]

As stated supra, in the light of existence of a legal mandatory pre-requirement and precondition of recording of formation of opinion which is in pari materia with 'reasons to believe' in section 281B, it was incumbent upon the Deputy Commissioner to arrive at his own satisfaction and not borrowed satisfaction by proper application of mind and consequently, the impugned order which is bald, vague, cryptic, laconic, unreasoned and non-speaking order deserves to be set aside, particularly having regard the undisputed fact that except for stating that he was of the opinion that it was necessary to attach the fixed deposits for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue, no other reasons have been assigned by the Deputy Commissioner in the impugned order. [Para 15]

headnotes.text: GST : Where on spot visit, flying squad opined that purchases made by writ-applicant from two parties were not genuine and hence, collected documents and books of account and passed order of provisional attachment of two bank accounts, having regard to fact that there was hardly a balance of Rs.22,065 in two bank accounts, there was no good reason to continue provisional attachment   The avowed object of exercise of power under section 83 for the purpose of provisional attachment of any property is to protect the interest of the Revenue.Ultimately, if sufficient material surfaces indicating the involvement of the writ-applicant in some bogus transaction, the next step in the process can always be a show-cause notice under section 73 or Section 74 of the Act, as the case may be. However, to provisionally attach all the bank accounts and that too those accounts in which there is hardly any balance would only cause undue hardship to the assessee   An order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course. It is one of the drastic measures which the authority may be compelled to take if the situation demands for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government Revenue.   When there are plethora of judgments explaining Section 83 in details, then why so much of litigation in the High Court. The only reason that can be attributed is the mechanical exercise of power under section 83 of the Act. This should stop at the earliest.   Union of India as well as CBDT were directed to issue appropriate instructions or guidelines at the earliest with respect to the exercise of power under section 83

Provisional attachment of bank accounts - Principal Additional Director General merely stated that powers conferred on concerned official under section 83 was invoked for provisionally attaching bank accounts of petitioner in order to protect interest of revenue - However, order did not show any basis for formation of opinion that provisional attachment was necessary to safeguard revenue's interest - No tangible material was disclosed - Order breached mandatory pre-conditions for exercise of powers under section 83 ibid [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 9, 10 and12] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank accounts - Some bank accounts having "0" credit balance - Provisional attachment of bank accounts was to be lifted provided cumulative amount appearing as credit balance in all bank accounts remitted to respondent/revenue, to protect its interests, pending adjudication [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 8 and 11] [In favour of assessee]GST : Provisional attachment of bank accounts should be lifted provided that cumulative amount appearing as credit balance in all bank accounts was remitted to revenue to protect its interests, pending adjudication

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, read with rule 159 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, read with rule 159 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Whether during pendency of any proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74, Commissioner after forming an opinion that it is necessary to do so for protecting interest of revenue, can provisionally attach any property including bank account belonging to taxable person - Held, yes - Whether these steps have to be taken in such manner as prescribed under rule 159(1) which deals with provisional attachment of property - Held, yes - Whether revenue or authority concerned needs to apply its mind before power is exercised - Held, yes - Whether an order of provisional attachment cannot be as a matter of course, rather, it is one of drastic measures which authority may be compelled to take if situation demands for purpose of protecting interest of Government revenue - Held, yes - Whether to provisionally attach all bank accounts and that too those accounts in which there was hardly any balance would only cause undue hardship to assessee - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where there was hardly a balance of Rs. 22 thousand in two bank accounts of applicant which had been provisionally attached, impugned order of provisional attachment of said two bank accounts was to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes [Paras 29, 43, 49 and 51]GST : An order of provisional attachment under GST is to be passed after proper application of mind, and cannot be a matter of course

Provisional attachment of bank accounts - Principal Additional Director General merely stated that powers conferred on concerned official under section 83 was invoked for provisionally attaching bank accounts of petitioner in order to protect interest of revenue - However, order did not show any basis for formation of opinion that provisional attachment was necessary to safeguard revenue's interest - No tangible material was disclosed - Order breached mandatory pre-conditions for exercise of powers under section 83 ibid [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 9, 10 and12] [In favour of assessee]GST : Order of provisional attachment of bank accounts of assessee was not sustainable as it was passed without disclosing any specific reason based on tangible material available with revenue

II Section 83 of the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery -  Provisional attachment - Whether on facts under heading 'Demands and recovery - Determination of tax' since nothing was demonstrated by department either in orders of attachment or in affidavit filed as to why exercise of such drastic power of attachment of bank accounts was necessary, provisional attachment of assessee's bank accounts was to be removed - Held, yes [Paras 16  17] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached on ground of alleged tax evasion - Petitioner contended that he had purchased goods from seller which had valid GST registration and that GST was paid at time of purchase - Request was made to authority to release bank account; however, same was not released - HELD : To protect interest of revenue, bank account was attached because petitioner did not have any freehold property and there was nothing which petitioner could have offered - On ground that ITC was availed on basis bogus and fake invoices issued by seller, summon was issued to petitioner to give statements and to produce documents - Power under section 83 is serious and harsh in nature, it should not be used as a tool to harass assessee nor should be used in any manner that it may have irresistible detrimental effect on business - Authority must ensure that action should not affect business activities of taxable person - Bank was to be directed not to permit petitioner to operate account to extent of tax amount and release attachment on furnishing of bond for balance amount - [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para's 8, 9, 9.3, 9.4 and 11] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars  Notifications : Circular No. CBEC - 20/16/05/2021 - GST/359

Attachment - Bank account - Renewal of attachment - Period of attachment having expired, department renewed attachment of bank account - Petitioners contended that there was no provision or jurisdiction with department to once again attach an account after expiry of attachment period - Petitioners also brought to notice department's Circular dated 2-9-2023 which prescribes time-frame for initiation and conclusion of proceedings - HELD : In view of Circular dated 2-9-2023, attachment of bank account was to be lifted [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Punjab Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where petitioners contended that there was no provision or jurisdiction with department to once again attach an account after expiry of attachment period, in view of Circular No. GST/INV/PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT/ADVISORY/2023-24, DATED 2-9-2023 prescribing time-frame for initiation and conclusion of proceedings, attachment of bank account was to be lifted

Attachment - Bank account - Renewal of attachment - Period of attachment having expired, department renewed attachment of bank account - Petitioners contended that there was no provision or jurisdiction with department to once again attach an account after expiry of attachment period - Petitioners also brought to notice department's Circular dated 2-9-2023 which prescribes time-frame for initiation and conclusion of proceedings - HELD : In view of Circular dated 2-9-2023, attachment of bank account was to be lifted [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Punjab Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]   CIRCULARS AND NOTIFICATIONS: Circular No. GST/INV/Provisional Attachment/Advisory/2023-24, Dated 2-9-2023

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Where period of one year has expired after order defreezing assessee's bank account was passed, concerned bank would not interdict operations of petitioner's bank account on basis of impugned order [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where period of one year has expired after order defreezing assessee's bank account was passed, concerned bank would not interdict operations of petitioner's bank account on basis of impugned order

Provisional Attachment - Attachment of bank account - Show Cause Notice was issued against petitioner-assessee by respondent-department under Section 83 - Respondent issued attachment orders on ground that petitioner had failed to discharge tax liability without any justification, further, respondent was of opinion that there was every chance that petitioner might default in paying ultimate tax, interest and penalty, for which a demand might be raised in assessment proceedings on completion - Petitioner filed instant writ petition seeking setting aside of bank account attachment order issued by respondent - Held:Supreme Court had opined that power to order a provisional attachment [under Section 83] of property of taxable person, including a bank account, was draconian in nature and conditions which were prescribed by statute for a valid exercise of power must be strictly followed - Further, apex court had further opined that exercise of power for ordering a provisional attachment must be preceded by formation of an opinion by Commissioner that “it is necessary so to do” for purpose of protecting interest of government revenue - Expression “necessary so to do for protecting government revenue” implicates that interests of government revenue could not be protected without ordering a provisional attachment - As aforesaid order applies with full force to facts of present case, therefore, attachments in FORM GST DRC-22 dated 05.04.2024 and order passed under Section 83 also dated 05.04.2024 were to be quashed [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 159 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Paras 3-6] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where petitioner-assessee challenged provisional attachment of bank account under Section 83 and apex court held that provisional attachment of bank account could only take place if it was necessary so to do for purpose of protecting interest of government revenue, therefore, following aforesaid judgement, provisional attachment order was to be set aside

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Operation for amount in excess - Bank account of petitioner was blocked to extent of refund of input tax credited alleging mismatch in payment made to supplier in respect of goods stated to have been exported - Department further doubted whether goods were procured by supplier in question and vehicles in which goods were transported had not entered Delhi and petitioner did not have necessary space to store goods - Department further contended that goods were procured from another supplier whose registration was cancelled - Petitioner argued that bank account was blocked by issuing letter to bank without passing order - HELD: An order under section 83 had been passed by department and such order freezing bank account was to be confined to extent of Rs. 50 lakhs and petitioner was to be entitled to operate bank account and withdraw any amount in excess of credit balance of Rs. 50 lakhs [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]GST : Order of provisional attachment being passed due to alleged mismatch in ITC payment, assessee was to be permitted to operate bank account for excess amount over that required for refund of ITC

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached on ground of alleged tax evasion - Petitioner contended that he had purchased goods from seller which had valid GST registration and that GST was paid at time of purchase - Request was made to authority to release bank account; however, same was not released - HELD : To protect interest of revenue, bank account was attached because petitioner did not have any freehold property and there was nothing which petitioner could have offered - On ground that ITC was availed on basis bogus and fake invoices issued by seller, summon was issued to petitioner to give statements and to produce documents - Power under section 83 is serious and harsh in nature, it should not be used as a tool to harass assessee nor should be used in any manner that it may have irresistible detrimental effect on business - Authority must ensure that action should not affect business activities of taxable person - Bank was to be directed not to permit petitioner to operate account to extent of tax amount and release attachment on furnishing of bond for balance amount - [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para's 8, 9, 9.3, 9.4 and 11] [In favour of assessee]GST : Power on provisional attachment under section 83 of CGST Act may have irresistible detrimental effect on business and hence, provisional attachment of bank account should be partially lifted on furnishing appropriate bond amount

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Extension of attachment period - Section 83(2) provides that provisional attachment made under sub-section (1) of section 83 shall cease to have effect after expiry of a period of 'one year' from date of order made under sub-section (1) - No fresh order having being passed by revenue authority to attach bank account on expiry of one year from date of provisional attachment of bank account, mere noting in file of concerned Officer could not constitute an order without a formal order as law may mandate being passed and most importantly such order being communicated to affected person, whose bank account is attached [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]GST : On expiry of one year from date of provisional attachment of bank account, no fresh order having being passed by Revenue Authority, mere noting in file of concerned Officer could not constitute an order for extension of attachment period  GST : For purposes of exercising power of provisional attachment under section 83, read with section 122(1A), of CGST Act, Commissioner would have a power to take action against any person, even if such a person is outside his jurisdiction

Provisional Attachment - Bank account - Every provisional attachment order shall cease to have effect after expiry of one year from date order had been passed under section 83(1) - After a year, Authority should defreeze assessee's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 5 and 8] [In favour of assessee]GST : Bank account of assessee provisionally attached under section 87 of CGST Act should be defreezed after expiry of a year

Provisional Attachment - Attachment of bank account - Show Cause Notice was issued against petitioner-assessee by respondent-department under Section 83 - Respondent issued attachment orders on ground that petitioner had failed to discharge tax liability without any justification, further, respondent was of opinion that there was every chance that petitioner might default in paying ultimate tax, interest and penalty, for which a demand might be raised in assessment proceedings on completion - Petitioner filed instant writ petition seeking setting aside of bank account attachment order issued by respondent - Held:Supreme Court had opined that power to order a provisional attachment [under Section 83] of property of taxable person, including a bank account, was draconian in nature and conditions which were prescribed by statute for a valid exercise of power must be strictly followed - Further, apex court had further opined that exercise of power for ordering a provisional attachment must be preceded by formation of an opinion by Commissioner that “it is necessary so to do” for purpose of protecting interest of government revenue - Expression “necessary so to do for protecting government revenue” implicates that interests of government revenue could not be protected without ordering a provisional attachment - As aforesaid order applies with full force to facts of present case, therefore, attachments in FORM GST DRC-22 dated 05.04.2024 and order passed under Section 83 also dated 05.04.2024 were to be quashed [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Rule 159 of Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017] [Paras 3-6] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment  -  Bank account- Lifting of attachment - limitation period - Petitioner ran footwear shop at Paramakudi - Business stood in spouse name - Petitioner maintained savings bank account with third respondent bank - First respondent issued provisional attachment under Section 83 attaching bank account, pursuant to which bank froze account - Petitioner challenged attachment contending that under Section 83(2) such attachment ceased after one year - Respondent did not dispute factual matrix - HELD : Statutory limitation in Section 83(2) mandated cessation of provisional attachment after one year - Continued freezing beyond prescribed period was impermissible - Impugned attachment was set aside and petitioner was permitted to operate account [Section  83  of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 10 to 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Adjudicating Authority by an order dated 9-2-2021 provisionally attached eleven bank accounts of assessee - Assessee approached High Court for interim directions for lifting provisional attachment so that subject bank accounts could become operable and petitioner-company was not only able to pay salaries and other dues concerning its employees but was also able to pay amounts claimed by department - Whether assessee was to be permitted to collect from bank accounts a sum of Rs. 2 crores to pay salaries of employees and balance amount available in bank accounts will be deposited with department - Held, yes [Para 3.3] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where Adjudicating Authority provisionally attached eleven bank account of assessee, assessee was to be permitted to collect from bank accounts Rs. 2 crores to pay salaries of employees and balance amount available in bank accounts will be deposited with department
