Provisional attachment - Bank account - Operation for amount in excess - Bank account of petitioner was blocked to extent of refund of input tax credited alleging mismatch in payment made to supplier in respect of goods stated to have been exported - Department further doubted whether goods were procured by supplier in question and vehicles in which goods were transported had not entered Delhi and petitioner did not have necessary space to store goods - Department further contended that goods were procured from another supplier whose registration was cancelled - Petitioner argued that bank account was blocked by issuing letter to bank without passing order - HELD: An order under section 83 had been passed by department and such order freezing bank account was to be confined to extent of Rs. 50 lakhs and petitioner was to be entitled to operate bank account and withdraw any amount in excess of credit balance of Rs. 50 lakhs [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Validity of - Competent Authority by an order passed under section 83 provisionally attached bank account of assessee - Assessee contended before High Court that no proceedings were pending against it under section 62 or 63 or 64 or 67 or 73 or 74 and hence jurisdictional fact for issuance of order of provisional attachment being non-existent, impugned order was ultra vires section 83 - HELD : Revenue had not disputed that no proceedings under section 62 or 63 or 64 or 67 or 73 or 74 had yet been initiated against assessee - Impugned order of provisional attachment required to be set aside with direction to Competent Authority to defreeze bank account of assessee immediately [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 4 and 5] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where Competent Authority provisionally attached bank account of assessee but no proceedings under section 62 or 63 or 64 or 67 or 73 or 74 had yet been initiated, impugned order required to be set aside

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority, under section 83, passed an order attaching bank of assessee and blocking credit available in electronic ledger - Whether section 83 empowers provisional attachment of property, subject to pendency of proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 or 74 Act; same does not contemplate, provisional attachment pending any proceeding - Held, yes - Whether order of attachment of bank account of assessee was prima facie without any authority of law - Held, yes - Whether there is no provision of law which empowers respondent authorities to block credit available in credit ledger of assessee - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]GST : Section 83 empowers provisional attachment of property, subject to pendency of proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 or 74 Act; same does not contemplate, provisional attachment pending any proceeding

Provisional attachment  -  Bank account- Lifting of attachment - Petitioner challenged provisional attachment of its bank accounts under Section 83 - DRC-22 recorded that Section 74 proceedings had been launched and froze PAN-linked accounts - A writ was filed before High Court - HELD: Section 83 applies only to protect revenue on a reasoned opinion based on tangible material - This draconian power requires cogent reasons - letters contain only a bald assertion of Section 74 proceedings, with no specific grounds - In fact, no proceedings under Section 74 were initiated - attachments are perverse, arbitrary and without basis in law - Provisional attachment notices dated 23 July 2025 are quashed and release directed within 48 hours, liberty to proceed afresh [Section  83,  read with section  74,  of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 7 to 11] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where by consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached, last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where by consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached, last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where by consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached, last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Current account and Cash credit account - Communication in Form DRC-22 was addressed by Principal Commissioner to Bank Manager directing that proceedings had been lodged against petitioner under section 83 of CGST Act and, therefore, current account of petitioner was to be provisionally attached - Petitioner submitted that by virtue of attachment of account, apart from debit transfers all accounts were debit freezed - Not only current account, but in fact cash credit account was also provisionally attached - On writ, HELD : On more than one occasion, Court had deprecated practice of respondent authorities in seeking to enforce tax liabilities by provisionally attaching cash credit account - Notice was issued to respondent/s - Till returnable date, there would be ad-interim relief [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 5, 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]GST : Revenue authority's practice of enforcing tax liabilities by provisionally attaching cash credit account, should be deprecated

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - By consecutive orders bank account of petitioner was provisionally attached - Last attachment order being passed over a year ago, bank should not interdict operation of petitioner's bank account [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Where period of one year has expired after order defreezing assessee's bank account was passed, concerned bank would not interdict operations of petitioner's bank account on basis of impugned order [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/section 83 of the Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Assessee filed instant petition contending that since no proceedings were pending against it, impugned order passed by revenue authority attaching its bank account was not sustainable - During course of hearing, assessee submitted that it had a credit balance of more than Rs. 1 crore in its bank account and that an appropriate amount therefrom could be retained as a security to safeguard interest of revenue - Whether, since entire disputed amount as of now was being secured by assessee, it was appropriate to direct respondent no. 3 to retain Rs. 45 lakhs from bank account in question as a security and thereupon provisionally lift debit freeze instructions in respect of said attached account of assessee - Held, yes [Para 9]GST : Where an order attaching bank account of assessee was passed in order to safeguard interest of revenue, it was appropriate to direct revenue to retain a part of amount lying in said account as security and thereupon provisionally lift debit freeze instructions in respect of bank account in question

Provisional attachment- Renewal/Revival of attachment - Assessee was subjected to provisional attachment under section 83 for 4th time - Assessee challenged same vide instant petition relying on judgement of supreme court in Kesari Nandan Mobile v. Asstt. CST [2025] 177 taxmann.com 481 (SC) - HELD: Supreme Court in Kesari Nandan (supra) clearly held that when statute does not provide for an extension, renewal, reissuance, revival, same cannot be done by authorities and such an action would amount executive overreaching statute - In light of same, impugned order attaching bank account of assessee was to be quashed and set aside - Authorities were to be directed to immediately de-freeze bank account of assessee [Section  83  of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Uttar Pradesh Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Haryana Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority having found during investigation that assessee had purchased scrap batteries from 16 suppliers, who were not traceable, and had availed input tax credit amounting to Rs. 13.38 cores on basis of invoices of 16 suppliers provisionally attached over cash credit account of assessee maintained with a bank - In said account assessee had debit balance - Assessee filed writ petition seeking relief in this regard - Whether the mandate of Section 83 is to attach amount lying in an account in the form of FDR or saving and it cannot be intention or purport of section 83 to attach an account having debit balance - Held, yes - Whether attachment of over cash credit account of assessee in teeth of intent and purpose of section 83 was bad - Held, yes - Whether impugned order of attachment deserved to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes - Whether GST Authorities were to be directed that they would proceed against assessee in accordance with judgment of Punjab and Haryana High Court rendered in case of Akhil Krishan Maggu v. Deputy Director, Directore General of GST Intelligence [2019] 111 taxmann.com 367 - Held, yes [Paras 10 to 12] [In favour of assessee]GST : The mandate of Section 83 is to attach amount lying in an account in the form of FDR or saving and it cannot be intention or purport of section 83 to attach an account having debit balance

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Petitioner, proprietor of a firm, received an attachment order evidencing that his bank account had been frozen at instance of GST authorities and despite his repeated requests, no information was disclosed by authority concerned as to why GST authority exercised such powers - However, it was found that no proceedings were pending against petitioner under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74 - Whether therefore, order provisionally attaching bank account of petitioner was without jurisdiction and was liable to be quashed and set aside; attachment was to be lifted and petitioner was to be permitted to operate his bank account - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 16]GST : Where no proceedings were pending against petitioner under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74, order provisionally attaching bank account of petitioner being without jurisdiction was to be lifted and petitioner was to be permitted to operate his bank account

Provisional Attachment of bank account - Recovery of excess ITC availed - Bank account of petitioner-assessee was attached at behest of department without any notice to them though proceedings initiated against excess availment of Input Tax Credit that was allegedly utilized for payment of tax, was still pending - Since no specific representation was made before concerned Departmental Authority for release of blocked funds in bank account of assessee, they should make a fresh representation to said authority who would consider same on merits as per law and would not attach funds lying in their other bank accounts till any final order that would be passed on such representation [Section 83, read with section 79, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 2 and 3, 6 to 9] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where bank account of assessee was attached at behest of Department without any notice to them, assessee should make a representation to departmental Authority who would consider same on merits as per law

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Kerala State Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority invoking powers under section 83 provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee - Supreme Court in case of Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2021] 127 taxmann.com 26 had occasion to consider exercise of powers under section 83 and after elaborate consideration laid down manner and mode in which powers are to be exercised and none of stipulations specified in above judgment were evident in order impugned and there was non application of mind to purport of power exercisable by Competent Authority under section 83, impugned order required to be stayed for a period of eight weeks - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where Competent Authority invoking powers under section 83 provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee, without application of mind and stipulations specified by Apex Court, impugned order required to be stayed

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 /Section 83 of the Maharashtra Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority vide order dated 6-12-2019 directed Bank Manager of assessee, where assessee held a bank account, not to allow any debt - Assessee filed writ petition seeking relief in this regard - It submitted that though impugned order did not refer to any provision of law, power for provisionally attaching bank account is under section 83 - Assessee further submitted that there were no proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74 against it as mentioned under section 83, which was necessary if attachment under section 83 was to be levied - Whether in view of judgment of Bombay High Court rendered in case of Kaish Impex Pvt. Ltd. v. UOI [Writ Petition No. 3145 of 2019, dated 20-1-2020]; wherein facts were identical to that of instant case, impugned order passed by Competent Authority attaching bank account of assessee deserved to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]GST : Where Competent Authority vide order dated 6-12-2019 directed Bank Manager of assessee not to allow any debt, since there were no proceedings under sections 62, 63, 64, 67, 73 and 74 against assessee, impugned order attaching bank account of assessee deserved to be set aside

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demands and recovery - Provisional attachment - Competent Authority vide order dated 24-8-2020 passed under section 83 provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee - He stated that in order to protect interests of revenue bank accounts were attached - Whether a bare perusal of order of provisional attachment would indicate that same was nothing but a result of mechanical exercise of power under section 83 - Held, yes - Whether attachment of bank accounts of assessee was ordered to be removed - Held, yes [Paras 3, 4 and 15][In favour of assessee]GST : Where Competent Authority vide order passed under section 83 provisionally attached bank accounts of assessee stating that in order to protect interests of revenue bank accounts were attached, impugned order was nothing but a result of mechanical exercise of power under section 83 and it was not sustainable in law

Provisional attachment - Cash credit account - Department contended that some of documents of petitioner were fake and hence input tax credit should be disallowed and penalty for same should be imposed - Notice was issued to bank of petitioner to provisionally attach cash-credit facility of firm - Petitioner contended that cash credit facility is not debt to be attached under section 83 of CGST Act, 2017 - Petitioner also contended that section 83 can be invoked only in certain circumstances for protecting interest of Government revenue - Department argued that since it was found from record that petitioner was paying GST from said cash credit account, in interest of revenue, they had provisionally attached said account - HELD: Cash credit facility is not a debt and, hence, cannot be attached - Provisions give adequate powers to petitioner to file objection for releasing bank account and hence Court cannot relief under writ jurisdiction [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/West Bengal Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 15 to 17] [In favour of assessee]GST : Cash credit facility is not a debt and, hence, cash credit account cannot be attached

Provisional attachment -  Scope of - Provisional attachment ceases to have effect after one year from order under section 83(1) of CGST Act, 2017 - Where no fresh attachment order had been issued, bank account was to be defreezed and to immovable properties were to be released [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]GST : Provisional attachment ceases to have effect after one year from order under section 83(1) of CGST Act, 2017

Provisional Attachment of bank account - Recovery of excess ITC availed - Bank account of petitioner-assessee was attached at behest of department without any notice to them though proceedings initiated against excess availment of Input Tax Credit that was allegedly utilized for payment of tax, was still pending - Since no specific representation was made before concerned Departmental Authority for release of blocked funds in bank account of assessee, they should make a fresh representation to said authority who would consider same on merits as per law and would not attach funds lying in their other bank accounts till any final order that would be passed on such representation [Section 83, read with section 79, of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 2 and 3, 6 to 9] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Bank account - Current account and Cash credit account - Communication in Form DRC-22 was addressed by Principal Commissioner to Bank Manager directing that proceedings had been lodged against petitioner under section 83 of CGST Act and, therefore, current account of petitioner was to be provisionally attached - Petitioner submitted that by virtue of attachment of account, apart from debit transfers all accounts were debit freezed - Not only current account, but in fact cash credit account was also provisionally attached - On writ, HELD : On more than one occasion, Court had deprecated practice of respondent authorities in seeking to enforce tax liabilities by provisionally attaching cash credit account - Notice was issued to respondent/s - Till returnable date, there would be ad-interim relief [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 5, 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment  -  Bank account- Lifting of attachment - Period 2024-25 - In exercise of powers under section 83, order of provisional attachment of one business bank account and one savings bank account was passed - One year period had expired since then - It was urged by assessee that in terms of section 83(2), provisional attachment had ceased to operate after expiry of one year from date of order of provisional attachment - HELD : Order of provisional attachment had ceased to operate after expiry of one year from date of order of provisional attachment in relation to business bank account which was referred in impugned order - So far as savings bank account was concerned, it was never directed to be attached under section 83 - From record, no justifiable material was found necessitating an order under section 83 attaching said savings bank account - Even if Form GST DRC-15 provides for provisional attachment of savings bank account, period of one year had also lapsed - Provisional attachment of both bank accounts was thus non-operational under provisions of section 83(2) [Section  83  of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Paras 10, 12, 13 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/ Section 83 of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Demand and recovery - Provisional attachment - Whether as per section 83, Commissioner can provisionally attach any property, including bank account, belonging to taxable person if he is of opinion that for protecting interest of Government revenue, it is necessary so to do - Held, yes - Whether however, provisional attachment would cease to have effect after expiry of a period of one year from date of order made under section 83(1) - Held, yes - Whether therefore, where order of provisional attachment of Bank Account of applicant maintained with State Bank of India had come to an end, as one year from date of order of attachment had been passed, applicant was to be permitted to operate his Bank Account forthwith - Held, yes [Paras 4 and 5]GST : Provisional attachment would cease to have effect after expiry of a period of one year from date of order made under section 83(1)

Provisional attachment -  Scope of - Provisional attachment ceases to have effect after one year from order under section 83(1) of CGST Act, 2017 - Where no fresh attachment order had been issued, bank account was to be defreezed and to immovable properties were to be released [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Delhi Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Provisional attachment - Cash credit account - Petitioner contended that cash credit account could not be provisionally attached as same dehors provision of section 83 of CGST Act, 2017 - Since attachment of cash credit account, not being property of taxpayer, order of provisional attachment of cash credit account of petitioner was to be quashed and setaside [Section 83 of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017] [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]GST : Cash credit account could not be provisionally attached as same dehors provision of section 83 of CGST Act, 2017  GST : Overlooking of settled position of law by Principal Commissioner was prima facie, contempt of court

facts.text:
The Competent Authority of the Gujarat Goods and Services Tax Department had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the petitioner under section 83.

On writ:

The Competent Authority provisionally attached under section 83 bank account of the assessee on the ground that it had created bogus records and claimed input tax credit for discharging the GST dues of about Rs. 121 crores.

The assessee, on writ petition filed before the High Court, contended that in terms of section 67 there could not be any attachment of future receivables so as to strangulate its entire business module and the recovery proceedings initiated by the department was contrary to the provisions of the GST Act.

The writ Court held that a sum of Rs. 5.68 crores, which was lying in the bank account of the assessee, was appropriated by the department and the assessee had also agreed to pay another sum of Rs. 1 crore against the estimated tax due of about Rs. 21 crores. The payment of Rs. 5.68 crores would amount to discharge of 27.05 per cent of the estimated tax dues. Therefore, there was no meaning in attaching the bank account further. It directed the assessee to deposit a sum of Rs. 1 crore within one week and on such deposit the attachment order was to be vacated. It also directed the Competent Authority to complete the investigation and issue appropriate show-cause notice as expeditiously as possible.

On writ appeal:

The Competent Authority, exercising under section 83, had attached the bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking relief in this regard.

The assessee filed instant writ petition challenging the order passed under section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 whereby the various bank accounts of the assessee were provisionally attached. However, no further orders were passed for recovering any dues. It was submitted by the department that the inquiries had revealed that the assessee was a non-existing person and had not cooperated in the investigation and hence order of provisional attachment was justified.

The applicant was a proprietor of a proprietary concern engaged in the business of trading of ferrous and non-ferrous metal scrap. It held a valid registration certificate under the provisions of the CGST Act and the GGST Act respectively.

A spot visit was carried out by the flying squad of the revenue department at the premises of the applicant. The department was prima facie of the view that the purchases made by the applicant from the JSK and UM were not genuine. In the course of the search carried out by the department, the registers, documents and books of account for the period between 1-7-2017 and 11-8-2020 were collected and taken into possession.

The Additional Commissioner passed an order under section 83 of provisional attachment of cash credit/current bank account and one savings bank account held by the applicant with the HDFC Bank Ltd.

Being dissatisfied with the order of provisional attachment, the applicant filed the instant writ-application.

■

Petitioners had issued cheques to respondent towards a payment. Meanwhile, the Commissioner of the CGST issued a communication to the bank and petitioner’s bank account was provisionally attached by the CGST Department under section 83 of the CGST Act, 2017, thereby prohibiting any debit transactions.

■

This order effectively froze the account and restricted all transactions. The same was confirmed by the bank’s letter, stating that a “STOP” had been marked on the account pursuant to the CGST attachment order and that no transactions could be permitted until further instructions were received from the department.

■

The petitioners duly informed the respondent of this attachment and requested that the cheques be not presented until the account was de-freezed.

■

Despite this, the respondent presented the cheques for encashment, leading to their dishonour and filed complaint under section 138 against the petitioners.

■

The petitioners filed petition seeking quashing of the summons and the consequential proceedings arising out of complaint case on ground that they informed the respondent about the attachment of their bank account by the CGST Department under section 83 of the CGST Act, 2017, as soon as it occurred. They contend that the cheques were issued with a mutual understanding that they would not be presented without prior intimation and consent. Despite this, the respondent presented the cheques for encashment, leading to their dishonour.

The Competent Authority had provisionally attached the assessee's bank account by passing order under section 83.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to de-freeze/withdraw restrictions placed on operations of bank account.

Subsequently the assessee sought leave to withdraw the petition with liberty to file objections in terms of sub-rule (2) of rule 159.

The Competent Authority for recovery of GST dues had provisionally attached various bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to release all bank accounts.

The assessee received a summons under section 70 of the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 from the authorities, directing the assessee to submit copy of GST payment along with other necessary details. The assessee appeared before the authority and submitted all necessary documents in response to the said summons. Thereafter another summons was issued which was replied by assessee. On the basis of reply furnished by assessee, the authority instructed the assessee to submit further documents, specific reasons and details as to why the input tax credit was wrongly claimed.

Subsequently, the proceedings were also initiated and a tax liability of certain amount was presumed by the authority since the assessee had claimed wrongful input tax credit and as such, with a view to safeguard the interest of revenue, by resorting to section 83 of the Act, the bank accounts were sought to be provisionally attached.

Instant writ petition was filed challenging the order of provisional attachment on the ground of violation of principles of natural justice. It was submitted by the assessee that to recover any amount of tax, interest and penalty, firstly, the assessment should be framed, and secondly, the demand notice should be issued and no conditions were fulfilled before attaching the bank account under section 83 of the CGST Act.

On the other hand, it was submitted by the department that the proceedings were already initiated under section 74 of Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 and to protect the interest of revenue, the bank account of assessee were attached by passing an order under section 83 of the Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017. Further, the subjective satisfaction which had been arrived at by an authority could not be requested to be set at naught in extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court in the absence of any mala fide in the petition. Such discretion of an authority could not be usurped by the Court under article 226 of the Constitution of India.

The Competent Authority passed orders under section 83 of provisional attachment of goods and two bank accounts of the assessee.

On writ:

The Competent Authority had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee under section 83 on the allegation that it without physical receipt of goods availed credit on basis of the invoices issued by the input supplier and thereafter paid GST on the basis of the output invoices without physical supply of the goods to the buyers.

Against the impugned order passed by the Competent Authority, the assessee filed a writ application.

It submitted that the allegation levied against it was to the effect that although the goods were not supplied, yet the tax was paid for the purpose of passing the credit. This was suggestive of the fact that, indisputably, no GST was payable, yet the same was paid. Section 9, which is the charging section, contemplates that the GST is payable only when the goods are supplied. The statement of output liability and input credit pertinent to it would indicate that for the period between July, 2017 and May, 2019, the total input credit availed of by it aggregated to Rs. 59.49 crores; whereas the total tax paid during the said period aggregated to Rs. 63.62 crores. The same was indicative of the fact that against the availment of credit of Rs. 59.49 crores, the tax amount to the tune of Rs. 63.62 crores came to be paid. Thus Rs. 4.13 crores had been paid in excess than the amount of credit availed of. If that be so, then there was no question of arriving at the satifaction by the Competent Authority that the interest of the government revenue was protected.

It further submitted that assuming for the moment that the allegation was true and correct and the credits were wrongly availed of, still the tax had been paid though it was not liable to be paid in light of the fact that there was no supply of goods. The availment of credits could be justified on two counts: (1) it was a revenue neutral satisfaction, and (2) the payment of tax although not payable yet was to be treated as if unavailable credits were reversed after they were wrongly availed.

The Competent Authority had attached provisionally under section 83 the bank accounts of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking relief in this regard.

It contended that the ingredients stated under section 83 were not attracted. The proceedings under section 62 or 63 or 64 or 67 or 73 or 74 were not pending consideration, which was one of the ingredients for passing attachment of bank account.

The revenue, on the other hand, relied on Annexure-D dated 27-8-2018 by which the assessee was asked to produce certain documents and the assessee had furnished the documents. Further the revenue relied on Annexure-E dated 17-10-2018 issuance of summons to the witness. The revenue submitted that both Annexures-D and E would fall under section 74.

A search and seizure operation dated 28-4-2023 was conducted under section 132(1) and it was found that several persons/entities were involved in hawala transactions through bogus RTGS and cryptocurrencies. Pursuant to the said search and seizure operation and on the basis of certain suspicious transactions, the accounts of the assessees were debit frozen to avoid leakage of revenue.

The assessees by way of instant petition, sought directions to de-freeze the bank accounts and to set aside the letter dated 30-4-2023 issued by the respondents.

The assessee submitted that as per the mandate of section 132(8-A), the freezing of bank accounts ceases to have effect after the expiry of a period of sixty days. He, therefore, submitted that since the maximum period for which the bank accounts could have been frozen had already expired on 30-6-2023, there was no reason to proscribe the assessees to operate the bank accounts under consideration.

The Competent Authority, pursuant to search of the premises of the assessee under sub-section (2) of section 67, passed an order of prohibition in respect of certain properties under rule 139(4). He further, in exercise of the powers vested under section 83, provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee and also the office premises.

On writ:

Bank accounts of assessee were provisionally attached to protect revenue's interest under section 231B

Subsequently, regular assessment was framed and total tax demand was raised against assessee.

The assessee filed instant writ petition claiming that amount attached standing to his credit over and above the demand raised against him should have been released by revenue on completion of assessment.

■

The assessee filed its return of income declaring income/loss of Rs. 10.69 lakhs.

■

The Assessing Officer passed an assessment order determining the income at Rs. 41.22 crores.

■

The assessee filed an appeal against the assessment order and also filed an application praying for stay of the demand issued under section 156.

■

The Deputy Commissioner rejected the application for stay of demand and directed the assessee to deposit 20 per cent of the disputed demand.

■

Thereafter, the Principal Commissioner also rejected the application for stay of the entirety of the disputed demand and directed the assessee to make a payment of at least 20 per cent of the demand immediately.

■

Meanwhile, the Deputy Commissioner passed an order attaching the assessee''s bank account.

■

In instant writ, the assessee challenged the order of attachment and sought for a direction to de-freeze the bank account.

The petitioner was engaged in the Business to Business ('B2B') e-commerce trading in 'white goods' including mobile handsets. The respondent No. 2 (Additional Director General of GST Intelligence) was conducting certain investigation in respect of Pal Overseas, a registered entity under the GST Act and also as regards other entities relating to the alleged issuance of bogus/fake invoices without supply of goods and were seeking to claim Input Tax Credit of Goods and Services Tax. It is stated that the petitioner was purchasing the mobile handsets from these suppliers and was selling to its customers. The respondent No. 2 conducted a search at the Head Office of the petitioner. During the search, the respondent No. 2 issued summons to the Associate Director of the petitioner Company and had recorded their statements.

The said representatives of petitioner Company responded to the notice, appeared before the Authorities and also made their statements, which had been duly recorded.

On 21-9-2020, the respondent No. 2 sought details of the bank accounts of the petitioner which were provided on the same day. It is stated that the respondent No. 2 attached the bank accounts of the petitioner purportedly in exercise of power under section 83.

The petitioner made representation in terms of rule 159(5) seeking release of attachment and defreezing of bank accounts, but such request was neither considered nor any order was passed as required under the applicable Rules.

On writ Petition:

The petitioner company carried on its business transactions through the current account registered with bank. On 5-6- 2018, the Additional Director General, Directorate General of Goods & Services Tax Intelligence (ADGGI) passed an Order to provisionally attach the current account of the petitioner maintained in the said bank under Section 83 of the CGST Act, 2017. The said first Order of the ADGGI was addressed to the Branch Manager of the said bank in order to freeze the functioning of the said account of the petitioners.

The said bank through a letter dated 11-6- 2018, informed the writ petitioner about the Order passed by the ADGGI which directed the bank to freeze the current account of the petitioners.

On 19-7- 2019, the said company by way of a letter made representation before the ADGGI, requesting to de-freeze the current account of the company which was earlier provisionally attached under Section 83. On 31-7-2019, the petitioner company wrote to the said bank praying for immediate de-freezing of the said account.

Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the inaction on the part of the respondents the writ petitioner preferred a writ application before the Court. . Thereafter, on 31-10- 2019, the Principal Additional Director General, Directorate General of Goods & Services Tax Intelligence (PDDGI) passed a fresh provisional order directing the said bank to provisionally attach the said current account of the petitioner.

The writ petitioners filed instant writ petition aggrieved by the orders passed by the Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence [DGGI], to provisionally attach the current bank accounts of the writ petitioner under Section 83.

The assessee-company had certain credits in the form of input tax credit as on 30-6-2017.

Under the GST Act there is a provision to pay tax either by cash or by way of credits which were available to the credit of a dealer as on 30-6-2017.

The Competent Authority called upon the assessee to pay interest amounting to Rs. 1.64 crores towards delay in payment of GST for seven months from July, 2017 to Jaunary, 2018 and thereafter issued a communication dated 3-5-2019 for attachment of bank account of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition praying to quash the impugned communication dated 3-5-2019 as illegal, arbitrary and violative of principle of natural justice. It stated that when it became liable to pay GST from July, 2017, it choose to pay the tax by way of input tax credit which stood to its credit as on 30-6-2017, but could not pay GST solely owing to technical glitch in department's portal.

The Competent Authority for recovery of Rs. 3 crore from the assessee had provisionally attached its six bank accounts.

The assessee filed a writ petition stating that it had a large amount of cash lying at its disposal with the concerned banks.

The Competent Authority, exercising under section 83, had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee.

The High Court, on writ petition filed by the assessee, by a judgment and order dated 20-12-2018 had set aside the impugned order of attachment and directed the Competent Authority to forthwith release the bank accounts of the assessee.

Despite the aforesaid position, the Competent Authority, by order dated 8-3-2019, once again had provisionally attached the very same bank accounts by an identical worded order.

The petitioner was the proprietor of the Firm running in the name and style of Global Corporation. He was involved in voluminous transactions of several parties and followed the law while conducting his business.

He received an attachment order and realized from the Office of the Principal Commissioner of Central GST, Mumbai that the Central Bank of India on 20-8-2020 freezed his current account with the Rajkot Main Branch and since then, he had not been allowed to operate the account.

The petitioner approached the Bank through its Manager and requested to let him be provided the necessary details for the reason of freezing his account. However, despite his repeated requests, no information was disclosed by the authority concerned as to why the GST authority exercised such powers. He was orally conveyed that because of voluminous transactions with the third party, which was involved in violation of the provisions of the CGST Act, his account has been frozen.

He moved an application under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The Reply received from the bank revealed that the information sought for could not be revealed on account of the fact that same would impede the process of investigation.

On Writ Petition before the High Court:

The Competent Authority, by an order dated 22-10-2018 passed under section 83, had provisionally attached the three bank accounts of the assessee.

The High Court, on writ petition filed by the assessee, by a judgment and order dated 20-12-2018 had set aside the impugned order of attachment and directed the Competent Authority to forthwith release the bank accounts.

Despite the aforesaid position, the Competent Authority, by order dated 8-3-2019, once again had provisionally attached the very same bank accounts by an identical worded order.

The Competent Authority had initiated some proceedings against the assessee under the provisions of Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and attached his saving bank account provisionally.

The assessee filed a writ petition seeking directions to the Competent Authority to dispose of the representation dated 18-6-2019 sent by him and duly received by the Competent Authority on 27-6-2019.

The Assistant Commissioner directed the assessee's bankers to freeze the assessee's accounts with them.

On writ:

The Competent Authority vide two separate orders dated 27-4-2021 provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee under section 83.

The assessee objected to the orders of provisional attachment by its representations dated 7-5-2021 and 17-5-2021 and sought for revocation thereof on diverse grounds.

The Competent Authority passed an order dated 21-5-2021, whereby objection raised to the orders of provisional attachment had been overruled and the prayer for revoking the said orders rejected.

On writ:

The Assessing Authority conducted a search at the business premises of the assessee, a proprietorship concern, and on the basis of the material found calculated the cumulative liability of the old concerns of assessee under the VAT Act on presumptive basis at Rs. 4.50 crores.

Thereupon the assessee offered its immovable property of Rs. 5 crores as security in order to avoid dispute till completion of the assessment proceedings.

However, the Commissioner by an order passed under section 45 provisionally attached the above immovable property of the assessee. He also provisionally attached the bank accounts of the assessee. He further issued garnishee notice under section 44 directing the bank of the assessee to make payment from the bank account of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition praying the High Court to quash and set aside the impugned order of provisional attachment of the bank accounts and garnishee notice.

Upon a search carried out against the assessee company, the Goods and Service Tax Authorities allegedly found that the assessee was engaged huge ITC fraud through fake purchases for 5 years.

The provisional attachment order dated 26-7-2021 invoking powers under section 83 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 was passed against the assessee. The provisional attachment order covered the properties as well as the bank accounts of the assessee. The said orders became the subject matter of challenge.

Prior to expiry date of 25-7-2022, the competent authority passed another provisional attachment order for second time on 8-7-2022.

In the instant writ petition before the Court, the second provisional attachment order was challenged.

A search action under section 132 was conducted upon a group case to which the assessee belonged. During search evidences indicating generation of unaccounted income to tune of certain amount was found. The department proceeded to provisionally attach assets of huge amount including bank deposits of the assessee.

The assessee filed a writ petition before the high court seeking lifting attachment of her bank deposits contending that the assessee had not been subjected to search, therefore, there was no justification for provisional attachment of her assets. The court granted permission to the assessee to operate her bank accounts.

On instant writ appeal to the high court the department contended that the case was directed to be listed by high court immediately after admission and order of lifting of provisional attachment was passed and that the revenue was not granted reasonable opportunity to put forth the facts in the form of counter affidavit. It further contended that the scope of provisional attachment under section 132(9B) was wide and should not be construed to be limited to searched persons alone and it would include any other persons to whom seized material might relate.

■

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. The seized amount was produced before the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court. On application by the Department under section 132A, the Court directed release of the amount to the Department. The Court directed release of the cash to them on furnishing a bond for the amount. The amount was accordingly released.

■

Upon investigation and being satisfied that there was no explanation for the cash nor was it accounted, and after recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under section 148. Finding that the expected demand on assessment including penalty would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores, the payment of which the assessees would evade, the competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessees under section 281B.

■

The Single Judge held that bank account was not a 'property' under section 281B, which could be subjected to provisional attachment and that the interest of the revenue stood secured by the security furnished before the Judicial First Class Magistrate's Court.

■

On writ appeal:

The Competent Authority for recovery of excise dues of Rs. 55 lakhs had provisionally attached bank accounts of the assessee.

On writ:

A search operation was conducted at the premises of the assessee-company, a wholly owned subsidiary of FCS, Taiwan. During search, several materials, digital data, books of account and documents were seized.

The Assessing Officer was of believe that the assessee was involved in various methods of tax evasion like unaccounted cash sales, purchase through shell companies etc. and thus attached the assessee's HSBC and DBS bank accounts after seeking approval from the Principal Commissioner under section 281B.

Later on, the DBS bank account was directed to be converted into fixed deposits and subsequently, the bank account of DBS Bank was released, whereas, the balance funds remained under attachment until further orders.

The assessee in instant writ petition challenged the continuing of the attachment of HSBC bank account and DBS bank accont even after a period of six months from date of order passed under section 132(9C) and contended that it had seriously jeopardized its business operation.

The Competent Authority had attached the bank accounts of the assessee-company.

On writ:

The petitioners assessee challenged the provisional attachment order made under section 281B by the respondent Commissioner attaching the two immovable properties, bank account and FD Rs. with the bank. It was submitted by the petitioner that the valuation of these two properties was Rs. 5.83 crores as per valuation of the approved valuer as against the estimated tax liability of Rs. 2.68 crores There was no justification for attaching the bank accounts and FD Rs. which very seriously affected the day to day business of the assessee. The value of aforesaid properties as per Departmental Valuer was Rs. 2.66 crores. The petitioner submitted that the attachment order was unconstitutional unlawful, ultra vires without application of mind.

A search under section 132 was conducted upon the assessee pursuant to which assessment proceedings under section 153A were initiated. During the course of said proceedings, the Deputy Commissioner had passed an order to provisionally attach the fixed deposit of the assessee by invoking section 281B.

On writ:

The petitioner was engaged in the business of manufacturing and supplying of various iron and steel products, viz., TMT bars, etc. and was paying goods and service tax in respect of the goods manufactured and supplied by it from the registered factory premises.

On 11-10-2018, the respondent- Assistant Commissioner of State Tax, visited the factory premises of the petitioner-company. During the course of such visit, he carried out comparison of the physical stocks of raw material and finished goods with the recorded quantity of the same and found that there was a stock difference, inasmuch as physical goods valued at Rs. 51,73,633 were found in excess in the factory premises when compared to the recorded quantity.

By an order of seizure dated 12-10-2018, the respondent attached the goods which according to him were found in excess on the factory premises of the petitioner.

It was the case of the petitioner that the respondent worked out the amount payable by the petitioner at Rs. 55,37,237 and thereafter on 22-10-2018, the bank accounts of the petitioner came to be attached by the first respondent.

It was the case of the petitioner that on account of seizure of its goods as well as attachment of the bank accounts, the petitioner was not in a position to carry on its day to day business and make payment of statutory dues like GST, Income tax, local taxes, etc.

The petitioner therefore, filed writ petition in High Court seeking defreezing of bank accounts and removal of attachment of goods.

■

The appellant stated that the sum of about Rs. 5 lakhs received from STC was declared under PMGKY; Form-I was filed; tax/surcharge/penalty of Rs. 2.48 lakhs was paid; and Rs. 1.25 lakhs was deposited in the interest-free PMGKY bond, leaving a balance of Rs. 1.28 lakhs with him.

■

Following notice under section 24(1) and enquiry, the Initiating Officer provisionally attached the appellant’s bank balance, investments, movable and immovable properties to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs, and also provisionally attached the Rs. 1.25 lakhs deposited in the PMGKY scheme; the matter was referred to the Adjudicating Authority.

■

The Adjudicating Authority, after hearing, set aside the attachment of immovable properties and confirmed attachment of the appellant’s bank account to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs; the reference was partly allowed.

■

In the instant appeal, the appellant argued that, considering the PMGKY payments and the bond deposit, attachment could not extend to the entire Rs. 5 lakhs and should be restricted to the balance amount; he accepted the release of immovable properties.

The Competent Authority for recovery of dues from the assessee, a private company, had provisionally attached the bank accounts of the directors.

On writ:

The Competent Authority levied the interest upon the assessee for filing the delayed Form GSTR-3B returns for the period of February and March, 2018.

The assessee filed a writ petition against the levy of interest.

During the pendency of the writ petition, the Competent Authority pursuant to an order dated 22-5-2019 had also attached the bank account of the assessee for non-payment of the interest.

A search and seizure operation was conducted by the department at the premises of the assessee pursuant to warrants of authorization dated 3-8-2005. On 4-8-2005, certain assets including jewellery, cash and fixed deposit receipts were seized and the assessee, by order passed under section 132(3), was restrained from operating its Savings Bank Accounts. Subsequently, the bank accounts of assessee were seized through withdrawal of cash by demand drafts. The assessee moved an application under section 132B(1) to department to adjust towards self-assessment tax, certain sums for assessment year 2005-06 and certain sum towards advance tax for assessment year 2006-07 from seized amount and to release the balance. The department, however, by passing order under section 132B, declined the assessee's request and stated that the amount was retained for the estimated liability. The assessee's writ was dismissed by the High Court observing that the department had taken a stand that there was estimated tax liability of approximately Rs. 10,00,000. On appeal, the assessee submitted that the factual scenario clearly showed that the authorities acted without jurisdiction in directing either to retain the amount after adjustment of the self-assessment and advance tax or also withdrawing the amount by demand drafts from the bank accounts. The revenue's case was that the money had been withdrawn in terms of 'Search and Seizure Manual, 1989', and that the adjustment that had been done was for existing liability and there was no appropriation in that sense because it could be done only after assessment was complete.

The assessee was engaged in the business of construction and sale of residential flats. It had not filed returns for the relevant assessment years.

The Commercial Tax Officer in exercise of powers under section 45 ordered provisional attachment of bank accounts of assessee for protecting interest of Government revenue

On writ:

■

During the demonetization period, a survey under section 133A of the Income-tax Act was conducted on 21-12-2021 at Axis Bank. Multiple dummy accounts controlled by two groups were found to have received large cash deposits. Statements under section 131 of the Income-tax Act recorded admissions that cash deposited in these dummy accounts did not belong to them and was used to convert demonetized currency and was deposited by into the Green Traders account and, on his instruction, was transferred through RTGS to the appellant.

■

Based on the material, the IO initiated action under section 24(1) of the PBPT Act, recorded reasons to believe in writing, and issued a show cause notice. The IO analyzed sworn statements and bank statements, treated Green Traders as benamidar and the appellant as beneficial owner, and passed a provisional attachment order with a reference to the Adjudicating Authority.

■

The Adjudicating Authority, by order dated 29- 12-2023 under section 26(3), confirmed the provisional attachment and answered the reference.

■

On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the appellant contended that the section 24(1) notice was invalid for lack of recorded or conveyed reasons; that the Initiating Officer acted solely on borrowed information from the Income Tax Department; that sum received via RTGS was consideration for earth-filling work at Bhavnagar and the appellant was unaware of the proprietor of Green Traders; and that there was no evidence linking the appellant to depositing cash in Green Traders’ account.

■

The Initiating Officer issued notice and made a provisional attachment under section 24(3) of bank accounts with Andhra Bank standing in the appellant’s name.

■

Thereafter, while passing an order under section 24(4)(a)(i), attachment was made to a different property, namely a bank account with Axis Bank of one P.

■

The Adjudicating Authority confirmed the Provisional Attachment Order.

■

On appeal to the Appellate Tribunal :

The assessee was a dealer in electrical components. On 2-8-2012 the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) inspected the assessee's business premises in terms of section 65 and noticed various defects and discrepancies in its account books. Thereupon he forcibly collected a cheque for an amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs from the assessee towards tax due on the alleged defects.

The assessee made a representation before the Assessing Authority concerned, wherein all the defects noticed had been explained and he had been requested to withhold the cheque amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs which was forcibly collected by the Commercial Tax Officer (Enforcement) at the time of inspection.

Thereafter the Assessing Authority having found that the department's bank had returned the above cheque unrealised issued a notice to the bank of assessee attaching its bank account for the recovery of the amount of Rs. 3.75 lakhs.

On writ:

■

The petitioners were farmers and were doing agricultural activities.They had sold agricultural goods out of the produce from the joint holding land with their uncle KBG and out of the sale proceedings, certain amount was deposited in the joint account of the petitioners with their uncle KBG. When the petititioner approached the Bank for withdrawal of the said amount, they were informed that there was attachment over the joint account for outstanding of their uncle by the Income Tax Department.

■

The petitioners had challenged the issuance of notice under section 226(3) whereby the authority had made attachment over the account.

■

Before commencement of CIRP, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Gautam Budh Nagar, under the Uttar Pradesh Revenue Code, 2006, initiated recovery proceedings for Rs. 9.39 crores (plus interest) towards RERA-related dues and, by letter dated 17.07.2023, directed attachment of all bank accounts of the Corporate Debtor. CIRP commenced on 09.08.2024. The Resolution Professional identified a bank account with Kotak Mahindra Bank (Respondent No.1) and, on 04.09.2024, requested change of authorised signatory and disclosure of all accounts.

■

The Bank confirmed on 24.09.2024 that the Resolution Professional had been recorded as authorised signatory, but on 23.10.2024 informed that the account had been placed under debit freeze and a lien marked to the extent of Rs. 9.39 crores (plus interest) pursuant to the 17.07.2023 attachment order. Despite being informed by the Resolution Professional about the Section 14 moratorium and being requested to remove the freeze, the freeze was not lifted.

■

Before the National Company Law Tribunal, the Resolution Professional sought de-freezing/removal of lien on the said account; the Bank responded that it had no independent claim and that the freeze was imposed and maintained strictly in compliance with the pre-CIRP statutory attachment order unless modified, stayed, or set aside by a competent forum.

Out of the amounts standing in the bank accounts of the petitioners in respect of which prohibitory orders had been issued, the Income-tax Department withdrew a major portion of the same from the bank by two pay orders.

On writ, the petitioners challenged the withdrawal on the ground of having been made without any authority of law as also the attachment and continuance of attachment of their accounts by the department:

■

The appellant filed an appeal under section 46(2) challenging the order passed under section 26(3), whereby attachment of her bank account to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs was confirmed while the immovable properties were released. The case arose from deposits of demonetized currency in the bank account of STC and transfer of Rs. 5 lakhs therefrom to the appellant’s account. The appellant admitted that the cash belonged to her and had been handed over for deposit in the bank account of STC and was thereafter retransferred through banking channels.The appellant further stated that out of Rs. 5 lakhs, she had paid Rs. 2.47 lakhs as tax, surcharge and penalty under PMGKY and deposited Rs. 1.25 lakhs in the interest-free PMGKY bond scheme, leaving a balance of Rs. 1.27 lakhs with her.

■

After enquiry, the Initiating Officer provisionally attached the appellant’s bank account and PMGKY bond deposit.

■

The Adjudicating Authority, while releasing the immovable properties, confirmed attachment of the bank account to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The Assessing Officer had attached two bank accounts of the assessee, i.e., pension account and other account.

The assessee preferred a writ petition for issuance of a direction to the Assessing Officer to lift the attachment of his bank accounts.

The Single Judge of the High Court by an order directed the Assessing Officer to lift the order of atttachment insofar as the pension of the assessee was concerned and made it clear that only the pension that was credited by the pension authority shall be allowed to be withdrawn. He further remanded back the matter to the Appellate Commissioner with a direction to dispose of the assessee's appeals within a period of three months.

On writ appeal:

■

The appellant filed an appeal under section 46(2) challenging the order passed under section 26(3), whereby attachment of her bank account to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs was confirmed while the immovable properties were released. The case arose from deposits of demonetized currency in the bank account of STC and transfer of Rs. 5 lakhs therefrom to the appellant’s account. The appellant admitted that the cash belonged to her and had been handed over for deposit in the bank account of STC and was thereafter retransferred through banking channels.The appellant further stated that out of Rs. 5 lakhs, she had paid Rs. 2.47 lakhs as tax, surcharge and penalty under PMGKY and deposited Rs. 1.25 lakhs in the interest-free PMGKY bond scheme, leaving a balance of about Rs. 1.27 lakhs with her.
