The section does not provide for any opportunity of being heard to the assessee before the guarantee is invoked. In this connection the observations of the Supreme Court in Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 300 ITR 403/169 Taxman 328 are apposite :

"If the statute conferring the power is silent with regard to the giving of a pre-decisional hearing to the person affected and the administrative decision taken by the authority involves civil consequences of a grave nature, and no full review or appeal on merits against that decision is provided, courts will be extremely reluctant to construe such a statute as excluding the duty of affording even a minimal hearing, shorn of all its formal trappings and dilatory features at the pre-decisional stage, unless, viewed pragmatically, it would paralyse the administrative process or frustrate the need for utmost promptitude. In short, this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands. The court must make every effort to salvage this cardinal rule to the maximum extent possible, with situational modifications. But, the core of it must, however, remain, namely, that the person affected must have reasonable opportunity of being heard and the hearing must be a genuine hearing and not an empty public relations exercise." (p. 666).

It is a moot point whether the aforesaid observations would be applicable before the invocation of the guarantee.

11.5-7 Direct acceptance of guarantee is not possible

The section envisages the situation where the assets are first attached and then a guarantee is accepted in lieu of the assets attached. It does not envisage a situation of acceptance of bank guarantee at the first stage itself without attachment of assets.

Section 281B empowers the Assessing Officer to make a provisional attachment of any property of the assessee during the pendency of any proceeding for the assessment or reassessment of any income, even though there is no demand outstanding against the assessee, if he is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so to protect the interests of the revenue. The order of provisional attachment will be made only after obtaining the approval of the Chief Commissioner or Commissioner or Director General or Director. This provision has been made in order to protect the interests of the revenue in cases where the raising of demand is likely to take time because of investigations and there is apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand. In other words, this section gives a power to be exercised during the pendency of any proceedings for assessment or reassessment, so that the assessee did not fritter away or secrete his resources out of the reach of the department when the assessment or reassessment is completed. The expression ‘for the purpose of protecting the interests of the revenue’ occurring in section 281B of the Act is very wide in its meaning. For that reason as a safeguard, prior approval of a higher authority like Chief Commissioner, Commissioner, Director General or Director, has been made a necessary condition. Further, the orders of provisional attachment must be in writing. However, there must be some material on record to show that the Assessing Officer has formed an opinion on the basis whereof it is necessary to attach the property in order to protect the interests of the revenue. The provisional attachment provided under section 281B is more like an attachment before judgment under the Code of Civil Procedure. It is a liability on the property. The Delhi High Court in Dar International v. Asstt. Director of Income- tax [1993] 114 CTR (Delhi) 172 has opined that the provision relating to making an attachment before judgment, i.e., before assessment order is made, is not illegal if the assessing authority is of the opinion that it is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue and the same is supported by supervening factors. However, the power conferred upon the Assessing Officer under section 281B is very drastic far-reaching power and that power has to be used sparingly and only on substantive weighty grounds and reasons. To ensure that this power is not misused, a number of safeguards have been provided in the section itself. One thing is clear that this power should be exercised by the Assessing Officer only if there is a reasonable apprehension that the assessee may default the ultimate collection of the demand that is likely to be raised on completion of the assessment. It should, therefore, be exercised with extreme care and caution. It should not be exercised unless there is sufficient material on record to justify the satisfaction that the assessee is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property with a view to thwarting the ultimate collection of the demand. Moreover, attachment should be made of the properties and to the extent it is required to achieve the above object. It should neither be used as a tool to harass the assessee nor should it be used in a manner which may have an irreversible detrimental effect on the business of the assessee. The Bombay High Court in Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 has opined that attachment should be made, as far as possible, of immovable properties if that can protect the revenue. Attachment of bank accounts and trading assets should be resorted to only as a last resort. In any event, attachment under section 281B should not be equated with attachment in the course of recovery proceedings.

In the premise of the above noted principles and having regard to the facts of this case, the question that arose for consideration was whether the second respondent had exercised the power conferred upon him under section 281B irrationally and without any justification. The facts stated in the counter affidavit of the second respondent and the correctness of which was not denied by the petitioner-assessee spoke for themselves and justified the drastic action taken by the second respondent by passing impugned orders under section 281B to protect the interest of the revenue. It was relevant to note that, according to the second respondent, the petitioner-assessee had so far received about Rs. 50.70 lakhs as donations of which only Rs. 20 lakhs was under attachment. Further, as could be seen from the impugned orders, it was open for the petitioner to operate its bank account except to the extent of balance as of that date and in that regard a communication dated 29-5-2001 was also sent to the concerned bank by the second respondent. Therefore, the assumption of the petitioner-assessee that the impugned order militated against its functioning and its charitable activities was not well founded.

However, the ITA 2025 has expanded the provision to include any person in possession of information related to specified assets.

17.5-5 Impracticable seizure of bank lockers and bank accounts [Section 247(4) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(3) of the ITA 1961)] While Section 132(1) of the ITA 1961 grants the power to seize money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable articles, Section 132(3) comes into play where it is not practicable to seize such assets. The Kerala High Court, in the case of ITO v. M. Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

17.5-6 Examination on oath of any other person present in the premises, etc. [Section 247(6) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(4) of the ITA 1961)]

Under the ITA 1961, the authorised officer could examine on oath only any person found to be in possession or control of any books of account, other documents, etc.

However, under the ITA 2025, the said authorised officer may also examine on oath any other person who—

(a)

Possesses or controls any information in electronic form or on a computer system

(b)

Has access to such a computer system

(c)

Is present in the premises; or

(d)

Is being searched.

In support of this amendment, the Ministry stated before the Select Committee that "During search, situations arise where a person though not possessing any books or other documents but is in the know of the business intricacies or is a key person managing business e.g. accountant, machine operator in the manufacturing industry, gatekeepers who are maintaining exit records, quality control persons who have complete production information and so on. Statements of such persons also become extremely important. Therefore, practically, these statements are relevant to conduct investigations. It is relevant to note that such statements are taken during the course of the search and at the premises being searched. Thus, the amendment has been rightly made to rationalise the provision."

A bare perusal of section 281B would show that two conditions are necessary for invoking it. Firstly, the existence of ‘opinion’ of the Assessing Officer that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue it is necessary to provisionally attach any property belonging to the assessee; and secondly, the previous approval of the higher authority concerned has been obtained before passing any order. Section 281B gives very wide power to the Assessing Officer enabling him to provisionally attach any property belonging to the assessee with the previous approval of the Commissioner if the Assessing Officer is of the opinion that for the purpose of protecting the interest of the revenue it is necessary to do so. [Para 8]

The Delhi High Court in the case of V.L.S. Finance Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 246 ITR 707/ 112 Taxman 295 has held that opinion means something more than mere retaining of ‘gossip’ or ‘hearsay’, it means the judgment of belief that is a belief or conviction resulting from what one thinks on a particular question. [Para 9]

So far as the question of opinion of the Assessing Officer was concerned, it was found that it was lacking in the instant case. The counter-affidavit sworn by ITO did not disclose any material on which requisite opinion to invoke the power under section 281 B could be formed. Only this much had been stated that FDRs valuing Rs. 44 lakhs were found. The nature and source of acquisition of those FDRs were required to be examined. The case of the assessee was that the aforesaid amount represented share application money received by the company. After filing of the counter-affidavit two more affidavits were also filed on behalf of the department. But in none of those affidavits any material or relevant circumstance had been mentioned on the basis of which it could be said that the assessee would not fulfil its obligation, namely, payment of demand of any tax which would be levied on it subsequently. Documents and account books, etc., seized by the officers of the Central Excise Department did not belong to the assessee-company nor did they relate to the business activities of the assessee-company. There was not a whisper even in any of the counter-affidavits that those documents belonged to the assessee. Such an averment was absent in the pleading of the department. The documents, thus, seized by the Central Excise Department and also requisitioned by the Income-tax Department did not relate to the business activities of either of the assessees. As a matter of fact, the enquiries on the basis of those documents were directed by the department against certain persons other than the assessees. [Para 10]

It is also settled that the powers vested with any authority under various provisions of law can be exercised only for the stated purpose and not for any other purpose. [Para 14]

Section 132(1)(c) permits search to be undertaken by the department if there is reason to believe that a person is in possession 'of any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing and such money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article or thing represents either wholly or partly income or property which has not been, or would not be, disclosed' for the purposes of the Act, referred to as 'the undisclosed income or property'. For the purposes of the instant petitions, the emphasis would be on the expression 'any money' and 'other valuable article or thing' as appearing in section 132(1). The context in which these words occur cannot possibly exclude money in a bank account. The contention that this could only mean 'cash' and not money in a bank account may be an attractive argument but not in the context in which the above expression occurs. It is certainly a valuable thing. In other words, a sum in a bank account is not outside the ambit of section 132(1) and can be subject to search and seizure. [Para 53]

Thus, a person could be in possession of undisclosed income not only in his or her own account but in someone else's account. In the context of the instant petitions, therefore, when pursuant to the search warrant, the department proceeded to search and seize not only valuable things etc. found in the premises of 'M' but also those in the accounts of the 8 petitioner companies as well as that of VS who was actively involved in the day to day management of various companies controlled by 'M' and worked closely with him, they could do so as long as they were satisfied that what constitutes M's undisclosed income was in the accounts of the 8 companies and VS. [Para 54]

The second proviso to section 132(1) read with section 132(3) permits the department to require the bank in which the account that is subject to search is located to freeze it since it may not be possible 'to take physical possession' immediately of such 'valuable article or thing and remove it to a safe place.' Section 132B deals with the powers of the authorised officer to deal with the valuable thing which has been so seized and the conditions on which the restraint placed may be lifted. [Para 55]

The assertion by petitioners that this is realization of the debt owed by the bank to the petitioners and that the amount therein cannot be transferred to the department is based on an incorrect understanding of the legal position under section 281B. The said provision states that in order to protect the interests of the revenue, it may be necessary to go in for a provisional attachment. Therefore, the direction issued to RBL by the department does not mean that the money is finally taken over by the revenue. It will undoubtedly be kept in a suspense account like a PD Account to await the final orders in the assessment proceedings and the issues raised as a consequence thereof. For this purpose, the argument that this does not constitute 'assets' or 'money' within the meaning of section 132(1) read with section 133 has not merit. [Para 57]

For the aforementioned reasons, both the petitions are dismissed. [Para 60]

In the case of S.K. Modi v. Union of India 2002 (144) ELT 59 (Delhi), the Hon’ble High Court had held that the principles of natural justice have to be complied with before order of attachment against petitioner could be passed.

u The Commissioner would then pass the orders for or against the attachment of the property after considering the submission of the assessee.

u The circular provides certain offences which may be considered for provisional attachment of property. Among others, offences like evasion of tax, short payment of service tax, claiming fraudulent refund or Cenvat credit, etc., have been mentioned.

u The circular also mentions that no proceedings under the Attachment Rules would be initiated in the cases where the service tax or Cenvat credit alleged is less than Rs. 25 Lakhs.

u On receipt of such orders, the Central Excise Officer would proceed with the provisional attachment of the property. It has been specifically mentioned that personal property of the assessee/partners/directors could not be provisionally attached. However, the circular provides that the immovable property used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached. Thus, if the property is being commercially used (whatever purpose) and not necessarily for the provision of services only, the same could be attached. Thus, in case the service provider has rented out his house or he is carrying on his business from the said property, the Central Excise Officer is free to attach the said property under the Attachment Rules as the same are being commercially used.

u The attachment of the immovable property (where available) must precede the attachment of any movable property. Also, the value of property attached must correspond as nearly as possible to the amount of pending revenue against the assessee. The valuation of properties like land, gold and securities would always be a matter of dispute since their values variate over a period of time.

u The assessee whose property has been provisionally attached should not cause to transfer the title or create a lien of a third party over such property. Having said this, it is important to mention that as is the case in Excise and Customs, in service tax also the secured creditor is entitled to preference over claim of revenue. The same has been upheld in the matter of UTI Bank Ltd. v. Dy. CCE [W.P. No. 39536 of 2005, dated 20-12-2006]. However, contrary to this, the circular provides that in case of provisional attachment, any debts, claims, etc., against the provisional attachment would be void. Thus, on a harmonious reading of both the provisions, it can be construed that any mortgage or any other charge created after the provisional attachment of the property would only be void against such provisional attachment.

u The circular also provides that the provisional attachment should not hamper the business of the assessee. Also, properties as is exempted by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, would also be exempt from provisional attachment under the Attachment Rules.

u Last but not the least, the property remains provisionally attached for a period of six months from the date of service of notice. Post which, an extension must be given for such attachment by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise (‘Chief Commissioner’). However, the total period of extension by the Chief Commissioner cannot exceed two years.

u The Attachment Rules provide for automatic release of the attached property if the assessee pays the dues with interest.

Thus, though the Attachment Rules empower the Central Excise Officer in relation to provisional attachment of property of an assessee, yet these provisions are not arbitrary and subjective. These provisions must be used only to safeguard the interest of the revenue and are to be enforced in a manner which is rational and not based on mere surmises or suspicion. The Circular has clearly spelt out that with more powers (to Central Excise Officer) comes more responsibility.

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY UNDER SERVICE TAX

Section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994 provides for provisional attachment of property belonging to service tax defaulters. The attachment is required to be done in the prescribed manner, the rules in relation to which were long overdue, since the section had come into force with effect from April 18, 2006. Recently, a new set of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 have been notified in this regard, which prescribe minimum and have left maximum gaps which will require CBEC’s instructions from time to time. The author, in this article, elaborates on the procedure of provisional attachment as per the Rules and CBEC’s instructions, in the form of FAQs.

Introduction

1. Attachment of property has been long-considered as an effective tool in ensuring better tax compliance. It ensures recovery of revenue from the department’s point of view and also acts as a strong deterrent for tax offenders. With the increasing gamut of service tax, the necessity for a provision for attachment of property was being long-felt. Accordingly, the Finance Act, 2006 inserted a new section 73C in the Finance Act, 1994, empowering and enabling the department to attach the assessee’s property in case of default. The provision though came into force with effect from April 18, 2006, the manner for effecting attachment remained to be prescribed. Accordingly, the provision remained virtually defunct since then. Recently, the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 have been notified vide Notification No. 30/2008-ST, dated August 1, 2008, which have come into force with effect from July 1, 2008. With the notification of these Rules, the provisions of section 73C have come into full force equipping the department with an effective tool against tax defaulters and ensuring better tax compliance.

Some FAQs

2. The provisions of section 73C and the new Provisional Attachment of Property Rules have emanated several issues which need a serious and thoughtful look. These have been elaborated in the form of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) as under :

(i) When can the provisions of attachment invoked ? - In terms of section 73C(1), the provisional attachment of property can be resorted to when:

(a )any proceeding under section 73 or section 73A is pending disposal, and

(b )the Central Excise Officer (i.e., the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise or the Commissioner of Central Excise) considers it necessary for the purpose of protecting the interests of revenue.

It is pertinent to note that proceedings under section 73 and 73A refer to-

(a )Recovery of service tax not levied or paid or short-levied or short-paid or erroneously refunded, and

(b )Deposit of service tax collected in excess of the amount assessed or determined.

Thus, proceedings for provisional attachment can be initiated only after issue of show-cause notice under section 73 or 73A.

As per the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provisional attachment of property may be invoked when any of the following offences is committed by a service provider or an exporter—

(a )Provision of a taxable service without the cover of an invoice or any other document, as prescribed, and without payment of tax;

(b )Provision of a taxable service without declaring the correct value for payment of service tax, where a portion of value of taxable service, in excess of invoice price, is received by him or on his behalf but not accounted for in the books of account;

(c )Taking of CENVAT credit without the receipt of goods or services specified in the document based on which the said credit has been taken;

(d )Taking of CENVAT credit on invoices or other documents which a person has reasons to believe as not genuine;

(e )Issue of service tax invoice or any other document, without providing or to be providing a taxable service, as specified in the said invoice or other document;

(f )Claiming of refund or rebate in a fraudulent manner such as on invoice or other documents which a person has reason to believe as not genuine.

The above acts/omissions shall entail proceedings under section 73 or 73A which may be followed by attachment of property under section 73C.

11. The new section 73C empowers a Central Excise Officer to provisionally attach the property during the pendency of recovery proceedings with prior permission of the Commissioner. The property may either be movable or immovable. The implication of the same is that the assessee cannot dispose of or mortgage or otherwise transfer the property.

Section 73C(2) provides that a provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of six months though it may be extended up to 2 years by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise.

This amendment is a departure from the liberal approach, which was practised so far. On the one hand, the Government wants to promote voluntary compliance, on the other hand, it seeks to enact the law of provisional attachment even before the completion of adjudication proceedings. The only silver lining is that the order of attachment has to be approved by highest authorities i.e., Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, as the case may be. Similar provisions are already there in other legislation e.g. section 281B of Income-tax Act, 1961. One only hopes that such provisions will be used sparingly and in extreme cases.

5-3 Undisclosed income or property under the Black Money Act also included [Section 247(1)(b) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(1)(c) of the ITA 1961)]

Under the ITA 1961, only the undisclosed income or property of the person which had not been disclosed or would not be disclosed under the Income-tax Act was sufficient to authorise officers to exercise the powers relating to search and seizure. However, under the ITA 2025, in addition to the above, the undisclosed income or property of such person which has not been, or would not be, disclosed under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, is also covered. And in this case also, the competent authorities can authorise the relevant subordinate officers to exercise the search and seizure powers enumerated in the law.

17.5-4 Information in relation to any asset in possession of any person [Section 247(1)(b) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(1)(c) of the ITA 1961)]

Under the ITA 1961, if any person was in possession of certain specified assets, and such assets represented, either wholly or partly, income or property which had not been disclosed for the purposes of the ITA 1961, then only the competent authorities could authorise the relevant subordinate authorities to exercise the search and seizure powers enumerated in the law.

However, the ITA 2025 has expanded the provision to include any person in possession of information related to specified assets.

17.5-5 Impracticable seizure of bank lockers and bank accounts [Section 247(4) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(3) of the ITA 1961)]

While Section 132(1) of the ITA 1961 grants the power to seize money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable articles, Section 132(3) comes into play where it is not practicable to seize such assets. The Kerala High Court, in the case of ITO v. M. Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

Section 281B relates to provisional attachment to protect revenue in certain cases. Khan [2000] 113 Taxman 568 (Guj.)]. Communication of reasons recorded for retention of books/documents - It is true that section 132(8) does not in terms provide that the Commissioner's approval or the recorded reasons on which it might be based should be communicated to the concerned person but since the person concerned is bound to be materially prejudiced in the enforcement of his right to have such books and documents returned to him by being kept ignorant about the factum of fulfilment of either of the conditions, it is obligatory upon the revenue to communicate the Commissioner's approval as also the recorded reasons to the person concerned. In the absence of such communication, the Commissioner's decision according his approval will not become effective [CIT v. Oriental Rubber Works [1983] 15 Taxman 51 (SC)].

Approval must be obtained before expiry of time-limit - Section 132(8) does not in terms empower the Commissioner to give ex post facto approval. Once the retention has become invalid, it cannot be validated by a subsequent grant of approval by the Commissioner [Hanuman Pershad Ganeriwala v. Director of Inspection [1974] 93 ITR 419 (Delhi); Sampatlal & Sons v. CIT [1984] 16 Taxman 144 (MP)].

The recording of reasons by the ITO for retention of books beyond the period of 180 (now 30) days and approval by the Commissioner of the same should take place before the expiry of 180 (now 30) days [Metal Fittings (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [1983] 14 Taxman 261 (Delhi)]. There cannot be a gap of a single day because section 132(8) only allows extension of time and not a fresh retention [Survir Enterprises v. CIT [1985] 22 Taxman 516 (Delhi)].

Retention of books/documents beyond specified period - Where, pursuant to search conducted in case of assessee u/s 132, title deeds were seized by ITOs and except statement filed that PCIT approved continued retention of books of account and other documents from time-to-time, there was nothing produced to substantiate that orders were issued permitting continued retention; retention of documents beyond 30 days of assessment order was not justified and revenue was to be directed to release title documents of assessee as expeditiously as possible [Udaya Sounds v. PCIT [2022] 138 taxmann.com 415/287 Taxman 251 (Ker.)].

Books can be returned pursuant to assessee's undertaking - The object of retention of books is not to penalise the assessee or to confiscate the books for ever. Where an undertaking had been obtained from the assessee-petitioner to the effect that as and when the department required the records they would be made available to it, a Single Judge would be justified in ordering the return of the books to the petitioner [Director of Inspection v. K. C. A. & Co. [1987] 32 Taxman 495 (J&K)].

Time-limit for handing over books/documents to jurisdictional AO - Period set out u/s 132(9A) is a measure to enable respective parties to adhere to process in an orderly fashion facilitating completion of assessment in time. Cash and bank balance are treated as movable property/asset. Property under section 2(26) of PBPT Act, 1988 means asset of any kind, whether movable or immovable and proceeds of a such property. It is our common knowledge that on many occasions cash forms part of the proceeds of a benami property which gets deposited in bank. In such a situation, depending on the origin of cash and intention behind such a transaction, the balance in the bank account represented by proceeds of a benami property could form benami property. In other words, if the bank balance has a nexus with the proceeds of a benami property, it can partake the character of benami property subject to benami transaction. There may a case where there is no bank balance except leaving a very small balance and there is no trace of utilization of cash withdrawn. Action can be taken to attach the small amount of cash balance in the bank and then other consequences would follow. There is no monetary limit to initiate benami proceeding.

3.1 Section 54 of Model GST Law provides that the tax officer shall proceed to recover the GST Demand by one or more of the modes mentioned below:

3.1.1 Adjust the GST Demand from any money owing to the taxpayer.

3.1.2 Detain and sell any goods belonging to or under the control of the taxpayer.

3.1.3 Garnishee proceedings. 3.1.4 Distrain any moveable or immovable property of the taxable person, and detain the same until the amount payable is paid; and in case, any part of the said amount payable or of the cost of the distress or of keeping of the property, remains unpaid for 30 days next after any such distress, the tax officer may cause the said property to be sold (before resorting to such mode, the tax officer is required to seek authorization from the competent authority).

3.1.5 Prepare a Recovery Certificate specifying the amount due and send it to the concerned district Collector in respect of the tax payer. The Collector shall then proceed to recover the amount specified there under from the tax payer as if it were an arrear of land revenue.

3.1.6 File an application to the appropriate Magistrate, who shall then proceed to recover the amount specified thereunder from the taxpayer as if it were a fine imposed by him.

(Author's remarks: To avoid causing any undue hardships on the tax payers, the Legislature should clearly spell out the sequence in which the aforesaid recovery modes are to be resorted to by the tax officers.)

3.2 Where the terms of any bond or any instrument executed by the tax payer provide that any amount due thereunder may be recovered in the aforesaid manner, such amount may, without prejudice to any other mode of recovery, be recovered in accordance with the aforesaid manner.

3.3 The Model GST Law also provides that the tax officers of the SGST3 or CGST4, during the course of recovery of their tax arrears, may also recover the amount(s) payable by the tax payer to the Central Government or State Government respectively.

3.4 Other provisions relating to tax recovery:

3.4.1 In terms of section 55, if a tax payer makes an application to either extend the time for payment or allow payment of any amount due (other than the amount due as per the liability self-assessed in any return) in monthly instalments (not exceeding 24), the jurisdictional Commissioner/Chief Commissioner may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, allow to do so subject to payment of interest with such restrictions and conditions as may be prescribed. Default in payment of any one instalment on its due date would result in the whole outstanding balance payable on such date becoming due and becoming payable forthwith and liable for recovery.

3.4.2 Section 56 of Model GST Law treats the transfer of property to be void in certain cases. In essence, this is similar to the section 281 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and provides that where a tax payer, after any tax has become due from him, (i) creates a charge on or (ii) parts with his property by way of sale, mortgage, exchange or any other mode of transfer in favour of any other person with the intention of defrauding the government revenue, such charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any amount(s) payable by such tax payer. However, this provision shall not affect any such charge or transfer if it is made (i) for adequate consideration and without notice of the pendency of proceedings against/ amount(s) payable by the taxpayer, or (ii) with the previous permission of the tax officer (popularly known as a No-Objection Certificate or NOC).

[Author's remarks: This section deals with cases of charge/transfer created on property(ies) post any tax has become due from the tax payer. The words 'with the intention of defrauding the government revenue' used in the section indicate that to treat any transfer of property as void, the obligation is on the tax officers to prove the fraudulent intention on the part of the taxpayer.]

3.4.3 In terms of the section 57 of Model GST Law, the GST Demand payable by a taxpayer shall be a first charge on the property of such taxpayer.

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY - PROVISIONS AND ANALYSIS

The Government vide Notification No. 30/2008, dated July 1, 2008 prescribed the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 (Attachment Rules). In this short but informative write-up, the author discusses the new Provisional Attachment of Property Rules under service tax, its fine prints and procedure. The author also discusses the powers given to the revenue along with the safeguards provided to the assessee under the new rules.

Introduction

1. The Government vide Notification No. 30/2008, dated July 1, 2008 prescribed the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 (‘Attachment Rules’). The rules were long pending since 2006 post introduction of section 73C in the Finance Act, 1994 (‘Act’) which provides for provisional attachment of property of a person during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 and section 73A of the Act.

The Attachment Rules are being seen as a tool of pressure creation in the hands of the department by the assessee and the issue of provisional attachment had been a matter of debate at the time of introduction of section 73C of the Act. However, it must be appreciated that these Rules contain provisions which provide cover to the innocent/genuine assessee from the wrath of provisional attachment of property.

Provisions of Attachment Rules & their implications

2. The Attachment Rules along with Circular No. F. No. 137/120/2006-CX4 (‘Circular’) provide the pre-conditions for the provisional attachment and the procedure thereof. The provisions provided in the whole scheme along with their implications are as follows :—

u The Attachment Rules are applicable with effect from July 1, 2008.

u The provisional attachment under the Attachment Rules can be enforced only during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 or 73A. Thus, a show- cause notice must have been served on the person under sections 73 and 73A first and then only Attachment Rules can be enforced. It must be noted that no attachment of property can be made by the revenue during the audit or enquiry stage.

u The Central Excise Officer need to forward a formal proposal to the Commissioner of Central Excise (‘Commissioner’) in the prescribed format wherein along with other factual details, the Central Excise Officer need to specify the reasons for provisional attachment of property and its value. There is a specific column provided in the format which requires the Central Excise Officer to list previous offences of the assessee. Thus, on a rational basis, it can be said that, in case of no previous offence scenario, the assessee could find favour with the revenue authority.

u The circular clearly provides that the provisional attachment is not a matter of wish of the Central Excise Officer but there should be sufficient justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. The circular based upon the recommendations of the 27th Report of the Standing Committee on Finance (Fourteenth Lok Sabha), provides for disciplinary action against the Central Excise Officer who uses his discretion in an illogical manner without sound reasons.

u The circular provides that normally, the proposal for provisional attachment must be forwarded within one month of the issue of show-cause notice. It has been upheld by the Hon’ble High Court in the case of Ani Elastic Industries v. Union of India 2008 (222) ELT 340 (Guj.), that where a power is conferred by a statute without mentioning the period within which it could be invoked, the same has to be done within a reasonable period, as all powers must be exercised reasonably and exercise of same within a reasonable period would be a facet of reasonableness. Accordingly, the proposal for provisional attachment must be issued within reasonable time and preferably before one month of issue of show-cause notice.

u The Commissioner after being satisfied that the proposal is fit for initiating actions of provisional attachment or even on his own motion, would cause service of a notice on the assessee for provisional attachment. It is pertinent to note that mere issuance of a notice is not a satisfactory performance and the notice must be served on the person for provisional attachment. The notice would provide the name, description, etc., of the property proposed to be attached provisionally and would also make a mention that till the disposal of the proceedings of provisional attachment, the assessee or his authorized agent should not cause the transfer of title or debase the title of such property.

procedure is to be adopted for the purpose :—

(i) Issue of Show-Cause Notice (SCN) - The proceedings for provisional attachment can be initiated only where SCN has been issued under section 73 or section 73A. In other words, the department cannot proceed to attach the property of the defaulter provisionally as and when it wishes to take action. The circular prescribes that normally, the proposal for attachment should be forwarded within one month’s period of the issue of SCN. (ii)Approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise: It is a prerequisite to seek approval of jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise, if at all, the Central Excise Officer 6 forms an opinion that it is necessary to attach the property of the noticee for protecting the interests of revenue. In order to seek approval, the concerned officer is required to prepare a proposal in the prescribed format 7. The same is to be forwarded to the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise for his approval. Thus, the Central Excise Officer cannot on his own proceed to attach the property.

Note : Where the proceedings under section 73/73A are pending before the Commissioner of Central Excise himself, he is empowered to make the order of attachment in accordance with the set procedure without seeking any further approval.

(iii) Giving of Opportunity for making submissions - On receipt of the proposal of attachment, the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise, or where he is acting on his own, and if he is satisfied that circumstances of the case justify provisional attachment, he may serve a notice on the person on whom a SCN is already served under section 73 or 73 A of the Act. The purpose of serving the present notice is to give the person concerned an opportunity to make submissions, in writing or in person or both, as to why the property belonging to him, and as may be specified in the notice, be not provisionally attached. According to the circular, the said notice should also specify the condition that the noticee should not sell, transfer, mortgage, charge, lease or otherwise alienate or encumber the property specified in the notice, till the decision of the said notice. In case of proposal for provisional attachment of immovable property, the notice should also be sent to the concerned registration authorities with a direction not to allow any sale, transfer, mortgage, etc., of the property.

Note : The person on whom the notice is served by the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise for provisional attachment of property is required to make submissions within fifteen days of serving of the notice.

(iv) Granting of Approval - Based on the materials placed before him, and after hearing the person concerned, the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise may grant approval to the provisional attachment of the property, within fifteen days of holding of personal hearing.

(v) Attachment of property - On receipt of approval from the Commissioner, the Central Excise Officer before whom the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending, may, by order in writing, proceed to attach the said property. Where proceedings are pending before the Commissioner himself and he has formed the opinion to attach the property, he shall order the attachment of the property, within fifteen days of holding of personal hearing.

Note : A copy of the order of provisional attachment should be served by the Central Excise Officer in the same manner as prescribed under section 37C of the Central Excise Act, 1944, as made applicable to service tax vide section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994.

(vi) Timing of Attachment - In terms of the circular, the provisional attachment of the property of the concerned person by arrest or distrain shall be made after sunrise and before sunset and not otherwise.

(vii) Inventory - The circular instructs that after provisional attachment of the property, the Central Excise Officer shall prepare an inventory of the property attached. He shall specify in the inventory the place where the property attached is lodged or kept and shall hand over a copy of the same to defaulter or the person from whose charge the property is distrained.

(viii) Attachment of property jointly held - In this respect, the Circular states that where the property to be provisionally attached consists of the share or interest of the concerned person in property belonging to him and another as co-owners, the provisional attachment shall be made by a notice to the concerned person prohibiting him from transferring the share or interest or charging it in any way.

In Dinesh Chand Surana v. Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax on 2 July, 2018, Madras High Court held that since the order passed under section 24(4) of the Act being an order of provisional attachment, the petitioner cannot be stated to have been aggrieved over such order, especially, when the adjudicating authority under the Benami Act has already initiated proceedings under section 24(4) of the Act. The person cannot be permitted to stall the adjudication proceeding under the Act.

In view of the above judicial pronouncements, it is recommended that the scope and application of Rule 86A of the CGST Rules be reviewed and clarified to prevent its use as a recovery mechanism. However, appropriate safeguards may continue to be retained to allow restriction of ITC utilisation in genuine cases involving fraud or wilful misuse of input tax credit, subject to due process and statutory limitations.

69. Powers to arrest to be applied judiciously Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, empowers authorised GST officers to arrest individuals for certain offences under the GST law. This provision is designed to prevent tax evasion and ensure compliance with the law.

The power to arrest relies solely on the Commissioner's "reason to believe" that an offence under clauses (a) to (d) of Section 132(1) has been committed. The ability to arrest based on "reason to believe" without stringent procedural checks opens the door to potential abuse and arbitrary detention.

It is recommended that the GST provisions be amended to seek specific approval from the Principal Chief Commissioner before arrests can be made. Further, the proper officers seeking approval must present written evidence justifying the arrest.

Recently, the Supreme Court expressed concerns about the ambiguity in Section 69. The Supreme Court instructed the Centre to refrain from employing "threat and coercion" tactics during search and seizure operations to recover GST from traders. It emphasised its commitment to interpreting the law in a manner that upholds individual liberties and prevents undue harassment of citizens. Thus, once implemented, these changes will address the concerns raised by the Hon'ble Supreme Court regarding the potential misuse of Section 69.

70. Offences should be mentioned explicitly

Section 132 of the CGST Act prescribes punishments for specified offences. However, certain clauses in this section raise concerns due to their broad, generic nature, which could lead to misuse and harassment.

Relevant text of the provision:

(h)

acquires possession of, or in any way concerns himself in transporting, removing, depositing, keeping, concealing, supplying, or purchasing or in any other manner deals with, any goods which he knows or has reasons to believe are liable to confiscation under this Act or the rules made thereunder;

(i)

receives or is in any way concerned with the supply of, or in any other manner deals with any supply of services which he knows or has reasons to believe are in contravention of any provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder;

(l)

attempts to commit, or abets the commission of any of the offences mentioned in [clauses (a) to (f) and clauses (h) and (i)] of this section,

These clauses are overly broad and generic. They do not require evidence of intentional tax evasion by the defaulter.

It is therefore recommended that the GST provisions be amended by removing them entirely from Section 132(1) to prevent their misuse. The GST provisions should be suitably amended so as to replace criminal liability for non-compliance with a token penalty, ensuring fairness in enforcement.

71. Malicious intent should be the basis for a penalty

The relevant text of Clause (c) of Section 132(1) of the CGST Act:

(c)

Avails input tax credit using the invoice or bill referred to in clause (b) or….

This provision penalises individuals availing input tax credit under the circumstances outlined in clause (b) of Section 132(1). It does not consider whether the individual acted with malicious intent (mens rea).

It is recommended that this clause be modified to adhere to the legal maxim "actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea," which means that an act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

Either the first part of clause (c) should be deleted entirely, or the term 'fraudulently' should be inserted at the beginning of clause (c) to limit its scope to deliberate offences. For unintentional non-compliance, the Government may consider imposing a token penalty rather than criminal liability.

72. No criminal proceedings for self-rectified defaults

Criminal proceedings under Section 132(1) of the CGST Act can be initiated even when the defaulter has voluntarily identified the default and corrected it before the proceedings are initiated.

It is therefore recommended that criminal action be restricted to cases where defaults persist when proceedings are initiated. In cases of self-rectification of defaults, the law may prescribe levying a token penalty for non-compliance instead of initiating criminal proceedings. This approach encourages proactive adherence to tax laws.

(ix) What procedure is to be followed for making an order for provisional attachment ? - As per rule 3, the following procedure shall be adopted in making provisional attachment of property :

(a )The Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise, on being satisfied that a provisional attachment is necessary in the interest of revenue, prepare a proposal in the prescribed format and forward the same to the jurisdictional Commissioner of Central Excise for his approval.

As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, normally the proposal should be forwarded within one month of the issue of show-cause notice.

In case the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending before the Commissioner of Central Excise, he himself shall initiate the attachment.

(b )The Commissioner of Central Excise may, on being satisfied, that the circumstances of the case justify provisional attachment, cause service of a notice on the person (in default). The notice shall state reasons for initiating provisional attachment and details of property to be attached.

(c )The notice shall require the person (in default) to make submissions, in writing or in person or both, within 15 days of service of the notice, as to why the property belonging to him and specified in the notice, should not be provisionally attached.

(d )The CBEC in its Circular dated July 1, 2008 has clarified that the said notice should also specify the condition that the noticee should not sell, transfer, mortgage, charge, lease or otherwise alienate or encumber the property specified in the notice, till the decision of the said notice. In case of proposal for provisional attachment of immovable property, the notice should also be sent to the concerned registration authorities with a direction not to allow any sale, transfer, mortgage, etc., of the property.

(e )After considering the materials placed before him, in writing or in person or both, by the person (in default), the Commissioner of Central Excise may grant approval to the provisional attachment of the specified property. As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, such an order should be made within 15 days of holding of personal hearing. Thereafter, the Central Excise Officer, before whom the proceedings under section 73 or 73A are pending, may order, in writing, to attach the said property.

(f )A copy of the order of provisional attachment shall be served on that person as per the provisions of section 37C of the Central Excise Act, 1944, as extended to service tax matters.

(x) For what period an order of attachment shall continue to be in effect ? - As per rule 6 of the Rules, an order of provisional attachment shall continue to be in force for a period of six months from the date of service of the order on the person in default, or till the date the entire ‘pending revenue’ along with interest thereon is paid, whichever is earlier. However, the aforesaid period of six months may be extended by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise, after recording reasons for the same in writing, for such further period(s) as he thinks fit. However, the total period of extension shall not exceed two years.

(xi) What procedure is to be followed in effecting attachment ? - Section 73C as well as the Rules, both are again silent on this issue. As per CBEC’s circular dated July 1, 2008, the following points merit consideration :

(a )The provisional attachment of the property of the concerned person by arrest or distrain shall be made after sunrise and before sunset and not otherwise.

(b )After provisional attachment of the property, the Central Excise Officer shall prepare an inventory of the property attached and specify in it the place where it is lodged or kept and shall hand over a copy of the same to defaulter or the person from whose charge the property is distrained.

(xii) Is the person whose property has been attached, obliged to exercise any restraint in respect of the said property ? - In terms of rule 5, the person whose property has been attached or his representative shall not mortgage, lease, transfer, deliver or deal with the attached property in any manner except with the previous approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise. The Rules, however, do not provide as to whether any action can be initiated if the person acts in definance of rule 5, and as to what shall be the position of the rights of the third party who deals unknowingly, with that person.

The CBEC’s circular, however, states that where a provisional attachment has been made, any private transfer or delivery of the property attached or of any debt, dividend or other moneys, contrary to such provisional attachment, shall be void as against all claims enforceable under the provisional attachment.

TAX RECOVERY

PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY UNDER SERVICE TAX PROVISIONS

ASHHOK SAXENA*

The Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 have been made effective to curtail growing tax evasion, particularly by the big service providers. Provisional attachment is to be resorted only in cases where the defaulted amount alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakhs. Being a harsh measure of extraordinary nature, it should not be applied routinely and, therefore, an elaborate procedure has been prescribed which needs to be followed before attachment of property. In this article, the modus operandi of these measures has been explained. The author is of the view that such measures though harsh, should not remain paper-measures because of the involvement of heavy-weights, but need to be implemented effectively if the interests of revenue are to be protected.

Introduction

1. Section 73C of the Finance Act, 1994 was inserted with effect from April 18, 2006 1 to provide for the provisional attachment of property. This provision was made effective with a view to protect the interests of revenue during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 2 or section 73A 3. Framing of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 4 is a step in the direction of implementing these provisions more comprehensively.

Keeping in view that the provisional attachment of property is a harsh measure directed towards the defaulting assessees, the CBEC has issued comprehensive instructions 5 so that no injustice is meted out.

Pending revenue

2. Provisional attachment of property is to be resorted to during the pendency of revenue which means the circumstances should exist where any service tax has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded and in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A. As regards justification for provisional attachment, the CBEC Circular states as under :—

"It is important to note that there should be sufficient justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The remedy of attachment being, by its very nature, extraordinary, has to be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. The grounds on which the Central Excise Officer entertains the reasonable belief that the notice would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any, should be clearly stated while seeking the approval of the Commissioner of Central Excise."

2.1 Amount alleged to be involved - There is a prescription regarding the amount of service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved for the provisional attachment of property. Presently, such amount should be more than Rs. 25 lakhs.

Offences which call for provisional attachment of property

3. The circular enumerates certain types of offences which if committed by a service provider or an exporter may be considered for provisional attachment of property. These are as under :—

uProvision of a taxable service without the cover of an invoice or any other document, as prescribed, and without payment of tax;

uProvision of a taxable service without declaring the correct value for payment of service tax, where a portion of value of taxable service, in excess of invoice price, is received by him or on his behalf but not accounted for in the books of account;

uTaking of CENVAT credit without the receipt of goods or services specified in the document based on which the said credit has been taken;

uTaking of CENVAT credit on invoices or other documents which a person has reasons to believe as not genuine;

uIssue of service tax invoice or any other document, without providing or to be providing a taxable service, as specified in the said invoice or other document;

uClaiming of refund or rebate in a fraudulent manner such as on invoice or other documents, which a person has reason to believe as not genuine.

Procedural aspects

4. An elaborate procedure is contemplated for provisional attachment of property, mainly because of the fact that such measures being extraordinary by nature, should not be resorted to as a routine. Following procedure is to be adopted for the purpose :—

(i) Issue of Show-Cause Notice (SCN) - The proceedings for provisional attachment can be initiated only where SCN has been issued under section 73 or section 73A. In other words, the department cannot proceed to attach the property of the defaulter provisionally as and when it wishes to take action. The circular prescribes that normally, the proposal for attachment should be forwarded within one month’s period of the issue of SCN.

In the course of business, various liabilities like dues to the Government and Statutory Agencies, like Sales Tax/VAT dues, etc. and now Goods and Service Tax (GST) under Central Goods and Service Tax Act, 2017 arise. The dues under GST arise as tax is collected from the recipient of supply of goods or services from the 'taxable person' ('dealer' under earlier Sales Tax/VAT laws and 'taxable person' under CGST Act, 2017) and it is the responsibility of such "taxable person" to deposit the tax collected with the Government. Section 83 empowered the Commissioner to attach the properties of the 'taxable person' to recover the dues. It is a general notion that the said dues, being the dues payable to the Government, have the priority or first right to recover from the properties of the taxable person over all other creditors' dues. This article discusses whether recovery of GST tax dues, in fact, has any priority under the law vis-a-vis other creditors.

CROWN DEBTS : It was held by the Supreme Court in the case of Dena Bankv. Bikhabhai Prabhudas Parekh & Co1 where the debts of the Government (Crown Debts) and Subjects conflict, the Debts due to Government get precedence and priority over all other debts except the Secured Creditors. The Court explained the doctrine of priority of 'Crown Debts' as under:

"What is common law doctrine of priority or precedence of crown debts? Halsbury, dealing with general rights of the crown in relation to property, states where the Crown's right and that of a subject meet at one and the same time, that of the Crown is in general preferred, the rule being "detur digniori" Herbert Brown states - "Quanta jus domini Regis et submit concurrent jus Regis preferred debt - Where the title of the king and the title of a subject concur, the king's title must be preferred. In this case detur digniori is the rule... where the titles of the king and of a subject concur, the king takes the whole... where the king's title and that of a subject concur, or are in conflict, the king's title is to be preferred" This common law doctrine of priority of State's debts has been recognised by the High Courts of India as applicable in British India before 1950 and hence the doctrine has been treated as "law in force" within the meaning of Article 372(1) of Constitution.

The principle of priority of Government debts is founded on the rule of necessity and of public policy. The basic justification for the claim for priority of state debts rests on the well recognised principle that the State is entitled to raise money by taxation because unless adequate revenue is received by the State, it would not be able to function as a sovereign government at all. It is essential that as a sovereign, the State should be able to discharge its primary governmental functions and in order to be able to discharge such functions efficiently, it must be in possession of necessary funds and this consideration emphasises the necessity and the wisdom of conceding to the State, the right to claim priority in respect of its tax dues.

However, the Crown's preferential right to recovery of debts over other creditors is confined to ordinary or unsecured creditors. The Common Law of England or the principles of equity and good conscience (as applicable to India) do not accord the Crown a preferential right for recovery of its debts over a mortgagee or pledgee of goods or a secured creditor. It is only in cases where the Crown's right and that of the subject meet at one and the same time that the Crown is in general preferred. Where the right of the subject is complete and perfect before that of the King commences, the rule does not apply, for there is no point of time at which the two rights are at conflict, nor can there be a question which of the two ought to prevail in a case where one, that of the subject has prevailed already. In Giles v. Grover 1832 131 ER 563 it has been held that the Crown has no precedence over a pledgee of goods. In Bank of Bihar v. State of Bihar and Ors. [AIR1971SC1210] , the principle has been recognised by this Court holding that the rights of the pawnee who has parted with money in favour of the pawnor on the security of the goods cannot be extinguished even by lawful seizure of goods by making money available to other creditors of the pawnor without the claim of the pawnee being first fully satisfied. Rashbehary Ghose states in Law of Mortgage - 'It seems a Government debt in India is not entitled to precedence over a prior secured debt."

Steps to secure recovery of demand in high demand cases - It has been the experience in the past that on several occasions, the Assessing Officers create huge demands against assessees without obtaining the details of any known assets of the asses¬see. With the passage of time and in the absence of such details, no concrete action gets taken to recover this demand. As a re¬sult, Department is burdened with the responsibility to recover the huge arrears existing in its records, with little possibility of actual recovery in many cases. As on 1-4-2004, the arrears increased by 20% to Rs. 87,885 crore while the objective was to reduce arrears by 20% as compared to the preceding year.

2. The Board has, therefore, decided that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakh and above in big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolka¬ta, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Pune and Bangalore and Rs. 1 lakh and above elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that the recovery, in full or in part, could become difficult, it shall be the responsibility of the Assessing Officer, during the assessment proceedings itself, to enquire into all assets of the assessee and place under provisional attachment, in terms of provisions of section 281B, before the assessment is completed, the assets sufficient to cover the demand in question (or to the maximum extent, as the case may be). After completion of the assessment, if the provisional attachment cannot be continued till recovery, the same assets can be considered for attachment, etc., under section 222/226. In each of these cases, the Assessing Officer shall mention in an Office Note to the Assessment Order in question, the efforts made to locate the assets of the assessee, the details of assets located, the details of assets placed under provisional attachment, etc.

3. In search and seizure cases, huge demands are raised under block assessment and the recovery of the same is tedious and time-consuming. In this regard, it is extremely important for Assessing Officers in Central Charges to explore the possibility of invoking the provisions of section 281B. At the time of prepa¬ration of Appraisal Report, the DDIT(Inv.)/ADIT(Inv.) should take particular care in identifying the properties of the assessees which could be attached under this section and make a specific mention of the same in the Appraisal Report itself.

4. It shall be the responsibility of all Assessing Officers to follow the above procedure. If any demand becomes irrecoverable due to the failure of the Assessing Officer to follow these guidelines, he shall be held accountable for the loss caused to the Government, regardless of his subsequent posting.

5. While making a review of scrutiny assessments, the Commission¬ers of Income-tax and Chief Commissioners of Income-tax concerned shall specifically comment on this aspect.—Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2-9-2004.

CLARIFICATION ONE

1. Attention is invited to Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2nd September, 2004, wherein the Board directed that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakhs and above in big cities and Rs. 1 lakh elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that recovery, in full or in part, would be difficult, the Assessing Officer should place assets of suitable value under provisional attachment under section 281B.

2. Since the issue of this Instruction, some apprehensions have been expressed regarding the potential for its indiscriminate use. The purpose of the Instruction was to draw attention to the statutory provision (section 281B) that has been in existence since 1975. To safeguard against any indiscriminate use, the Board desires that the provisions of section 281B should be resorted to only in cases where there is a reasonable likelihood of the recovery becoming difficult due to inadequacy of assets. Where there are sufficient assets to cover the demand, the provisions of section 281B should not be resorted to, except under exceptional circumstances warranting the same, and after strictly complying with the conditions incorporated in section 281B.—F. No. 404/22/2004-ITCC, dated 5-11-2004.

During the relevant assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) disallowed the claim of the assessee on the ground that section 54F applied only to individuals and HUF and not to a trust. On appeal, the CIT(A) allowed the assessee's claim. Aggrieved by the order, the AO preferred an appeal to the Delhi Tribunal. The Tribunal held that it was a fact that the assessee was a private trust, established for the benefit of specific individuals. The trust income is taxable if it is the income of the beneficiary; it is not the case with a charitable trust. Furthermore, a charitable trust is treated as an AOP because its beneficiary is the public at large. In fact, if the beneficiary of the charitable trust is identified, the trust loses its charitable character.

In the instant case, the trust purchased certain land, and the sale of the flat thereon, through collaboration, generated income from capital gains. Against this, a residential house was purchased, and an exemption under Section 54F was claimed. If the assessee trust were not in existence, the same transaction would have been carried out in the name of beneficiaries therein, and the benefit would certainly be given to those beneficiaries under Section 54 of the Act as claimed.

Therefore, the order passed by the CIT(A) in granting relief under Section 54F of the Act, as claimed by the assessee under the facts and circumstances, was found to be just and proper.

21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.

22. Donations received through Ketto platform transferred to personal & family account rightly taxed under Section 56(2)(x): ITAT

Ms. Rana Ayyub Shaikh v. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 174 taxmann.com 277 (Mumbai - Trib.)

The assessee, a journalist and columnist for The Washington Post newspaper, raised donations from three campaigns on the Ketto platform. The assessee withdrew the said donation in her or her family member's account. A substantial amount of donations was transferred from her father's and sister's accounts to the assessee's account.

The Assessing Officer found that despite the time spent of more than one year from the first campaign, the assessee had unutilised funds of approximately ? 2.4 crores, for which no separate accounts were maintained, making it impossible to segregate the funds used for each campaign. The account in which the assessee or her family members withdrew the money was a personal savings account. Moreover, instead of engaging in relief work, the assessee opened a new account and invested in a fixed deposit in her own name. She also incurred personal expenditure from the same savings account in which the funds were received.

Assessing Officer (AO) further held that the donations allegedly received for Covid relief were taxable as the income of the assessee under section 56(2)(x). On appeal, the CIT(A) confirmed the view of the AO. The aggrieved assessee filed the instant appeal before the Tribunal.

Existing law means any law, notification, order, rule or regulation, relating to levy and collection of duty or tax on goods or services or both passed or made before commencement of CGST Act/SGST Act by Parliament or any authority or person having power to make such law, notification, order, rule or regulation - section 2(48) of CGST Act and SGST Act.
