PROVISIONAL ATTACHMENT OF PROPERTY - PROVISIONS AND ANALYSIS

The Government vide Notification No. 30/2008, dated July 1, 2008 prescribed the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 (Attachment Rules). In this short but informative write-up, the author discusses the new Provisional Attachment of Property Rules under service tax, its fine prints and procedure. The author also discusses the powers given to the revenue along with the safeguards provided to the assessee under the new rules.

Introduction

1. The Government vide Notification No. 30/2008, dated July 1, 2008 prescribed the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008 (‘Attachment Rules’). The rules were long pending since 2006 post introduction of section 73C in the Finance Act, 1994 (‘Act’) which provides for provisional attachment of property of a person during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 and section 73A of the Act.

The Attachment Rules are being seen as a tool of pressure creation in the hands of the department by the assessee and the issue of provisional attachment had been a matter of debate at the time of introduction of section 73C of the Act. However, it must be appreciated that these Rules contain provisions which provide cover to the innocent/genuine assessee from the wrath of provisional attachment of property.

Provisions of Attachment Rules & their implications

2. The Attachment Rules along with Circular No. F. No. 137/120/2006-CX4 (‘Circular’) provide the pre-conditions for the provisional attachment and the procedure thereof. The provisions provided in the whole scheme along with their implications are as follows :—

u The Attachment Rules are applicable with effect from July 1, 2008.

u The provisional attachment under the Attachment Rules can be enforced only during the pendency of any proceedings under section 73 or 73A. Thus, a show- cause notice must have been served on the person under sections 73 and 73A first and then only Attachment Rules can be enforced. It must be noted that no attachment of property can be made by the revenue during the audit or enquiry stage.

u The Central Excise Officer need to forward a formal proposal to the Commissioner of Central Excise (‘Commissioner’) in the prescribed format wherein along with other factual details, the Central Excise Officer need to specify the reasons for provisional attachment of property and its value. There is a specific column provided in the format which requires the Central Excise Officer to list previous offences of the assessee. Thus, on a rational basis, it can be said that, in case of no previous offence scenario, the assessee could find favour with the revenue authority.

u The circular clearly provides that the provisional attachment is not a matter of wish of the Central Excise Officer but there should be sufficient justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interest of the revenue. The circular based upon the recommendations of the 27th Report of the Standing Committee on Finance (Fourteenth Lok Sabha), provides for disciplinary action against the Central Excise Officer who uses his discretion in an illogical manner without sound reasons.

u The circular provides that normally, the proposal for provisional attachment must be forwarded within one month of the issue of show-cause notice. It has been upheld by the Hon’ble High Court in the case of Ani Elastic Industries v. Union of India 2008 (222) ELT 340 (Guj.), that where a power is conferred by a statute without mentioning the period within which it could be invoked, the same has to be done within a reasonable period, as all powers must be exercised reasonably and exercise of same within a reasonable period would be a facet of reasonableness. Accordingly, the proposal for provisional attachment must be issued within reasonable time and preferably before one month of issue of show-cause notice.

u The Commissioner after being satisfied that the proposal is fit for initiating actions of provisional attachment or even on his own motion, would cause service of a notice on the assessee for provisional attachment. It is pertinent to note that mere issuance of a notice is not a satisfactory performance and the notice must be served on the person for provisional attachment. The notice would provide the name, description, etc., of the property proposed to be attached provisionally and would also make a mention that till the disposal of the proceedings of provisional attachment, the assessee or his authorized agent should not cause the transfer of title or debase the title of such property.

The second significant aspect of sub-rule (5) is the mandatory requirement of furnishing an opportunity of being heard to the person whose property is attached. This is in consonance with the principles of natural justice and ensures that a fair procedure is observed. Sub-rule (5) provides for a post provisional attachment right of:

(i)

Submitting an objection to the attachment;

(ii)

An opportunity of being heard. Sub -rule (5) contains clear language to the effect that a person whose property is attached is entitled to two procedural entitlements: first, the right to submit an objection on the ground that the property was not or is not liable to be attached; and second, an opportunity of being heard to the person filing an objection. This is a clear indicator that in addition the filing of an objection, the person whose property is attached is entitled to an opportunity of being heard. It is not open to the Commissioner, as has been stated in the present case, to hold the view that the only safeguard under sub-rule 5 is to submit an objection without an opportunity of a personal hearing. Such a construction would be plainly contrary to sub-rule 5 which contemplates both the submission of an objection to the attachment and an opportunity of being heard. The opportunity of being heard can be availed of as a matter of right by the person whose property is attached. Both the right to submit an objection and to be afforded an opportunity of being heard are valuable safeguards. The consequence of a provisional attachment is serious. It displaces the person whose property is attached from dealing with the property. Where a bank account is attached, it prevents the person from operating the account. A business entity whose bank account is attached is seriously prejudiced by the inability to utilize the proceeds of the account for the purpose of business. The dual procedural safeguards inserted in sub-rule 5 of rule 159 demand strict compliance.

The Commissioner who hears the objections must pass a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the objections. To allow the Commissioner to get by without passing a reasoned order will make his decision subjective and defeat the purpose of subjecting it to judicial scrutiny. The Commissioner must deal with the objections and pass a reasoned order indicating whether, and if not, why the objections are not being accepted. Sub-rule 6 of rule 159 allows for the release of a property which either was or is no longer liable for attachment. The form in which such an order has to be passed, namely form GST DRC-23, states that 'now there is no such proceeding pending against the defaulting person which warrants attachment' of the account or as the case may be, the property. Sub -rules 5 and 6 do not expressly contemplate a situation in which the person whose property is attached can object on the ground that the attachment is in excess of the amount likely to be due for which proceedings have been launched under the Act. Nor does it provide for a specific opportunity to the taxable person to offer any alternative form of security in lieu of the attachment. Such an opportunity must be read into the provision to allow for a fair working in practice. Whether any alternative security that is furnished by the taxable person should be accepted and if so, its sufficiency, is a matter for the Commissioner to determine. Undoubtedly, the taxable person may not have a right to demand that only a particular form of security must be accepted. The Commissioner has to decide whether the form of security offered would secure the interest of the revenue. Where the taxable person sets up the plea that the extent of the attachment is excessive or where the taxable person offers an alternative form of security, these are also matters which ought to be determined by the Commissioner in the exercise of powers under rule 159(5). The scope of objection can also extend to the nature of the property which is being provisionally attached. Now, it is in this backdrop that it needs to be determined whether the petition under article 226 was maintainable and if it was, whether Commissioner exercised the powers under section 83 read with rule 159 in accordance with law. The above acts/omissions shall entail proceedings under section 73 or 73A which may be followed by attachment of property under section 73C. (ii) Is there any threshold limit for invoking attachment provision ? - Neither section 73C nor the Rules lay down any threshold limit for initiating attachment proceedings. However, the CBEC’s Circular No. 103/06/2008-ST, dated July 1, 2008, provides that it should be resorted to only in a case where the service tax or CENVAT credit alleged to be involved is more than Rs. 25 lakh.

(iii) Against whom can the provisions of attachment be invoked ? - As per section 73C, provisional attachment can be ordered in respect of any property belonging to a person on whom a notice has been served under section 73(1) or 73A(3). It may be noted that under section 73(1), a notice can be served on the person chargeable with the service tax which has not been levied or paid or which has been short-levied or short-paid or the person to whom service tax has been erroneously refunded, whereas, a notice under section 73A(3) can be served on - (1) a person liable to pay service tax who has collected any amount in excess of the service tax assessed or determined and paid on any taxable service from the recipient of the taxable service, or (2) any person who has collected any amount as service tax, which is not required to be collected, from any other person.

(iv) Which property can be attached under the provision of service tax ? - As noted in FAQ 3, provisional attachment under section 73C can be ordered in respect of any ‘property’ belonging to the specified person. Rule 2(c) of the Rules defines the term ‘property’ to include immovable property. Further, rule 4(2) of the Rules provides that movable property shall be attached only if the immovable property is not sufficient to protect the interest of revenue.

The CBEC, vide its circular dated July 1, 2008, has clarified that immovable property/properties which is/are used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached.

(v) Can personal property(ies) of proprietor/partner(s)/ director(s) be also attached ? - As per proviso to rule 3(3) of the Rules, personal property of proprietor or partners or directors, as the case may be, shall not be attached. As per rule 2(d), ‘personal property’ means any movable or immovable property belonging to a proprietor or partner or director, which is not in relation to business activity.

Accordingly, the CBEC in its circular dated July 1, 2008 has also clarified that any movable or immovable property which is in personal use of the sole proprietor/partner/director cannot be attached.

(vi) What shall be the extent of attachment ? - In terms of rule 4(1), the provisional attachment of property shall be to the extent it requires to protect the interest of revenue. In other words, the value of property attached shall be as nearly as may be equivalent to that of the amount of ‘pending revenue’.

The term ‘pending revenue’ is defined under rule 2(b) to mean "any service tax that has not been levied or paid or has been short-levied or paid or erroneously refunded in respect of which a notice has been served under sub-section (1) of section 73 or sub-section (3) of section 73A". Thus, the term ‘pending revenue’ refers to the amount demanded in the proceedings under section 73 or 73A.

(vii) What can be the possible justification to hold a view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary ? - If the Central Excise Officer reasonably believes that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, any of his property(ies) liable to attachment, it can be considered as sufficient justification necessitating attachment of property. The belief must, however, be based on substantial grounds.

(viii) What precautions should the Central Excise Officer take before initiating attachment proceedings ? - Although section 73C and the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, are both silent in this regard, the CBEC has in its circular dated July 1, 2008, stated emphatically that the remedy of attachment is of extraordinary nature and should be resorted to in the utmost circumspection and with maximum care and caution. There should be sufficient justification to hold the view that the provisional attachment of property is necessary to protect the interests of revenue. The Central Excise Officer should, in his proposal for attachment, clearly state the grounds on which he entertains the reasonable belief that the person in default would dispose of, or remove, the property and the sources of his information, if any.

The circular further states that appropriate disciplinary action shall be initiated against the officers who may be found to have exercised the powers of provisional attachment of property frivolously and without sound reasons.

Recovery of Tax

3.1 Section 54 of Model GST Law provides that the tax officer shall proceed to recover the GST Demand by one or more of the modes mentioned below:

3.1.1 Adjust the GST Demand from any money owing to the taxpayer.

3.1.2 Detain and sell any goods belonging to or under the control of the taxpayer.

3.1.3 Garnishee proceedings. 3.1.4 Distrain any moveable or immovable property of the taxable person, and detain the same until the amount payable is paid; and in case, any part of the said amount payable or of the cost of the distress or of keeping of the property, remains unpaid for 30 days next after any such distress, the tax officer may cause the said property to be sold (before resorting to such mode, the tax officer is required to seek authorization from the competent authority).

3.1.5 Prepare a Recovery Certificate specifying the amount due and send it to the concerned district Collector in respect of the tax payer. The Collector shall then proceed to recover the amount specified there under from the tax payer as if it were an arrear of land revenue.

3.1.6 File an application to the appropriate Magistrate, who shall then proceed to recover the amount specified thereunder from the taxpayer as if it were a fine imposed by him.

(Author's remarks: To avoid causing any undue hardships on the tax payers, the Legislature should clearly spell out the sequence in which the aforesaid recovery modes are to be resorted to by the tax officers.)

3.2 Where the terms of any bond or any instrument executed by the tax payer provide that any amount due thereunder may be recovered in the aforesaid manner, such amount may, without prejudice to any other mode of recovery, be recovered in accordance with the aforesaid manner.

3.3 The Model GST Law also provides that the tax officers of the SGST3 or CGST4, during the course of recovery of their tax arrears, may also recover the amount(s) payable by the tax payer to the Central Government or State Government respectively.

3.4 Other provisions relating to tax recovery:

3.4.1 In terms of section 55, if a tax payer makes an application to either extend the time for payment or allow payment of any amount due (other than the amount due as per the liability self-assessed in any return) in monthly instalments (not exceeding 24), the jurisdictional Commissioner/Chief Commissioner may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, allow to do so subject to payment of interest with such restrictions and conditions as may be prescribed. Default in payment of any one instalment on its due date would result in the whole outstanding balance payable on such date becoming due and becoming payable forthwith and liable for recovery.

3.4.2 Section 56 of Model GST Law treats the transfer of property to be void in certain cases. In essence, this is similar to the section 281 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and provides that where a tax payer, after any tax has become due from him, (i) creates a charge on or (ii) parts with his property by way of sale, mortgage, exchange or any other mode of transfer in favour of any other person with the intention of defrauding the government revenue, such charge or transfer shall be void as against any claim in respect of any amount(s) payable by such tax payer. However, this provision shall not affect any such charge or transfer if it is made (i) for adequate consideration and without notice of the pendency of proceedings against/ amount(s) payable by the taxpayer, or (ii) with the previous permission of the tax officer (popularly known as a No-Objection Certificate or NOC).

[Author's remarks: This section deals with cases of charge/transfer created on property(ies) post any tax has become due from the tax payer. Going forward, in commercial deals, the transferee's of property(ies)could seek to request for such NOCs to ensure that the property(ies) charged/transferred to them have not been charged/transferred with a fraudulent intention. The words 'with the intention of defrauding the government revenue' used in the section indicate that to treat any transfer of property as void, the obligation is on the tax officers to prove the fraudulent intention on the part of the taxpayer.]

3.4.3 In terms of the section 57 of Model GST Law, the GST Demand payable by a taxpayer shall be a first charge on the property of such taxpayer.

Such PA shall cease to have effect after the expiry of 1 year from the date of the PA order.

Steps to secure recovery of demand in high demand cases - It has been the experience in the past that on several occasions, the Assessing Officers create huge demands against assessees without obtaining the details of any known assets of the asses¬see. With the passage of time and in the absence of such details, no concrete action gets taken to recover this demand. As a re¬sult, Department is burdened with the responsibility to recover the huge arrears existing in its records, with little possibility of actual recovery in many cases. As on 1-4-2004, the arrears increased by 20% to Rs. 87,885 crore while the objective was to reduce arrears by 20% as compared to the preceding year.

2. The Board has, therefore, decided that in cases where demand of Rs. 5 lakh and above in big cities like Delhi, Mumbai, Kolka¬ta, Chennai, Ahmedabad, Hyderabad, Pune and Bangalore and Rs. 1 lakh and above elsewhere, is likely to be created and it appears that the recovery, in full or in part, could become difficult, it shall be the responsibility of the Assessing Officer, during the assessment proceedings itself, to enquire into all assets of the assessee and place under provisional attachment, in terms of provisions of section 281B, before the assessment is completed, the assets sufficient to cover the demand in question (or to the maximum extent, as the case may be). After completion of the assessment, if the provisional attachment cannot be continued till recovery, the same assets can be considered for attachment, etc., under section 222/226. In each of these cases, the Assessing Officer shall mention in an Office Note to the Assessment Order in question, the efforts made to locate the assets of the assessee, the details of assets located, the details of assets placed under provisional attachment, etc.

3. In search and seizure cases, huge demands are raised under block assessment and the recovery of the same is tedious and time-consuming. In this regard, it is extremely important for Assessing Officers in Central Charges to explore the possibility of invoking the provisions of section 281B. At the time of prepa¬ration of Appraisal Report, the DDIT(Inv.)/ADIT(Inv.) should take particular care in identifying the properties of the assessees which could be attached under this section and make a specific mention of the same in the Appraisal Report itself.

4. It shall be the responsibility of all Assessing Officers to follow the above procedure. If any demand becomes irrecoverable due to the failure of the Assessing Officer to follow these guidelines, he shall be held accountable for the loss caused to the Government, regardless of his subsequent posting.

5. While making a review of scrutiny assessments, the Commission¬ers of Income-tax and Chief Commissioners of Income-tax concerned shall specifically comment on this aspect.—Instruction No. 8/2004, dated 2-9-2004.

Sub- section (1) of section 74 empowers the proper officer to serve a notice on a person chargeable with tax where it appears that—

(i)

Any tax has not been paid;

(ii)

Tax has been short paid;

(iii)

Tax has been erroneously refunded; or

(iv)

Input tax credit has been wrongly availed or utilized by reason of fraud, wilful statement or suppression of fact to evade tax. [Para 45] Sub-section (1) enables the proper officer to issue a notice to show cause for the recovery of tax, interest payable under section 50 and the penalty equivalent to the amount of tax specified in the notice. Sub-sections (2), (3) and (4) lay down procedural provisions which are to be followed by the proper officer. Secondly, under sub-section (5) of section 74, before the service of a notice under sub-section (1), the person who is chargeable with tax may pay the tax together with interest and a penalty equivalent to fifteen per cent of the tax on the basis of their own ascertainment of the tax or as ascertained by the proper officer and inform the proper officer of the payment having been made upon receipt of the information. Sub-section (6) stipulates that the proper officer shall not serve any notice under sub-section (1) in respect of the tax so paid or any penalty payable under the provisions of the Act or the Rules. [Para 46]

On the other hand, when the proper officer is of the opinion that the amount which has been paid under sub-section (5) falls short of the amount which is actually payable, a notice under sub-section (1) is to issue for the amount which falls short of what is actually payable. Sub-section (8) contains a stipulation that where a person who is chargeable with tax under sub-section (1) pays the tax together with interest and a penalty of twenty-five per cent of the tax within thirty days of the issuance of the notice, all proceedings in respect of the notice shall be deemed to be concluded. Under sub-section (9), the proper officer after considering the representation of the person chargeable to tax is authorized to determine the amount of tax, interest and penalty due and to issue an order. A period of five years is stipulated by sub-section (10) for the issuance of an order in sub-section (9). Sub-section (11) stipulates that upon service of an order under sub-section (9), all proceedings in respect of the notice shall be deemed to be concluded upon the person paying the tax with interest under section 50 and a penalty equivalent to 50 per cent of the tax within thirty days of the communication of an order. These provisions indicate how sub-sections (5), (8) and (11) operate at different stages of the process. [Para 47]

Now in this backdrop, it becomes necessary to emphasize that before the Commissioner can levy a provisional attachment, there must be a formation of 'the opinion' and that it is necessary 'so to do' for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue. The power to levy a provisional attachment is draconian in nature. By the exercise of the power, a property belonging to the taxable person may be attached, including a bank account. The attachment is provisional and the statute has contemplated an attachment during the pendency of the proceedings under the stipulated statutory provisions noticed earlier. An attachment which is contemplated in section 83 is, in other words, at a stage which is anterior to the finalization of an assessment or the raising of a demand. Conscious as the legislature was of the draconian nature of the power and the serious consequences which emanate from the attachment of any property including a bank account of the taxable person, it conditioned the exercise of the power by employing specific statutory language which conditions the exercise of the power. The language of the statute indicates first, the necessity of the formation of opinion by the Commissioner; second, the formation of opinion before ordering a provisional attachment; third the existence of opinion that it is necessary so to do for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue; fourth, the issuance of an order in writing for the attachment of any property of the taxable person; and fifth, the observance by the Commissioner of the provisions contained in the rules in regard to the manner of attachment. Each of these components of the statute are integral to a valid exercise of power. In other words, when the exercise of the power is challenged, the validity of its exercise will depend on a strict and punctilious observance of the statutory preconditions by the Commissioner. While conditioning the exercise of the power on the formation of an opinion by the Commissioner that 'for the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue, it is necessary so to do', it is evident that the statute has not left the formation of opinion to an unguided subjective discretion of the Commissioner. The formation of the opinion must bear a proximate and live nexus to the purpose of protecting the interest of the government revenue. [Para 48]

The department could not show any material either from the counter-affidavit or from the supplementary affidavits to justify the action of the assessing authority under section 281B. Only this much was submitted by them that certain enquiries with regard to the nature and source of gifts in favour of the petitioner No. 2 were to be enquired into. That was the only ground which was stated in the counter-affidavit and was urged by the department. That ground was wholly insufficient to invoke section 281B. In every case, where the assessment has to take place, it is the bounden duty of the Assessing Officer to make such enquiries as are necessary to complete the assessment. Apart from the above the assessee-company was newly born assessee on the file of the Income-tax Department as it was incorporated only on 9-12-2001 and indisputably it filed returns of income up to the assessment year 2003-04, which were finalized by the department. There was no history of the assessee-company to show that on any occasion earlier it failed to discharge its liability. Apart from the above as has been held by the Bombay High Court in the case of Gandhi Trading v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 239 ITR 337 that the attachment of the bank accounts is the last resort. The department if it is of the opinion that the assessee is likely to dispose of its property to thwart the payment of income-tax dues, the department should provisionally attach the immovable property of such assessee first. Resort to blanket attachment of the entire bank accounts of an assessee has serious consequence on its rights to carry on the business. The action of the department in such circumstances should not give an impression to any body that it has indulged in any manner to hamper the business activities of the assessee. Power has been conferred under the said section to protect the interest of the revenue. Only so much asset or amount which would satisfy the future demand should be provisionally attached under section 281B leaving other assets including the amount standing in the bank account to enable the assessee to carry on the business. The passing of the impugned order in the instant case, amounted to stopping the business activities of the assessee, which instead of advancing the purpose of section 281B frustrated the interest of the revenue. [Para 15]

Even assuming that the Assessing Officer had power to attach the bank accounts provisionally, it does not give licence to conduct assessment proceedings at his leisure when the department was so apprehensive as to resort its power under section 281B which is to be used sparingly. It is expected in such matter from the department to conclude the assessment proceedings within a reasonable period. It is difficult to approve the callous approach of the Assessing Officer in such matters not to conclude the assessment proceedings within a reasonable period of time. [Para 16]

PROCEEDS OF BENAMI PROPERTY DEPOSITED IN BANK

Cash and bank balance are treated as movable property/asset. Property under section 2(26) of PBPT Act, 1988 means asset of any kind, whether movable or immovable and proceeds of a such property. It is our common knowledge that on many occasions cash forms part of the proceeds of a benami property which gets deposited in bank. In such a situation, depending on the origin of cash and intention behind such a transaction, the balance in the bank account represented by proceeds of a benami property could form benami property. In other words, if the bank balance has a nexus with the proceeds of a benami property, it can partake the character of benami property subject to benami transaction. There may a case where there is no bank balance except leaving a very small balance and there is no trace of utilization of cash withdrawn. Action can be taken to attach the small amount of cash balance in the bank and then other consequences would follow. There is no monetary limit to initiate benami proceeding.

The notes/disclaimers in Clause 3 of Form 3CA/Clause 5 of Form 3CB must not exceed 1000 characters. (1) Whether Conversion Charges paid in cash to as payee's bank account was frozen by attachment order of ESIC?

Where the assessee-company had paid conversion charges to a company in cash as a bank account of the said company was frozen by an order of attachment passed by the ESI department, the assessee was entitled to exemption under rule 6DD and; thus, no disallowance under section 40A(3) was called for. What is crucial while testing such a claim and the applicability of section 40A(3) is the facts of each particular case. Therefore, a decision cannot be taken without referring to facts. The assessee seeks to bring its case under two limbs, namely, there was no banking facility and it was a business expediency. The assessee by stating that there was no banking facility does not seek to bring their case under clause (j) of rule 6DD but on account of the factual position. On 29-11-2002, the Punjab National Bank sends a letter to SLM directing them to close the bank account with State Bank of India and directs them to do all banking transactions only through the Punjab National Bank. This direction has come because the said Bank was appointed as the operating agency to implement a scheme of revival of SLM as framed by the BIFR. Therefore, SLM cannot flout the direction. The said company was carrying on business and it appears that the assessee was one of the major entities with whom they had entered into agreement. There was an agreement for 'conversion job-work' dated 1-4-2003. Even prior to that, on 27-2-2004, the Punjab National bank informs SLM that their bank account with them has been attached pursuant to an order passed by the Employees State Insurance Corporation, Madurai and the interest payable towards Punjab National Bank cannot be serviced from the very same account. On receipt of the letter on 2-4-2004, SLM writes to the assessee informing this development and requesting them to pay cash for meeting the wages, salary and other expenses for their unit to run smoothly. Further, they have represented for payment of additional conversion charges depending upon the quality of the product as they have incurred lot of expenses in modernising the machineries. These factors led to the assessee effecting payments in cash. The words 'extent of banking facilities available' in proviso to section 40A(3) has to be interpreted in the facts of a given case and all such cases will not be covered under clause (j) of rule 6DD which has been subsequently deleted. In the instant case, banking facility was available but the bank account of SLM could not be operated by the very bank themselves because of an order of attachment passed by the ESI department. SLM virtually came to the assessee with the begging bowl and requested to effect payment in cash. The assessee has entered into an agreement for conversion on job work basis. The assessee is required to act as a prudent businessman, so that the job-work is completed to his satisfaction with optimum quality. This has led the assessee to effect payments in cash The argument of the revenue is on the ground that in order to avoid the attachment of the bank account the assessee has effected payment in cash. It is to be noted that what is relevant to be seen insofar as section 40A(3) is concerned is the conduct of the assessee and not the payee and the question would be did the assessee have a reasonable cause to effect payment in cash. If the assessee has a reasonable Explanation, then the proviso under section 40A(3) would stand attracted and the assessee would be entitled to relief. It maybe true that merely because the payee is identifiable, it will automatically exonerate the assessee. The Court is not laying down any such broad principle. The fact that the payee was identifiable and not a fictitious person would go to show the bona fides of the transaction. This is what is required to be considered from the angle of a commercially expedient and prudent business house [Pr. CIT v. Sumukha Synthetics [2020] 119 taxmann.com 234 (Madras)]

(2) Is Section 40A(3) attracted where cash payments were made when bank accounts of the assessee were frozen by the Income Tax Department under Section 226(3)?

Where the Income Tax Department froze the bank account of the assessee under section 226(3) in those circumstances, the assessee would be entitled to exemption under rule 6DD in respect of cash payment and, therefore, no disallowance under section 40A(3) could be made.. Conclusion

3. It is astonishing to note that the Provisional Attachment of Property Rules, notified after more than two years of the basic provision of section 73C coming into force, appear to have been drafted hastily, leaving a number of issues unanswered. The CBEC has, however, endeavoured to fill the gaps simultaneously by issuing the circular on the same date. Most obviously, these gaps had already been reckoned by the CBEC. It would have been better if the issues answered by the circular were also incorporated in the Rules making them comprehensive and complete. Departmental circulars being administrative instructions do not get legislative ratification as in case of Rules.

Therefore, a Superintendent of Central Excise is also a Central Excise Officer as contemplated under section 73(1) ibid. Now, can a Superintendent of Central Excise adjudicating a matter within his monetary jurisdiction make a proposal as contemplated under rule 3(1) ibid ?

A considered answer to the above query will be that a Superintendent of Central Excise cannot make a proposal as contemplated under rule 3(1) ibid. Reasons for this position are as follows: The term 'Central Excise Officer' mentioned in section 73(1) ibid is a general category, whereas the expressions 'Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise' used in rule 3(1) ibid are specific expressions. The rule of interpretation applicable in such situations is 'Specialia generalibus derogant'. Where a special provision is made on a certain matter, that matter is to be excluded from the general provision. (See: Venkateshwar Rao v. Govt. of Andhra Pradesh AIR 1966 SC 828; CIT v. Shahzada Nand & Sons [1966] 60 ITR 392 (SC); State of Gujarat v. Patel Ramajibhai Danabhai AIR 1979 SC 1098, etc.).

The above position is also fortified by the contrast in the expressions used in section 73(1) and rule 3(1). Section 73(1) uses the expression "the Central Excise Officer is of opinion that", while the expressions in rule 3(1) are "the Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is satisfied that …". Thus, the mental state necessary under rule 3(1) is that of satisfaction which is much higher than the opinion as contemplated under section 73(1), and the former is expected of an officer of a higher level than the one entertaining an opinion. There again, the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise is supposed to make a proposal for attachment 'after due verification of the facts, and the circumstances of the case', which further underlines the gravity of the matter. It should be so, because attachment of property is a very serious matter and the same should be resorted to only in highly necessary and appropriate cases.

Analysis

4. In summary, it can be said that the term 'Central Excise Officer' mentioned in section 73(1) ibid denotes an Assistant Commissioner of Central Excise or the Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise, and not any officer of Central Excise below the rank of an Assistant Commissioner.

This does not, however, mean that attachment of property cannot be resorted to in a case where adjudication is pending before a Superintendent of Central Excise. (Even in monetary terms attachment may be vital if there are several cases pertaining to the same assessee pending before a Superintendent/Superintendents). In such cases, the Commissioner of Central Excise can cause service of notice for attachment on his own satisfaction, under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008. If attachment of property is felt necessary in a matter pending before a Superintendent of Central Excise, the Superintendent will have to inform the Commissioner accordingly, not under rule 3(1) of the Service Tax (Provisional Attachment of Property) Rules, 2008, but in general terms. Commissioner will have to call for the file under section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994 (read with section 12E of the Central Excise Act, 1944), examine the matter, record his satisfaction under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 ibid, and proceed to issue notice for attachment. But if the Superintendent makes a proposal under rule 3(1) ibid, such proposal will be incompetent, and if the Commissioner acts on such a proposal per se without examining the matter and recording his own personal satisfaction under sub-rule (2) of rule 3 ibid, and proceeds to issue notice for attachment, the whole proceedings will be incompetent and vitiated and will be liable to be struck down by a competent Court of law, for lack of satisfaction on the part of the Commissioner.

RBI;

(b)

SBI;

(c)

Any subsidiary of SBI;

(d)

Any bank as may be appointed by RBI as its agent under section 45(1) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

11.5-3 Release of guarantee

Where the AO is satisfied that the guarantee is not required anymore to protect the interests of the revenue, he shall release that guarantee forthwith.

11.5-4 Acceptance of guarantee is mandatory

Once the assessee furnishes the guarantee satisfying the aforesaid conditions the AO is bound to revoke the attachment. This is because section 281B(3) provides that the AO 'shall' by an order in writing revoke such attachment.

11.5-5 Satisfied

The AO has to be 'satisfied' that the guarantee for an amount lower than the FMV is sufficient.

The term 'satisfied' has been explained as follows:

It is not the personal whim, wish, view or opinion or the ipse dixit of the President de hors the material but a legitimate inference drawn from the material placed before him which is relevant for the purpose. In other words, the President has to be convinced of or has to have sufficient proof of information with regard to or has to be free from doubt or uncertainty about the state of things indicating that the situation in question has arisen [S. R. Bommai v. UOI AIR 1994 SC 1918/[1994] 1 SCC 3 (SC)].

However, once he is satisfied it appears that he has no discretion not to reduce the amount of guarantee.

11.5-6 Opportunity of being heard

The section does not provide for any opportunity of being heard to the assessee before the guarantee is invoked. In this connection the observations of the Supreme Court in Sahara India (Firm) v. CIT [2008] 300 ITR 403/169 Taxman 328 are apposite :

"If the statute conferring the power is silent with regard to the giving of a pre-decisional hearing to the person affected and the administrative decision taken by the authority involves civil consequences of a grave nature, and no full review or appeal on merits against that decision is provided, courts will be extremely reluctant to construe such a statute as excluding the duty of affording even a minimal hearing, shorn of all its formal trappings and dilatory features at the pre-decisional stage, unless, viewed pragmatically, it would paralyse the administrative process or frustrate the need for utmost promptitude. In short, this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save in very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands. The court must make every effort to salvage this cardinal rule to the maximum extent possible, with situational modifications. But, the core of it must, however, remain, namely, that the person affected must have reasonable opportunity of being heard and the hearing must be a genuine hearing and not an empty public relations exercise." (p. 666).

It is a moot point whether the aforesaid observations would be applicable before the invocation of the guarantee.

11.5-7 Direct acceptance of guarantee is not possible

The section envisages the situation where the assets are first attached and then a guarantee is accepted in lieu of the assets attached. It does not envisage a situation of acceptance of bank guarantee at the first stage itself without attachment of assets.

■ It is the grievance expressed by the assessees that since the department has resorted to such draconian measure of provisional attachment of their properties, not for the first time, but for the fourth time, due to which, their business has almost come to a standstill, since, the properties, which were attached by the department were all the properties, which they have offered as securities to the banks, and because of such mortgaged properties were came to be attached, the banks are refusing to part with further working capital loans, at any moment, they would declare the assessees as non performing assets, if this situation continues, it will jeopardize the entire business of the assessees and it would also have a cascading effect of 5000 workers loosing their job, resulting in 5000 families landing on streets suffering for food and shelter. Thus, from the above backgrounds of the case it is clear that the first charge holders of the properties are the bankers and the department are only the second charge holders of the assessees’ properties. Therefore, the first charge holders of the assessees’ properties, being the bankers, the assessees have to first satisfy the bankers, for availing loan facility and only the bankers are satisfied they would come forward to lend loan facility to the assessees. The assessees have earned good reputation and credibility amongst the general public, based on which, the bankers have come forward to extend the loan facility and this is a continuous arrangements entered into between the bankers and the assessees, for the sake of running the business smoothly, and when the banks, having extended working capital loan facility to the assessees, certainly, they will monitor the same so as to protect their interest. The question of non-repayment would arise due to deficit in service of working capital loan extended to the assessees. Therefore, the department could have enabled the assessees to get their working capital loans extended by the bankers, and thereafter, monitor the assessees, whether such loan is being utilized by the assessees for the purpose, for which, such additional loan is extended, and by doing so, the interest of the revenue, is not going to be affected in any away, rather, it would promote much financial gain, and thereby, the interest of the revenue would also be safeguarded. Therefore, the department ought to have acted in such a way, in order to protect the interest of the revenue. Whereas, in the instant case, it is seen that, on earlier occasions, i.e., on 28.02.2022, 23.08.2022 and 17.02.2023, the department has issued the attachment orders and the same got lapsed on 27.08.2022, 22.02.2023 and 16.08.2023 respectively. Finally, for the fourth time, the department has issued the provisional attachment orders dated 16.08.2023 and the reasons assigned is that to protect the interest of the revenue.(Para 9)

■

Hence the Court posed a question to the department, whether the intention of the department is really to protect the interest of the revenue or whether to close down the business of the assessees by resorting to such draconian action. In reply to the said question, the department stated that it has no intention to cause hindrance or obstacles to the assessees’ running their business and the department is mainly concerned only about the safeguarding the interest of the revenue and in matters of revenue, there is no place for consideration of equity.(Para 10)

Khan [2000] 113 Taxman 568 (Guj.)]. Communication of reasons recorded for retention of books/documents - It is true that section 132(8) does not in terms provide that the Commissioner's approval or the recorded reasons on which it might be based should be communicated to the concerned person but since the person concerned is bound to be materially prejudiced in the enforcement of his right to have such books and documents returned to him by being kept ignorant about the factum of fulfilment of either of the conditions, it is obligatory upon the revenue to communicate the Commissioner's approval as also the recorded reasons to the person concerned. In the absence of such communication, the Commissioner's decision according his approval will not become effective [CIT v. Oriental Rubber Works [1983] 15 Taxman 51 (SC)].

Approval must be obtained before expiry of time-limit - Section 132(8) does not in terms empower the Commissioner to give ex post facto approval. Once the retention has become invalid, it cannot be validated by a subsequent grant of approval by the Commissioner [Hanuman Pershad Ganeriwala v. Director of Inspection [1974] 93 ITR 419 (Delhi); Sampatlal & Sons v. CIT [1984] 16 Taxman 144 (MP)].

The recording of reasons by the ITO for retention of books beyond the period of 180 (now 30) days and approval by the Commissioner of the same should take place before the expiry of 180 (now 30) days [Metal Fittings (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [1983] 14 Taxman 261 (Delhi)]. There cannot be a gap of a single day because section 132(8) only allows extension of time and not a fresh retention [Survir Enterprises v. CIT [1985] 22 Taxman 516 (Delhi)].

Retention of books/documents beyond specified period - Where, pursuant to search conducted in case of assessee u/s 132, title deeds were seized by ITOs and except statement filed that PCIT approved continued retention of books of account and other documents from time-to-time, there was nothing produced to substantiate that orders were issued permitting continued retention; retention of documents beyond 30 days of assessment order was not justified and revenue was to be directed to release title documents of assessee as expeditiously as possible [Udaya Sounds v. PCIT [2022] 138 taxmann.com 415/287 Taxman 251 (Ker.)].

Books can be returned pursuant to assessee's undertaking - The object of retention of books is not to penalise the assessee or to confiscate the books for ever. Where an undertaking had been obtained from the assessee-petitioner to the effect that as and when the department required the records they would be made available to it, a Single Judge would be justified in ordering the return of the books to the petitioner [Director of Inspection v. K. C. A. & Co. [1987] 32 Taxman 495 (J&K)].

Time-limit for handing over books/documents to jurisdictional AO - Period set out u/s 132(9A) is a measure to enable respective parties to adhere to process in an orderly fashion facilitating completion of assessment in time. Thus, time limits set out u/s 132(9A) are not only for purposes of section 132(8) and 132(9) but also to facilitate reasonable time to AO to complete assessment where identities of Investigating Officer and AO are different [Agni Estates & Foundations (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2021] 126 taxmann.com 14 (Mad.)].

u The circular provides certain offences which may be considered for provisional attachment of property. Among others, offences like evasion of tax, short payment of service tax, claiming fraudulent refund or Cenvat credit, etc., have been mentioned.

u The circular also mentions that no proceedings under the Attachment Rules would be initiated in the cases where the service tax or Cenvat credit alleged is less than Rs. 25 Lakhs.

u On receipt of such orders, the Central Excise Officer would proceed with the provisional attachment of the property. It has been specifically mentioned that personal property of the assessee/partners/directors could not be provisionally attached. However, the circular provides that the immovable property used for commercial purpose may be provisionally attached. Thus, if the property is being commercially used (whatever purpose) and not necessarily for the provision of services only, the same could be attached. Thus, in case the service provider has rented out his house or he is carrying on his business from the said property, the Central Excise Officer is free to attach the said property under the Attachment Rules as the same are being commercially used.

u The attachment of the immovable property (where available) must precede the attachment of any movable property. Also, the value of property attached must correspond as nearly as possible to the amount of pending revenue against the assessee. The valuation of properties like land, gold and securities would always be a matter of dispute since their values variate over a period of time.

u The assessee whose property has been provisionally attached should not cause to transfer the title or create a lien of a third party over such property. Having said this, it is important to mention that as is the case in Excise and Customs, in service tax also the secured creditor is entitled to preference over claim of revenue. The same has been upheld in the matter of UTI Bank Ltd. v. Dy. CCE [W.P. No. 39536 of 2005, dated 20-12-2006]. However, contrary to this, the circular provides that in case of provisional attachment, any debts, claims, etc., against the provisional attachment would be void. Thus, on a harmonious reading of both the provisions, it can be construed that any mortgage or any other charge created after the provisional attachment of the property would only be void against such provisional attachment.

u The circular also provides that the provisional attachment should not hamper the business of the assessee. Also, properties as is exempted by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, would also be exempt from provisional attachment under the Attachment Rules.

u Last but not the least, the property remains provisionally attached for a period of six months from the date of service of notice. Post which, an extension must be given for such attachment by the Chief Commissioner of Central Excise (‘Chief Commissioner’). However, the total period of extension by the Chief Commissioner cannot exceed two years.

u The Attachment Rules provide for automatic release of the attached property if the assessee pays the dues with interest.

Thus, though the Attachment Rules empower the Central Excise Officer in relation to provisional attachment of property of an assessee, yet these provisions are not arbitrary and subjective. These provisions must be used only to safeguard the interest of the revenue and are to be enforced in a manner which is rational and not based on mere surmises or suspicion. The Circular has clearly spelt out that with more powers (to Central Excise Officer) comes more responsibility.

11. Some Substantive provisions :

Section 3 – Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 3 of the Ordinance places a blanket ban on Unregulated Deposit Schemes and prohibits deposit taker from promoting, operating, issuing any advertisement soliciting participation or enrolment in or accepting deposits in pursuance of an Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 4 – Fraudulent default in Regulated Deposit Schemes

Section 4 of the Ordinance prohibits deposit taker, while accepting deposits under a Regulated Deposit Scheme, from commission of fraudulent default in the repayment or return of deposit on maturity or in rendering any specified service promised against such deposit.

It may be noted that Section 4 is not applicable to companies (as per proviso to Section 27 of the Ordinance)

Section 5 – Wrongful inducement in relation to Unregulated Deposit Schemes

Section 5 of the Ordinance prohibits any person from knowingly making any statement, promise or forecast which is false, deceptive or misleading in material facts or deliberately conceal any material facts, to induce another person to invest in, or become a member or participant of any Unregulated Deposit Scheme.

Section 6 – Certain scheme to be Unregulated Deposit Scheme

Section 6 of the Ordinance provides that prize chit or a money circulation scheme banned under the provisions of the Prize Chits and Money Circulation Scheme (Banning) Act, 1978 shall be deemed to be an Unregulated Deposit Scheme under this Ordinance.

Section 7 – Provisional Attachment

The power for provisional attachment in cases of contravention of section 3 has been vested with a Competent Authority. This Competent Authority is an officer appointed by appropriate Government who is not below the rank of Secretary to that Government.

As per section 7(3) of the Ordinance, where the Competent Authority, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing), on the basis of such information and particulars as may be prescribed that any deposit taker is soliciting deposits in contravention of section 3, he may, by order in writing, provisionally attach the deposits held by the deposit taker and the money or other property acquired either in the name of the deposit taker or in the name of any other person on behalf of the deposit taker.

It is pertinent to mention that section 7(3) of the Ordinance is not properly drafted and does not provide for giving any show cause notice to the deposit taker prior to provisionally attaching deposits. Not providing an opportunity of being heard prior to provisional attachment tantamount a contravention of principles of Natural Justice and vitiates the pre-requisites of a fair trial. As this law will evolve, there is a high possibility that section 7(3) may be read down by the Courts to the extent it fails in providing a show cause notice prior to provisional attachment. It will be tested in future.

Section 14 and 15 – Confirmation of attachment by Designated Court

(i)

Section 14 of the Ordinance requires the Competent Authority to file an application before the Designated Court for making the provisional attachment absolute within a period of 30 days (which may extend upto 60 days) from the date of the order of provisional attachment. This period may be extended up to sixty days, for reasons to be recorded in writing.

(ii)

As per section 15(1) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall then issue notice to the deposit taker or any person whose property is attached under section 14, to show cause, within a period of 30 days, as to why the order of attachment should not be made absolute and the properties so attached be sold.

(iii)

As per section 15(2) of the Ordinance, the Designated Court shall issue notice to all other persons represented to it as having or being likely to claim any interest or title in the property to appear on the same date as persons referred to in section 15(1) to raise objections, if they so desire, to the attachment of the property.

Upholding Delhi High Court judgment which held that moratorium under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) will apply to the order of Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the Supreme Court has observed that IBC will override anything inconsistent contained in any other enactment, including the Income Tax Act.

In order to curb misuse of Input Tax Credit by bogus invoices, rule 86B of CGST Rules has been inserted w.e.f. 1-1-2021 to provide that at least 1% of tax liability shall be paid in cash in certain situations. As per CBI&C, this provision will affect less than 0.5% of total taxpayers and genuine taxpayers will not be affected at all.

Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules, the registered person shall not use the amount available in electronic credit ledger to discharge his liability towards output tax in excess of 99% of such tax liability, in cases where the value of taxable supply other than exempt supply and zero-rated supply, in a month exceeds fifty lakh rupees:

(b)

the registered person has received a refund amount of more than one lakh rupees in the preceding financial year on account of unutilised input tax credit under section 54(3)(i); or

the registered person has received a refund amount of more than one lakh rupees in the preceding financial year on account of unutilised input tax credit under section 54(3)(ii); or

the registered person has discharged his liability towards output tax through the electronic cash ledger for an amount which is in excess of 1% of the total output tax liability, applied cumulatively, upto the said month in the current financial year; or

the registered person is - (i) Government Department; or (ii) a Public Sector Undertaking; or (iii) a local authority; or (iv) a statutory body.

11.1-3e Whether the amendment encourages search and seizure without recording of reason to believe? - Prima facie, answer is no, because there is no change in law in respect of recording of reason to believe before authorization of search. There is no additional power given to income-tax authority to conduct search without recording reasons. The specified authority is obliged to record the reason. However, only difference is that now such authority need not disclose the reason to any person, authority or the Appellate Tribunal. If search proceeding is challenged before High Court, such authority is bound to disclose the reason to High Court, if asked to do so.

However, in past, in many cases, search was conducted without recording concrete reason. In some cases, it was also found that the reason was recorded subsequent to the search proceeding or based on the material found during the search. In such circumstances, Court had struck down the order passed by the authorities treating it as illegal or invalid.

In terms of the amendment, now income-tax authorities are not required to disclose the reason to any person, authority or Appellate Tribunal. Therefore, in absence of transparency in process of decision making and recording reason by income tax authorities, it may encourage the search without recording a reason or recording reason subsequently.

In such cases only remedy available is to file a Writ petition before jurisdictional High Court which may be a costly affair.

17.5-5 Impracticable seizure of bank lockers and bank accounts [Section 247(4) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(3) of the ITA 1961)] While Section 132(1) of the ITA 1961 grants the power to seize money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable articles, Section 132(3) comes into play where it is not practicable to seize such assets. The Kerala High Court, in the case of ITO v. M. Shajahan [1976] 104 ITR 347 (Kerala), held that action under section 132(3) for a bank account is indeed permissible when it is not practicable to seize the asset. The Court observed that monies deposited in a bank, by virtue of the debtor-creditor relationship between the bank and the customer, are impracticable to seize in the physical sense. The money becomes the bank's property, and the customer merely has the right to demand repayment. Therefore, a prohibitory order under section 132(3) is the appropriate mechanism to prevent the assessee from dealing with such funds. The Court further clarified that while the proper procedure is to address the order to the customer (assessee) directing them not to deal with the money, with a copy communicated to the bank, an order directly issued to the bank would still have the same effect of preventing the assessee from operating the account. This is because section 132(3) also allows the officer to take "such steps as may be necessary for ensuring compliance with this sub-section."

In contrast to bank accounts, the treatment of bank lockers under Section 132 is distinct. The Kerala High Court in M. Shajahan (supra), while discussing the nature of bank deposits, also touched upon bank lockers. The Court noted that with regard to securities and valuables deposited for safe custody in a locker, "the property in them remains with the customer." This implies that the contents of a bank locker are considered to be in the assessee's possession, even if physically held by the bank for safe custody. Therefore, if the contents of a locker are found to be undisclosed assets during a search, they can be directly seized under section 132(1)(iii). If, for some reason, direct seizure is not immediately practicable (e.g., due to lack of immediate access or valuation issues), then a prohibitory order under section 132(3) can be issued to prevent the assessee from operating the locker.

This distinction is crucial as for bank accounts, a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) is the primary mode of attachment due to the nature of the debtor-creditor relationship, making physical seizure impracticable. For bank lockers, direct seizure under Section 132(1) is possible; only if that is impracticable is a prohibitory order under Section 132(3) resorted to.

Under the ITA 1961, there was no explicit mention of bank lockers and bank accounts under Section 132. But, it was understood that the said items may fall within the ambit of the phrase "other valuable article or thing", if other conditions of section 132 are satisfied.

However, the ITA 2025 has explicitly included bank lockers and bank accounts under section 247(4), wherein the seizure of such items is not practicable.

17.5-6 Examination on oath of any other person present in the premises, etc. [Section 247(6) of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 132(4) of the ITA 1961)]

11. State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act; Section 53 of IBC doesn't override Section 48 of GVAT Act: SC

IBC | State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 157/174 SCL 250 (SC)

In the landmark ruling, the Supreme Court held that the State is a secured creditor for tax purposes under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

In the instant case, the following questions were placed before the Supreme Court:

(a)

Is State a secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes under Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act)?

(b)

Whether Section 53 of IBC overrides Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT (GVAT Act) or not?

The Apex Court held that the State is a secured creditor under the GVAT Act. Section 3(30) of the IBC defines the secured creditor as "a creditor in favour of whom security interest is created".

The court further held that such security interest could be created by the operation of law. The definition of a secured creditor in the IBC does not exclude any Government or Governmental Authority. Therefore, the State will be treated as the secured creditor under IBC for tax purposes.

In view of the above, the Supreme Court concluded that State is a secured creditor for VAT under GVAT Act, and Section 53 of IBC doesnot override Section 48 of the GVAT Act.

With regard to the overriding effect of Section 53 of the IBC, it was held that Section 48 of the GVAT Act is not contrary to or inconsistent with Section 53 or any other provisions of the IBC. Section 53 of the IBC deals with the distributions of the asset. As per Section 53, proceeds from the sale of the liquidation assets shall be distributed in the order of priority and within such period as prescribed in the provision.

Under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), the debts owed to a secured creditor, which would include the State under the GVAT Act, shall rank equally with other specified debts, including debts on account of workman's dues for 24 months preceding the liquidation commencement date.

The term "Secured Creditor", as defined under the IBC, is comprehensive and wide enough to cover all types of security interests, namely, the right, title, interest or a claim to the property created in favour of or provided for a secured creditor by a transaction, which secures payment or performance of an obligation and includes mortgage, charge, hypothecation, assignment and encumbrance or any other agreement or arrangement securing payment or performance of any obligation of any person.

In view of the statutory charge in terms of Section 48 of the GVAT Act, the claim of the tax department of the State squarely falls within the definition of "Security Interest" under Section 3(31) of the IBC, and the State becomes a secured creditor under Section 3(30) of the Code.

69. Powers to arrest to be applied judiciously Section 69 of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017, empowers authorised GST officers to arrest individuals for certain offences under the GST law. This provision is designed to prevent tax evasion and ensure compliance with the law.

The power to arrest relies solely on the Commissioner's "reason to believe" that an offence under clauses (a) to (d) of Section 132(1) has been committed. The ability to arrest based on "reason to believe" without stringent procedural checks opens the door to potential abuse and arbitrary detention.

It is recommended that the GST provisions be amended to seek specific approval from the Principal Chief Commissioner before arrests can be made. Further, the proper officers seeking approval must present written evidence justifying the arrest.

Recently, the Supreme Court expressed concerns about the ambiguity in Section 69. The Supreme Court instructed the Centre to refrain from employing "threat and coercion" tactics during search and seizure operations to recover GST from traders. It emphasised its commitment to interpreting the law in a manner that upholds individual liberties and prevents undue harassment of citizens. Thus, once implemented, these changes will address the concerns raised by the Hon'ble Supreme Court regarding the potential misuse of Section 69.

70. Offences should be mentioned explicitly

Section 132 of the CGST Act prescribes punishments for specified offences. However, certain clauses in this section raise concerns due to their broad, generic nature, which could lead to misuse and harassment.

Relevant text of the provision:

(h)

acquires possession of, or in any way concerns himself in transporting, removing, depositing, keeping, concealing, supplying, or purchasing or in any other manner deals with, any goods which he knows or has reasons to believe are liable to confiscation under this Act or the rules made thereunder;

These clauses are overly broad and generic. They do not require evidence of intentional tax evasion by the defaulter.

It is therefore recommended that the GST provisions be amended by removing them entirely from Section 132(1) to prevent their misuse. The GST provisions should be suitably amended so as to replace criminal liability for non-compliance with a token penalty, ensuring fairness in enforcement.

71. Malicious intent should be the basis for a penalty

The relevant text of Clause (c) of Section 132(1) of the CGST Act:

(c)

Avails input tax credit using the invoice or bill referred to in clause (b) or….

This provision penalises individuals availing input tax credit under the circumstances outlined in clause (b) of Section 132(1). It does not consider whether the individual acted with malicious intent (mens rea).

It is recommended that this clause be modified to adhere to the legal maxim "actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea," which means that an act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

Either the first part of clause (c) should be deleted entirely, or the term 'fraudulently' should be inserted at the beginning of clause (c) to limit its scope to deliberate offences. For unintentional non-compliance, the Government may consider imposing a token penalty rather than criminal liability.

72. No criminal proceedings for self-rectified defaults

Criminal proceedings under Section 132(1) of the CGST Act can be initiated even when the defaulter has voluntarily identified the default and corrected it before the proceedings are initiated.

It is therefore recommended that criminal action be restricted to cases where defaults persist when proceedings are initiated. In cases of self-rectification of defaults, the law may prescribe levying a token penalty for non-compliance instead of initiating criminal proceedings. This approach encourages proactive adherence to tax laws.

Extension of Inverted Duty Structure (IDS) refund to 'input services' and 'capital goods'

Section 54(3) of the CGST Act, read with Rule 89(5) of the CGST Rules, prescribes the mechanism for granting refunds of unutilised input tax credit (ITC) arising from an inverted duty structure. However, the statutory formula restricts the scope of 'Net ITC' exclusively to input tax credit availed on input goods, explicitly excluding input services and capital goods from the refund computation.

As a result, taxpayers operating under an inverted tax structure accumulate substantial unutilised ITC on account of input services (such as job work, freight, utilities, professional services, etc.) and capital goods, which remain permanently blocked. While large enterprises are generally able to absorb such accumulation due to diversified product portfolios and higher-rated outward supplies, MSMEs and smaller manufacturers, particularly those engaged in single-product or low-margin businesses, face severe working capital constraints due to the non-refundability of such credits.

The adverse impact of this restriction has been further exacerbated by recent GST rate rationalisation measures, which have reduced output tax rates without a corresponding alignment of input tax rates, intensifying inverted duty structures across several sectors.

In this context, it is recommended that the refund mechanism under Rule 89(5) be suitably amended to include input services and capital goods within the scope of 'Net ITC' for the purpose of inverted duty structure refunds. Such a measure would align the refund framework with the fundamental GST principle of tax neutrality, prevent tax cascading, and significantly improve liquidity, thereby promoting ease of doing business and enhancing manufacturing competitiveness.

67. IDS refunds should be allowed for inputs and outputs at the same GST rate

Under Section 54 of the CGST Act, taxpayers are entitled to claim refunds for accumulated input tax credit on account of an inverted duty structure (IDS), i.e., where the rate of tax on inputs exceeds the rate of tax on outward supplies. However, tax authorities have often denied refunds under Section 54(3) read with Rule 89 of the CGST Rules, where the input tax rate on certain goods exceeds the output tax rate, even when the principal input and output attract the same GST rate. This has created uncertainty and impacted cash flow for businesses.

Recent judicial developments indicate a more purposive interpretation of the IDS provisions. In Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. vs. Assistant Commissioner of Central Tax [2025] 174.taxmann.com 1 (Karnataka), the Karnataka High Court observed that an IDS refund cannot be denied merely because some inputs are taxed at a higher rate than the output, so long as the principal input and the outward supply attract the same GST rate and the accumulation of ITC is otherwise attributable to the rate structure.

Further, during the 56th GST Council meeting, the government indicated its intent to simplify IDS refund processes, hinting at regulatory changes in the near future. Taxpayers can anticipate a more streamlined and predictable mechanism for claiming IDS refunds, potentially reducing litigation and enhancing liquidity management.

68. Blocking of the electronic credit ledger with zero or negative ITC may be reviewed

Rule 86A of the CGST Rules was inserted videNotification No. 75/2019- Central Tax, dated 26-12-2019, empowering the GST authorities to restrict the utilisation of ITC in the ECL under exceptional circumstances.

In practice, instances have been observed where tax authorities have blocked the ECL on a negative basis, i.e., restricted utilisation of ITC in excess of the balance actually available in the ECL at the time of passing the order. Such negative blocking effectively prevents utilisation of future credits, leading to severe cash-flow constraints for taxpayers, particularly during audits or verification proceedings.

Recently, the Supreme Court dismissed the Revenue's Special Leave Petition in Kings Security Guard Services (P.) Ltd. 174 taxmann.com 982, thereby affirming the decision of the Delhi High Court. The High Court, relying on its earlier ruling in Best Crop Science (P.) Ltd. [2024] 166 taxmann.com 654, held that Rule 86A of CGST Rules is not a machinery provision for recovery of tax or dues under CGST Act but an emergent measure for protection of revenue by temporarily not allowing debit of available ITC in ECL order disallowing debit from ECL, in excess of ITC available in ECL at the time of passing the order.

In view of the above judicial pronouncements, it is recommended that the scope and application of Rule 86A of the CGST Rules be reviewed and clarified to prevent its use as a recovery mechanism. However, appropriate safeguards may continue to be retained to allow restriction of ITC utilisation in genuine cases involving fraud or wilful misuse of input tax credit, subject to due process and statutory limitations.

92. Malicious intent should be the basis for levying penalty

The relevant text of Clause (c) of Section 132(1):

(c) Avails input tax credit using the invoice or bill referred to in clause (b) or….

This provision penalises individuals availing input tax credit under circumstances outlined in clause (b) of Section 132(1). It does not consider whether the individual acted with malicious intent (mens rea).

It is recommended that this clause be modified to adhere to the legal maxim "actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea," which means that an act is not guilty unless the mind is guilty. Either the first part of clause (c) should be deleted entirely or the term 'fraudulently' should be inserted at the beginning of clause (c) to limit its scope to deliberate offences. For unintentional non-compliance, impose a token penalty instead of criminal liability.

93. Criminal proceedings for self-rectified defaults

Criminal proceedings under Section 132(1) can be initiated even when the defaulter has voluntarily identified the default and corrected it before the proceedings are initiated.

It is recommended that criminal action be restricted to cases where defaults persist when proceedings are initiated. In cases of self-rectification of defaults, the law can prescribe to levy a token penalty for non-compliance instead of initiating criminal proceedings. This approach encourages proactive adherence to tax laws.

Sometimes, in Indirect tax cases, the tax authorities exercise the rights over the taxpayer's goods and properties in their possession and try to recover the dues based on such property. In this regard, it is important to refer to a recent judgment in the case of Sundaresh Bhatt, Liquidator, ABG Shipyard.17

The facts before the Hon'ble Supreme Court were that ABG Shipyard ("ABG") had imported certain goods which were stored in the Customs Bonded Warehouse and Container Freight Station. ABG had also availed the benefit of the Export Promotion Capital Goods Scheme ("EPCG Scheme"). An insolvency resolution process was initiated against ABG, and the liquidator sought to dispose of the goods lying at the customs warehouse. The Customs Department issued notices to ABG seeking demand of customs duty for non-fulfilment of the obligation under the EPCG Scheme. ABG approached the NCLT seeking directions to dispose of the goods. The application was allowed stating that Customs Department would allow ABG to remove the goods from the warehouse, and the Customs was free to lodge a claim before the liquidator. In the meantime, Customs Department also issued notice to ABG under Section 72(1) of the Customs Act seeking to demand customs dues in respect of goods warehoused.

At this juncture, it would be pertinent to discuss Sections 71 and 72 of the Customs Act. Section 71 of the Customs Act states that goods warehoused shall only be taken out of a warehouse on (i) clearance for home consumption or (ii) export, or (iii) removal to another warehouse or (iv) as provided under the Customs Act. Thus, Section 71 of the Customs Act allows the removal of goods from a warehouse only under four specific situations. Section 72 of the Customs Act is a recovery provision in relation to warehoused goods. It allows an officer of customs to demand duty along with interest and penalties on goods (i) which have been improperly removed from the warehouse, (ii) where goods which have been kept in the warehouse beyond the period allowed and (iii) where goods have been kept under a bond but have not been cleared for home consumption or export.
